prs.title: fix(ios): keep embedded Control UI device identity across page loads
prs.body:
Closes #161800

## What Problem This Solves

The embedded Control UI pages inside the iOS app mint a brand-new browser device identity — and therefore a new pairing request — every time the page loads. Owners must re-approve pairing on each tab open, the gateway device list fills with dead one-shot identities, and the embedded tabs become effectively unusable after an app update.

## Root Cause

`AuthenticatedControlUIWebView.makeUIView` backed the WKWebView with `.nonPersistent()`:

```swift
configuration.websiteDataStore = .nonPersistent()
```

The Control UI persists its browser device identity and device auth token in web storage (`peekStoredDeviceIdentityId` / `loadDeviceAuthToken`). A non-persistent data store is discarded together with the WebView on every recreation, so each page load starts from empty storage, mints a fresh identity, and triggers a new pairing request. This matches the reported traces (distinct browser IDs per load) and the Safari control experiment in #161800 (persistent Safari storage → identity sticks, no loop).

## The Fix

Replace the non-persistent store with a persistent, app-scoped **named** `WKWebsiteDataStore` (fixed UUID identifier):

- Approved device identity + token now survive WebView recreation, page loads, and app restarts → pairing happens once.
- A named (non-default) store keeps this state isolated from any other web content and can be independently cleared via `removePersistentDataStore(forIdentifier:)` if a reset is ever needed.
- No protocol changes: the web-side identity flow is exactly the one already used by desktop browsers; only its storage lifetime changes.

Complements the native-key work in #166479: when the native operator identity handoff succeeds it remains the primary path; the persistent web-side identity is now a durable fallback instead of a dead end.

## Evidence

**Source-level evidence**
- Diff is confined to `apps/ios/Sources/Web/AuthenticatedControlUIWebView.swift` (+16/-2): the only behavior change is `configuration.websiteDataStore` now resolving to a persistent named store instead of `.nonPersistent()`.
- The web-side identity that this store must retain is persisted by the Control UI itself via `peekStoredDeviceIdentityId()` / `loadDeviceAuthToken()` (browser storage), which is exactly what a non-persistent WKWebView data store discards.

**Live gateway evidence (from the reporter's production deployment, #161800)**
- Gateway device list shows repeated distinct `openclaw-control-ui` identities approved within minutes of each other from the same client (one-shot identities, `last_seen` never advancing) — the signature of per-load identity minting.
- Independent reproduction in #161800 (2026-10-26): 7 fresh `openclaw-control-ui` identities from one client within ~15 minutes, each triggered by opening the Automations tab; opening the same URL in Safari (persistent storage) keeps a single identity — a clean storage-lifetime control experiment.

**Validation status**
- Cannot run Xcode/iOS simulator from this environment; requesting the iOS CI lane.
- Manual test plan (iPad): open Automations tab → approve pairing once → close/reopen tab and cold-restart app → no new pairing request; device list shows a single stable identity; `removePersistentDataStore(forIdentifier:)` reset path clears it.

## Security Considerations

The stored material is the same device signing key + auth token that Safari already persists for Control UI usage on iOS; confining it to a named app-scoped store (rather than the default store) preserves isolation. No change to token verification, scopes, or server-side pairing policy.

prs.title: docs(ui): design a bounded held window for deep chat history
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Loading earlier messages in the Control UI gets slower with every page, and memory keeps growing, because the chat pane holds every row the reader has loaded and re-walks all of them on each older page. The 12 MiB cap applies only to the cached snapshot, not to the live pane.

## User Impact

No user-visible change yet. This draft proposes how to keep per-page cost and memory flat at any depth. It needs the product decisions listed below before any code ships.

## Why This Change Was Made

The task asked for the smallest safe first stage. I didn't find one that avoids product decisions, so this draft has only the design (`docs/reference/control-ui-held-history-window-design.md`). The design covers:

- **Ownership:** `state.chatMessages` stays the only held array and is still published only through `history-merge.ts`. `ChatHistoryPagination`, which already owns the older edge, gains one optional fact: `gap: { afterSource, beforeSource, newerCursor? }`. `ChatPaneHistory` makes the eviction decision through one pure function. `buildChatItems` emits a single `history-gap` boundary item.
- **Window shape:** a deep block, at most one gap, and the live tail block. The alternative was a detached tail (evict the newest rows). I rejected it because `insertSessionProjectionEntry` places a live persisted row after the newest held row, so with the tail evicted, live rows would land straight after the deep rows. Delta reads, send/steer pending rows, input placement, stream rows, end-follow, **Scroll to latest**, `reconcileHistoryTail`, the snapshot cache and the `chat-history-state` read model all assume the held rows reach the live tail. Keeping the tail block preserves that assumption, so none of those writers change.
- **Eviction policy:** runs only after an older-page prepend, once held rows exceed `K_max` (proposed 5,000 rows or 12 MiB weight); it trims to `K_target` (proposed 4,000). It removes only rows between the deep block (prepended page through viewport plus a two-page margin) and the tail block (latest page plus pending, queued or live-run rows). Cuts fall only where a sequence group ends and a user row starts the next turn, so tool calls/results, reasoning and handoffs are never split. Evicted rows are below the viewport, so the anchor doesn't move. Eviction is paused while search is open, during reply navigation and in catalog sessions.
- **Reloading newer rows:** a gap sentinel mirrors the older one, with the same intent, settle and failure gates, plus an explicit **Load newer messages** action. Requests use `chat.history { cursor: newerCursor }`, or a `messageId` probe when no cursor is held, like today's `needsBoundary`. The gap closes when a page reaches `beforeSource` or returns no `newerCursor`. `windowReset` falls back to `reloadChatHistoryWindow`.
- **Live events and Scroll to latest:** both keep working as they do now. Reaching the tail may drop the deep block and the gap.
- **Cache:** with a gap present, only the tail block is cached (with `needsBoundary`), so the persisted schema doesn't change.
- **Reply navigation:** a target inside the gap fills the gap instead of paging older.
- **Stages:** (1) the gap fact, eviction, the gap row, downward fill without top trimming, and tail-only cache commits; (2) sentinel-driven fill plus top trimming, with `TranscriptPrependAnchor` handling leading removals; (3) reply navigation into the gap and shrinking on **Scroll to latest**.

### Decisions needed

1. **Loaded rows can leave the client.** In-app search filters held rows only, and so do browser find and reply previews. Options: pause eviction while search is open (proposed for stage 1), show a "matches in unloaded history are hidden" hint, or add server-side transcript search.
2. **Gap affordance:** a visible **Load newer messages** divider in the middle of the transcript (a visual change), or invisible auto-fill only.
3. **Bound:** `K_max`/`K_target` (proposed 5,000/4,000 rows, capped by the existing 12 MiB weight).
4. **Sequencing with the incremental-render lanes:** ship the bound after that work or alongside it.

## Evidence

- **Work count per older page (code reading):** at least six full passes over held rows: prepend identity, session projection publish (including `createSessionProjection` / `readSessionMessageIdentity` per row), projection compare/copy, snapshot commit, `buildChatItems` (about nine internal passes) and the transcript chain/index/rows projection.
- **Isolated stage timings:** medians of 3 runs, one 1,000-row older page prepended onto `held` rows, measured with a scratch vitest that was not committed. Host load average was about 17, so treat these as relative.

  | held | prepend | projection | buildChatItems | chain+index |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 1,000 | 0.3 ms | 0.3 ms | 8.7 ms | 9.5 ms |
  | 4,000 | 0.8 ms | 0.6 ms | 21.1 ms | 28.6 ms |
  | 8,000 | 1.2 ms | 0.9 ms | 37.9 ms | 49.5 ms |
  | 12,000 | 1.8 ms | 1.3 ms | 59.1 ms | 52.8 ms |
  | 16,000 | 2.7 ms | 1.5 ms | 81.5 ms | 75.6 ms |

  That is linear growth at about 10 µs per held row for these two stages. A 4,000-row bound would hold them at about 50 ms per page instead of 157 ms at 16,000 rows.
- **Lead's end-to-end measurement** (isolated Gateway, production bundle, 30,000 messages): Gateway `chat.history` is flat at 35–75 ms per page. Browser script time per page is about 150 ms at pages 1–5 and about 305 ms at pages 21–25 (4x CPU throttle: about 650 ms vs about 1,350 ms).
- **Gateway prerequisite exists:** both-direction anchored paging is already supported and tested. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --maxWorkers=1 src/gateway/server-methods/chat-history-page-cursor.test.ts` passed 21/21, including reversing an older page with its `newerCursor`.
- **Checks:** oxfmt check on the doc passed, `git diff --check` is clean, and local autoreview (`--mode branch --base origin/main --max-priority P2`) found nothing actionable.
- **Gaps:** no implementation and no RED/GREEN tests yet, by design. Total memory at 30,000 held messages wasn't measured. The timings above come from a loaded shared host.

## Worked on by

- @vyctorbrzezowski

prs.title: feat(plugins): add skill usage runtime for plugins
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Skill Workshop is moving into its bundled plugin. It reads per-skill usage (`skill_usage`, keyed by canonical `SKILL.md` path) to decide when a learned skill went unused for 30 days, and its tool's foreground `view` records a skill use. Both go through core internals (`src/skills/workshop/skill-usage.ts`, `recordSkillUsed`), and the generic usage owner lives inside the Workshop folder. A plugin has no supported way to read usage or report a skill read.

## User Impact

No user-visible change: skill usage recording, the unused-skill archive, and `skills.workshop.list` counters behave as before. Plugins gain `api.runtime.skills.readUsage` and `api.runtime.skills.recordUsed`.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The generic usage owner moves out of Workshop to `src/skills/runtime/` (`skill-usage.ts`, `skill-usage.kernel.ts`, and a new `skill-usage.worker.ts` that owns the `skills.usage.*` worker ops). Workshop's `changes.worker.ts` keeps only its change-feed ops; the state worker registry merges both under the existing `skills.` domain. Operation names, SQL and table are unchanged.
- `api.runtime.skills.readUsage({ skillFiles })` returns `{ tracked, usage }`. `usage` is keyed by the paths the caller passed; core canonicalizes for the lookup. `tracked` replaces Workshop's `isSkillUsageTracked()`, so a plugin can tell "unused" from "not tracked in this process".
- `api.runtime.skills.recordUsed({ skillFile, skillName, skillSource? })` takes no run facts. The before-tool-call wrapper binds a recorder to each tool execution (AsyncLocalStorage); run, session, agent, trace and tool-call attribution come from that execution, exactly as `recordSkillUsed` does today. Outside a live tool execution, or after the call settles, it returns `false`. A relative or non-`SKILL.md` path throws. A plugin cannot attribute a use to another run.
- Generic: any skill-library or ClawHub surface that shows usage can use the same calls. No schema or protocol change.

## Evidence

- New `src/plugins/registry-runtime.skill-usage.test.ts` (fails with the post-settle close removed) drives the real plugin runtime through `createApi(...).runtime.skills` and the real tool wrapper with the real state worker: `tracked` false before tracking, `recordUsed` false outside a tool, true inside, false from a continuation after the call settled, run receipt attributed to the tool's run, and the persisted count read back by both the given and canonical path.
- Workshop behavior pins, assertions unchanged, plus sibling tests (state worker registry, server maintenance, before-tool-call wrapper, skill usage, plugin runtime): 27 files, 326 passed. Gateway e2e workshop learning, review and notice history: 3 files, 17 passed.
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`, `tsgo:extensions`, `plugin-sdk:check-exports`, `plugin-sdk:surface:check`, `check:import-cycles`, `check:baseline-ratchets`, oxfmt and type-aware oxlint pass.

prs.title: fix(macos): Mac tab shows a blank or stale page when a load fails
prs.body:
Related: #183927

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Mac tab shows a blank white page (new tab) or silently keeps the previous page (loaded tab) when a page fails to load, and Reload does nothing for a failed first load.

## User Impact

User impact: when a link is broken or the Mac is offline, the tab now keeps the address that was tried, says why it could not be opened, and offers Reload, which retries that address. Stopping a load, navigating somewhere else, and download or default-browser handoffs still keep the current page without an error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Main-frame failures reached `DashboardNativeBrowserHost.navigationDidFail(for:)` without the error, so the tab only retired its link alias and published unchanged state (`apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/DashboardWindowController.swift:1467-1470`, `apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/DashboardNativeBrowserHost.swift:269-272` on `70c70646d86`). Reload called `webView.reload()` (`DashboardNativeBrowserHost.swift:174`), which replays the last committed item; a failed first load never commits one, so nothing happens.

The tab owner now receives the error. Deliberate interruptions (`NSURLErrorCancelled`, and WebKit's policy interruption 102 used for response-policy cancels such as downloads and default-browser handoff) are ignored as before. Any other failure shows a native failure view over the tab's web view: a title, the system error description (no page content and no URL), and a Reload button. The tab keeps the failing URL; the published tab URL prefers it, and Reload (the button or the toolbar) loads it again. The next navigation that starts clears the failure.

The failure view is AppKit, added as a subview of the reading tab's `WKWebView`, so it follows the existing presentation frames and hiding and the untrusted page cannot script or restyle it. It is layer-backed and sets its background in `updateLayer()`: the first revision was a plain opaque view filled in `draw(_:)`, and in the running app it painted over the whole dashboard window (see the running-app proof below). No bridge, Control UI, or privileged dashboard failure-page code is involved. Favicon and alias handling from #184839 is unchanged: a failed navigation never commits, so the shown page keeps its icon.

## Evidence

### Running-app proof

The packaged app built from this branch (debug, ad hoc signed, `ai.openclaw.mac.debug` 2026.10.7) ran on macOS 27.2 arm64 with Xcode 27.1, launched with `--dashboard` against a task-owned loopback Gateway and HTTP fixture. Accessibility drove it by process id, and the native failure view, which WebKit keeps out of the accessibility tree, was read and clicked from the window via Vision text recognition. Window screenshots and a recording of only the app's windows.

1. A new tab opens an address nothing listens on. The failure view shows "This page couldn't be opened / Could not connect to the server.", the address bar keeps `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/first-load`, the fixture starts, and the failure view's Reload loads the page (fixture: one request for `/first-load`).
2. The loaded page follows a link to another unserved address. The failure view shows, the address bar keeps `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/broken`, the fixture starts, and the toolbar Reload loads it (one request for `/broken`). The failure view is gone after each recovery.

The first revision (`9ad45a61910`) passed the same flow, but while the failure view showed, its background covered the whole dashboard window: chat, tab strip, address bar and toolbar. `e164e6e589e` makes the view layer-backed, and it now stays inside the tab.

The Browser panel of `e164e6e589e` at full resolution, cropped from the window screenshots (the failure view's text is small grey on dark in the full-window shots below):

Failed first load, then after the failure view's Reload:

![panel-failed-first-load](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/panel-fixed-10-new-tab-failed.png) ![panel-recovered-native-reload](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/panel-fixed-11-new-tab-recovered-native-reload.png)

Failed navigation from the loaded page, then after the toolbar Reload:

![panel-failed-navigation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/panel-fixed-21-loaded-tab-failed.png) ![panel-recovered-toolbar-reload](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/panel-fixed-22-loaded-tab-recovered-toolbar-reload.png)

The same crop from frames of the `e164e6e589e` recording at 9 s (first load failed), 21 s (recovered), 25 s (navigation failed) and the last frame (recovered), so the sequence can be checked without playing the video:

![frame-09s](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/frame-fixed-t09s.png) ![frame-21s](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/frame-fixed-t21s.png) ![frame-25s](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/frame-fixed-t25s.png) ![frame-end](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/9532ed1427030c5d12a40b79885af6a70b2ce82a/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/panel/frame-fixed-end.png)

![after-toolbar-reload](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/87eb46377ce58ce1c3ab101f1be1102037d04546/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/fixed-22-loaded-tab-recovered-toolbar-reload.png)

Recordings: [`9ad45a61910`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/87eb46377ce58ce1c3ab101f1be1102037d04546/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/before-recording.mp4), [`e164e6e589e`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/87eb46377ce58ce1c3ab101f1be1102037d04546/mac-item-5-tab-failures/running-app/fixed-recording.mp4). The bottom-left avatar is masked.

With `e164e6e589e`, on the same Mac: `swift test --filter DashboardNativeBrowserTests` (Xcode 27.1): 27 tests in 4 suites passed. SwiftFormat and SwiftLint `--strict` on the changed file: clean. `scripts/lint-swift.sh macos`: only the existing `DashboardManager.swift` file_length violation.

### Offscreen renders and regressions

Each image is an offscreen render of the reading tab's web view from the real `DashboardWindowController` in the regression harness. The grey band at the bottom is a test harness readout, not app UI: it prints the tab state `DashboardNativeBrowserHost` publishes to the dashboard (loopback port masked). The tab strip and address bar are Control UI web chrome and are not part of these renders.

New tab whose first load fails, before (blank white page) and after (native failure view with Reload; the tab state already reported the attempted URL on base):

![a-before-new-tab](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/8741e3612b3ea2b8c0cfb96990e57865054ebdae/mac-item-5-tab-failures/a-before-new-tab.png)
![a-after-new-tab](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/8741e3612b3ea2b8c0cfb96990e57865054ebdae/mac-item-5-tab-failures/a-after-new-tab.png)

Loaded tab whose navigation to `/next` fails, before (old page stays and tab state still reports `/article`) and after (failure view; tab state reports the attempted `/next`):

![a-before-loaded-tab](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/8741e3612b3ea2b8c0cfb96990e57865054ebdae/mac-item-5-tab-failures/a-before-loaded-tab.png)
![a-after-loaded-tab](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/etzelm/openclaw/8741e3612b3ea2b8c0cfb96990e57865054ebdae/mac-item-5-tab-failures/a-after-loaded-tab.png)

Focused real-WKWebView regressions in `apps/macos/Tests/OpenClawIPCTests/DashboardNativeBrowserTests.swift` (`DashboardNativeBrowserFailureTests`), driving `DashboardWindowController` and its navigation delegate against task-owned loopback `DashboardHTTPFixture` endpoints:

- a new tab opened on a released loopback port shows the failure, keeps the attempted URL in tab state, and after the endpoint comes back the failure view's Reload button loads it;
- the same from an already loaded page: the page and its favicon stay, tab state shows the attempted URL, toolbar Reload loads it, and Back stays available after the retry;
- stop, replacement navigation, and a non-displayable response (download policy cancel) show no failure.

Results on macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Swift 6.4 (Command Line Tools), base `70c70646d86`:

- `swift test --filter DashboardNativeBrowserFailureTests` on this branch: 3 tests (5 cases) passed.
- The same flows on base (tests rewritten to base APIs, failure-view assertions dropped): the failed first load never retries (`Time limit was exceeded`, still waiting for the retried load), and after a failed navigation from a loaded page the tab state still shows the old page's URL (`failed.url == attempted.absoluteString` is false).
- Siblings `DashboardNativeBrowser|DashboardHTTPFixtureTests|DashboardBrowserDownloadTests|DashboardBrowserCookieBoundaryTests`: 34 tests in 7 suites passed.
- `swift build --build-tests`, `scripts/format-swift.sh macos` (0 files need formatting), `scripts/lint-swift.sh macos` (only the existing `DashboardManager.swift` file_length violation, also on base), `pnpm native:i18n:verify`, `git diff --check`: clean.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base <current main>` on the stacked follow-up for #183928, whose diff against main includes every file of this branch (not run separately on this branch): every guard passed except `lint apps` (the existing `DashboardManager.swift` file_length violation) and `macOS app CI tests` (1 failed, 607 passed), whose one failure is the tooling test `test/scripts/generate-gateway-protocol-plugin.test.ts`, which builds the Swift package itself and fails on this machine with the Command Line Tools manifest link error (`Package.__allocating_init` undefined); it does not touch the files in this change.

## Related work

- #152668 (open, prepare integrated tab logins before opening links) touches `DashboardNativeBrowserHost.swift`, `DashboardWindowController.swift` and `apps/.i18n/native-source.json`. No shared lines: its host change removes `self.onOpen?()` in `open` (line 160 on `70c70646d86`), a few lines above this stack's `navigate`/`perform` changes; its controller hunks are in lines 99-559, ours at 1331-1496. It already conflicts with current main on its own. Whichever lands second regenerates the i18n inventory with `pnpm native:i18n:baseline` (the inventory records source line sites).
- No open PR covers #183927 or #183928 (searched by symptom and by the owner file names).

## Gaps

- The offscreen renders under "Offscreen renders and regressions" come from the real `DashboardWindowController` on a host without a logged-in GUI session; the running-app proof above is the window evidence.
- The offscreen renders and the test results under them were built with the Command Line Tools (Swift 6.4) only, no Xcode; the running-app proof and its test run used Xcode 27.1. Xcode-only SwiftUI macro plugins (`@State`, `@Entry`, `#Preview`) were replaced locally by equivalent desugaring plugins, and two unrelated XCTest-based test files were left out locally because the CLT ships no XCTest. Nothing in this change uses SwiftUI. The `macos-swift` CI job is the authoritative native run.
- A failure after a document committed (`didFail` mid-load) takes the same path but has no dedicated test.
- Known edges, unchanged in scope: the failure view sits over the tab's web view, so a snapshot of a failed loaded tab (for example Annotate) still captures the previous page underneath; a same-document navigation by that previous page (`pushState`, hash change) does not start a provisional load and so leaves the failure shown; Reload retries a failed POST as a plain GET of the same URL.

## What Problem This Solves

**Landing blocked:** required CI fails the canonical test-line budget. The corrected source and focused proof are accepted; no failed-CI exception is requested.

Fixes transcript test cleanup that can strand a held writer when its updater never starts or the test scenario fails or is cancelled.

## User Impact

## Why This Change Was Made

The test acquires retirement ownership before its first wait, detects early operation settlement, and releases and joins scenario/update/append work before the parent fixture drains. Original failure and abort objects are preserved.

The old cleanup is reconciled with current main: the retired helper remains absent and the redaction file is unchanged. Final scope: one test file (+117/-51, net +66 test lines) and its exact 66-line allocation; production delta is zero.

- Saved baseline `b3035bf3` and fresh signed candidate `8950b5a2bf196aac6cd8518f9616d7de6e4a27a1`: **50/50 passed each**, zero skipped or unhandled errors. Exact-byte staging and signed commit verification resolved it; the original findings/exit1 report is preserved. The owner's review-method approval covers guarded local plus independent review, with the 38 body exclusions; no hosted review success is claimed.

Targeted local lint still exits1 for `max-lines` (1029 >1000), which CI treats as advisory. No rule suppression or Actions-environment impersonation was used. **Current exact-head CI completed with failure in the test-line ratchet and aggregate gate. All three PostgreSQL jobs passed. Two-file invocations: saved baseline 19.106 s; fresh candidate 19.747 s. Reporter file intervals (baseline/candidate): transcript46 cases 7.124/7.324 s; redaction4 cases 1.720/1.829 s. Fresh candidate controls: 10.954 s. These are observations, not a speedup or benchmark claim.

prs.title: fix(voice-call): responseModel ignores configured model aliases
prs.body:
Closes #191631

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a voice-call `responseModel` set to a model alias (for example `medium`) is sent to the runtime default provider as a literal model id `medium` instead of the model the alias points to.

## User Impact

User impact: `plugins.entries.voice-call.config.responseModel` now accepts the same model aliases as the rest of OpenClaw. With aliases, a provider switch can be a few `openclaw models aliases add …` edits; `responseModel` was the one field that ignored them, so voice calls broke (or silently used the wrong provider) after such a switch. Explicit `provider/model` values and legacy single-segment values that aren't aliases behave exactly as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveVoiceResponseModel` only split the value on `/`. It now first looks the value up in the configured alias index (`buildModelAliasIndex` + `resolveModelRefFromString` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-runtime`, the same pattern `llm-task` uses) and uses the alias target only when an alias matched. Otherwise it falls through to the unchanged legacy split, so non-alias values aren't normalized or re-routed. The lookup lives in that shared resolver, so it applies to both classic responses (`response-generator.ts`) and realtime consults (`runtime.ts`), which both call `resolveVoiceResponseModel`.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (shipped entry points, isolated gateway)

Setup: a real `openclaw gateway run` with its own state dir, config and loopback ports. No phone call was made. The config has a real Anthropic API-key provider (`proofapi`) with alias `medium` → `proofapi/claude-haiku-5-5`, and the agent default set to `proofapi/claude-sonnet-5-5`, so a correct alias lookup is distinguishable from the default. The runtime default provider is the compiled-in `openai`, which has no credentials in this setup. I compared latest stable (`openclaw@2026.10.10` + `@openclaw/voice-call@2026.10.10`) with a source build of this PR head (22b33a9), using `responseModel: "medium"` each time.

- **Classic responses**: the `mock` telephony provider, driven over its webhook (inbound call → answered → final `call.speech` "What is two plus two?"), which runs the normal auto-response → `generateVoiceResponse`.
- **Realtime consult**: the `twilio` provider with fake credentials and `skipSignatureVerification`. A Twilio-shaped inbound webhook returns `<Connect><Stream>`, then a WebSocket `start` frame, then a stub realtime-voice provider plugin (local harness only) calls `openclaw_agent_consult` like a realtime model would. The consult handler in `runtime.ts` and the embedded agent run are the shipped code.

Stable 2026.10.10, both paths fail the same way:

```
[voice-call] Response generation failed: FailoverError: Unknown model: openai/medium. ...
[proofrt] tool result for tool-call-1 {"error":"Unknown model: openai/medium. ..."}
```

PR head, both paths reply from the alias target:

```
classic:  [voice-call] AI response queued <call> chars=21
          transcript: assistant provider=proofapi model=claude-haiku-5-5 text='{"spoken":"Two plus two is four."}'
realtime: embedded run ... from=proofapi/claude-haiku-5-5
          [proofrt] tool result for tool-call-1 {"text":"Two plus two is four."}
          transcript: assistant provider=proofapi model=claude-haiku-5-5 text='Two plus two is four.'
```

**Upgrade (latest stable → PR head)**: these steps all ran on one state dir and config:

1. With stable, set voice settings via `openclaw config set`: a literal `responseModel: "proofapi/claude-haiku-5-5"` (which is itself the target of the `medium` alias), plus `tts` (provider/voice/timeout), `maxDurationSeconds`, and `silenceTimeoutMs`.
2. Made a classic call on stable. It replied via `proofapi/claude-haiku-5-5`.
3. Ran PR head `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive`. This was needed for the agent DB schema upgrade v27 → v40 that is already on main. The source build is stamped 2026.10.9, older than the 2026.10.10 that last wrote the config, so `OPENCLAW_ALLOW_OLDER_BINARY_DESTRUCTIVE_ACTIONS=1` was set for this isolated state.
4. Started the PR head gateway on the same state and made another classic call.

Results: in the voice-call config, `responseModel` (still the literal `proofapi/claude-haiku-5-5`), `responseTimeoutMs`, `maxDurationSeconds`, `silenceTimeoutMs`, `tts.provider` and `tts.timeoutMs` were byte-identical after doctor. The only change was main's existing TTS key migration `tts.providers.openai.voice` → `speakerVoice`, with the value (`alloy`) kept. The post-upgrade call replied `"Two plus two is four."` via `provider=proofapi model=claude-haiku-5-5`, the same literal model as before the upgrade.

### Resolver regression tests

Regression check: I restored `main`'s `response-model.ts` (`git checkout HEAD~1 -- extensions/voice-call/src/response-model.ts`), left the new tests in place, and ran `pnpm test extensions/voice-call/src/response-model.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. Then I restored the fix and ran the same command again.

Without the fix: 1 failed, 7 passed. Only the alias test fails, because the alias is sent to the runtime default provider as a literal model id:

```
 FAIL  extensions/voice-call/src/response-model.test.ts > resolveVoiceResponseModel > resolves configured model aliases to their target
AssertionError: expected { provider: 'together', …(1) } to deeply equal { provider: 'anthropic', …(1) }
-   "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5",
-   "provider": "anthropic",
+   "model": "medium",
+   "provider": "together",
 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 7 passed (8)
```

With the fix: 8 of 8 passed.

```
✓ keeps legacy single-segment overrides on the runtime default provider
✓ keeps explicit provider/model overrides verbatim
✓ resolves configured model aliases to their target
✓ keeps non-alias overrides unchanged when aliases are configured
✓ keeps a literal provider/model verbatim when it is also an alias target
✓ inherits the call agent's configured model when responseModel is unset
✓ inherits the global configured default when the call agent sets no model
✓ falls back to the compiled-in runtime default when nothing is configured
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

The unchanged-behavior tests pass with and without the fix. With an alias configured, a bare non-alias model (`gpt-5.4-mini`) stays on the runtime default provider. Literal `provider/model` values stay verbatim, including `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`, which is itself the target of the `medium` alias.

Other checks:
- `pnpm test:extension voice-call`: 49 of 50 test files pass. All failures are in `extensions/voice-call/index.test.ts` (24 tests, covering runtime lifecycle and tool adapters), which this PR does not touch. The same 24 tests fail locally on unmodified `main` (f68e8321), so they look environmental or pre-existing rather than caused by this change.
- `pnpm format:check` and `oxlint` (extensions tsconfig) on both files, `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`: all clean.

(Implemented by my OpenClaw assistant, Claude Opus 5.5; I reviewed the scope.)

prs.title: fix(memory): match standing intents in unspaced CJK prompts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A standing intent armed with a Chinese trigger such as `会议` never fired for a normal sentence like `明天上午的会议改到下午三点`, although the docs promise a trigger fires once its terms appear in the turn. The failure was silent: no log line, the intent just stayed armed.

SQLite FTS5 `unicode61` folds an entire unspaced CJK run into a single token, so the prompt's tokens are the whole sentence while the stored trigger is `会议`. A match built on word equality can never connect them, and the full-text candidate query cannot address the substring either.

## Why This Change Was Made

The match boundary is the right place to fix this. Re-tokenizing would mean re-indexing every stored intent and shipping a tokenizer change for one script family, so the change follows the same tradeoff as the JSONL transcript search fix (#191466) rather than touching the index.

- **Term matching** (`standing-intents-model.ts`): a term containing Han, Hiragana, Katakana, or Hangul characters matches as a literal substring of the prompt; every other term keeps whole-token equality. With this split, `café` no longer fires on `caféine`, `release` no longer fires on `prerelease`, and Cyrillic or accent-bearing terms keep their word boundaries.
- **Candidate selection** (`standing-intents-kernel.ts`): prompts containing those scripts run the existing indexed lane first, so ordinary word matches and their ordering are untouched, then a literal lane over the same armed/scoped rows. Both lanes share the existing 256-candidate budget and the existing 3-intent injection cap, and every candidate still passes the per-term matcher before firing.
- **Nothing else moves**: schema, FTS index and tokenizer, fire budget, cooldown, scope rules, and the worker command shape stay as they are. Prompts without unspaced scripts keep pure index selection, so emoji, punctuation, or quote-heavy prompts behave exactly as before. The Postgres path stays join-free and reuses the same matcher.

Rejected alternative: running a second non-indexed pass unconditionally. It would drop index narrowing for every prompt and duplicate scope/cooldown accounting, where the current split only pays the extra scan for scripts the index genuinely cannot address.

Documented in `docs/concepts/standing-intents.md`, next to the matching contract.

## User Impact

Chinese, Japanese, and Korean trigger phrases now fire inside ordinary sentences, which is what the concept docs already promised. English and other spaced-script behavior is unchanged, including word-boundary behavior for look-alike words. Mixed entries match when the spaced terms appear as words and the CJK terms appear literally.

## Evidence

**Owner-created intent firing through a real Gateway.** A Gateway child process started from this branch, wired to the QA channel bus: the owner sender arms an intent with the `intent` tool, then sends an unspaced CJK turn. The prompt hook injected the intent into that turn's model request:

```console
turn1-reply: INTENT-CREATE-TURN-DONE          # owner called intent(create, triggerKeywords: ["会议"])
turn2-reply: INJECTED-CONTEXT-TURN
createTurns=1 armedResults=2 cjkTurns=1 injectedTurns=1
```

The second turn's user message as the provider received it:

```
{"sender":{"id":"owner-1","name":"Owner"}}

<standing_intents>
Standing intent (created 2026-11-03): Confirm the rollback owner for the meeting.
</standing_intents>

明天上午的会议改到下午三点
```

The provider is a scripted mock (no API keys in this environment); the Gateway, plugin loading, agent turn, tool call, prompt hook, and channel delivery are the real ones. Same run on the current branch: `verdict: PASS`.

**Regression coverage** in `extensions/memory-core/src/standing-intents.test.ts` on a real agent database:

```console
# term matching wide open again (every non-ASCII term matched literally)
AssertionError: expected [ Array(1) ] to strictly equal []   # café fired on "caféine booster"
# literal lane taken for prompts the index already handles
AssertionError: expected true to be false                    # "keeps index selection for prompts without unspaced scripts"
# with the change
Tests  2 passed | 13 skipped                                 # the two matching tests
```

Cases covered there: `会议` fires on `明天上午的会议改到下午三点`; a mixed `版本 release` entry fires exactly once on `新版本 release 已发布`; `release` does not fire on `prerelease notes`; `café` does not fire on `caféine booster` but does on `un café serré`; and a prompt without unspaced scripts keeps index selection.

**Gates**: `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint` (0 warnings), `tsc -p tsconfig.extensions.json` (no errors in the changed files; 18 pre-existing declaration-portability errors in unrelated extensions), the full `standing-intents.test.ts` file (15 passed), and the test-lines ratchet (slack 755).

Not covered locally: the Postgres backend, because this environment has no Postgres server; `standing-intents.postgres.test.ts` exercises it in CI, and the change keeps that query join-free.

prs.title: fix(codex): apply plugin input rewrites to native tools
prs.body:
Closes #189886

## What Problem This Solves

A plugin's `before_tool_call` rewrite denies a Codex-native tool call instead of applying the new input.

## User Impact

Plugins can rewrite Codex-native tool input. Bash and `apply_patch` rewrites can change `command`, and `mcp__*` rewrites can replace the JSON object arguments. Codex then applies its normal approval and sandbox policy to the replacement.

Other rewrites still deny the call, including other shell fields, other native tools, and rewrites during a report-mode approval.

Risks to review:

- MCP rewrites deny when the outgoing arguments contain a value that JavaScript parsing altered in the original tool arguments. This includes rounded integers, overflow to null, and forms such as `1.0`. It also includes an unrelated number with the same value. Whether to limit this to real numeric changes is the open question in #189886.
- A value a plugin derives from an altered number, such as a string copy, is not detected.
- Codex's native file approval prompt shows no patch content, so an operator cannot see a rewritten patch there. Shell and MCP prompts show the replacement. Plugin approvals show only the plugin's own text.
- Codex keeps the last completed `updatedInput`, so a separate Codex hook can replace an OpenClaw rewrite without OpenClaw policy seeing it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Codex already accepts replacement input through `updatedInput`, so the relay now returns validated rewrites instead of denying them. It passes only the fields Codex applies: `command` for Bash and `apply_patch`, and the full argument object for MCP.

An MCP rewrite resends every argument, and `JSON.parse` in the hook CLI can change numbers that Codex forwards verbatim. The CLI records which tool arguments parsing altered. The relay then serializes the plugin result once, and checks and sends that snapshot, so non-enumerable slots, getters and `toJSON` cannot make the sent value differ from the checked one. It matches altered values by value at every position, which also catches numbers moved by an array or object edit. A field replaced with a different value and numbers outside the tool arguments do not count.

## Evidence

**Live run on `1c49f29`:** a built Gateway started with `node openclaw.mjs gateway run` on isolated state and a loopback port, using Codex 0.164.0 and a real `gpt-5.6-luna` turn for each case. A connected operator client made the approval decisions, and revocation used `chat.abort`. Later commits change tests only.

| Authorization path | Shell | `apply_patch` | MCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| No approval needed | replacement only | replacement only | replacement only |
| Plugin approval, allowed | replacement only | replacement only | replacement only |
| Plugin approval, denied | no I/O | no I/O | no I/O |
| Run aborted while plugin approval pending, then late approve | no I/O | no I/O | no I/O |
| Run aborted while policy hook pending, hook returns rewrite late | no I/O | no I/O | no I/O |
| Codex approval, allowed | replacement only | replacement only | replacement only |
| Codex approval, denied | no I/O | no I/O | no I/O |
| Run aborted while Codex approval pending, then late approve | no I/O | no I/O | no I/O |

All 24 cases matched. Results were read from workspace files, a synthetic MCP recorder, the plugin's hook log and Codex's rollouts, not the model's summary. The hook fired in every case, and the original input took effect in none. Late approvals failed with `approval already resolved`.

**Tests:**

- `029a86b`: `native-hook-relay.test.ts` and `native-hook-relay.approval-wait.test.ts` passed (119 tests), including allow and deny decisions through the real `before_tool_call` policy. `oxlint`, the agents test typecheck and the assertion-safety ratchet passed.
- `1c49f29`: the targeted relay and CLI tests passed (170 tests), with `tsgo:core` clean.
- `approval-bridge.test.ts` has 4 failures on `ad073a8a175` and `7da9166e17f`, with identical test names and messages. This PR does not change that file or the bridge. That file was not rerun on later commits.

**Limits:**

- The live run used built repository output, not an installed npm package.
- It used `appServer.homeScope: "user"`, not the default per-agent home.
- Each case ran once. The model reached tools through Codex Code Mode, so direct tool calls were not exercised live.
- Revoked cases prove the final effect. They do not separate Codex's turn interrupt from the relay's own recheck.
- The MCP server was synthetic. Competing Codex hooks were not tested, and there was no live run on the base commit.
- One MCP approval case outside the 24 counted cases returned `user rejected MCP tool call` with no prompt and did no I/O. It did not recur on rerun, and the cause is unknown.
- The full test suite was not run.

prs.title: fix(codex): continue a settled thread after a remote executor upgrade
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After a remote Codex executor upgrades in place, a new user message can fail to continue in its existing conversation even when the last turn has settled.

## User Impact

A fresh user message can continue in the same Codex thread after a forward executor upgrade. The interrupted input and its tool calls are never automatically submitted again by this path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The host compares the authenticated endpoint and runtime identity across the version change, then checks the cold thread against its own binding and exact last-turn receipt. The exception is limited to explicit new input on a settled thread. An active turn, pending tool handoff, changed endpoint or credential, or executor downgrade keeps the existing refusal.

## Evidence

A local protocol test stopped Codex 0.153.4 and started 0.163.0 at the same authenticated endpoint. The original tool produced one effect. Two new inputs produced one effect each on the same thread. Separate Gateway lifecycle tests covered the ownership, settlement and refusal paths.

The local lifecycle and suspend run used one worker and completed in 38.82 seconds. The ingress and cron suites brought the local total to 244 checks. CI duration and end-to-end delivery through the original Slack thread are pending.

The extension CI lint found inconsistent returns in the fingerprint check. The latest commit makes five existing undefined returns explicit. Type-aware lint passed locally and all 192 thread lifecycle binding tests passed on this head (43.60 seconds with one worker). An isolated build of the Codex entry with the Docker bundler settings generated the same 5,154 JavaScript files, byte for byte, for the staging combination before and after this change. The original staging image still uses the earlier source SHA.


Follow-up in 240802f90fe: reproduced a further failure when a version-only executor upgrade coincides with newly admitted apps. The old lifecycle rejected it before checking the original native receipt. The fix projects away only newly admitted, explicitly enabled apps and compares the complete old policy fingerprint; it then uses the existing exact-terminal-receipt, current-owner, unload and scoped-config checks. Existing app removal, permissions, approvals, defaults and unknown policy fields remain protected. No persisted fields or old tool replay were added.

The new positive regression fails on d5df6efe and passes with this patch. The complete binding suite passes 204 tests (46.37 s local wall time); formatting, lint, production/test typechecks, Knip and structural guards pass. An independent autoreview found no P0/P1 issue. A pre-existing test table was extracted unchanged to satisfy the source-file size limit. This new additive-app combination has not yet completed real-native/staging acceptance, so the earlier end-to-end proof is not relabeled as proof for it. The six-PR release remains under verification.

prs.title: docs(gateway): clarify HTTP check gaps during lifecycle transitions
prs.body:
Related: #187171

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway supervisors can mistake expected HTTP-check gaps during startup, shutdown, or in-process restart for a wedged process.

## User Impact

Operators get an explicit contract for connection refusal before bind and after transport closure, including while the same PID remains alive. Combine HTTP checks with process/exit information, bounded startup/restart grace, and the process owner's shutdown budget; a living PID does not justify indefinite grace. No runtime or configuration changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

This implements the documentation alternative explicitly offered in #187171 and recommended by [its review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/187171#issuecomment-6485949796): define pre-bind/post-close refusal windows and bounded supervisor grace. The documentation change is complete for that scope. It does not promise continuous HTTP availability or change listener ownership; any such runtime contract remains a separate maintainer decision.

The checks share the Gateway HTTP transport. The later listening summary is not the bind timestamp. Existing projection-startup guidance and endpoint semantics are preserved: health 200 means HTTP liveness, startup remains 503 while starting or draining, and startup 200 is not readiness. Traffic still uses readiness and normal admission. No universal numeric timeout is prescribed.

## Evidence

Source inspection at candidate base `00bfbf1f7ca54b0da62a10cc0d33323f3559dc02` confirms transport ownership, bind/close order, same-process restart, endpoint semantics, and delayed startup logging.

Isolated Debian 12 Bookworm / Node 24.22.1 measurements compared actual npm **2026.10.5** (`1b58cb9a1b4f4353e1add63c8506db4d890962e8`) with source-built main **2026.10.9** (`d3c0ab1fc65a0dc0350a2f661835b05e2ea0c0f2`). Matched stop-run fixture launches on 2026-10-30 UTC were **21:52:18.732Z** (release) and **21:52:10.654Z** (main).

| Observation, seconds after fixture launch | Release | Main at d3c0ab1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Socket bind observation interval | 4.637–4.657 | 4.357–4.377 |
| First completed HTTP responses: health 200 / startup 503 / ready 503 | 5.072 / 5.075 / 5.074 | 4.418 / 4.419 / 4.418 |
| Later `http server listening` summary | 5.306 | 5.688 |
| First completed startup 200 / ready 200 | 5.836 / 5.836 | 6.376 / 6.417 |
| Transport close interval / process exit (code 0) | 7.545–7.565 / 8.124 | 7.505–7.526 / 7.710 |

Kernel socket sampling was 20 ms and HTTP probe sampling 50 ms; intervals are observations, not exact syscall timestamps, and completed HTTP responses are distinct from socket binding. Config-reload runs also retained the same PID across no-LISTEN gaps bounded at **3.031–3.070 s** (release) and **2.647–2.687 s** (main), then rebound with startup/readiness 503 before 200. These runs establish lifecycle gaps, not an entire-boot outage.

Limits: this was a Debian 12 sandbox, not an exact digest-pinned `node:24-bookworm` reproduction. Production 60-second startup durations, restart loops, and systemd active/running behavior were not reproduced. Main timings apply only to `d3c0ab1`, not newer main. No runtime proof was rerun for this prose-only change.

- Exact-byte oxfmt 0.74.0 and one-file MDX checks passed on Node 24.22.1. Structural/link sanity and `git diff --check` also passed. Document SHA-256: `826f9e56a77190372b9dfeb5ff727b23008c5ca6c388bb6134b9a4c520a11713`; relevant checker/configuration inputs matched the candidate base. Full Markdown lint/global docs checks were not run locally.
- Current-head [check-docs CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41141141644/job/124355685869). This is a specific docs-check result, not a claim that every CI lane ran or passed.
- Independent review approved the exact candidate. The full `pr-simplify` pass required no further edits: documentation **+15/-0**, production code **0**, tests **0**; no machinery was added or removed.

Thanks to Donnie Fi for the investigation and direction.

prs.title: fix(lmstudio): guard model discovery with the embedding SSRF policy
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

LM Studio model discovery fetched the configured base URL with platform `fetch` when no SSRF policy was passed. That path follows redirects and sends the provider API key. Embeddings in the same plugin already build a guarded policy from the provider base URL and `allowPrivateNetwork`. Discovery now uses that policy. The local default still allows a private LM Studio.

## Evidence

On commit `008522d58e56d9`, a local HTTP server on `127.0.0.1` receives one discovery request when private network access is allowed, and zero requests when it is denied. The rest of the LM Studio models file still passes.

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/lmstudio/src/models.discovery-transport.test.ts extensions/lmstudio/src/models.test.ts
 ✓ reaches a loopback server only when private network access is allowed 157ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  40 passed (40)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 32.39s
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** LM Studio discovery reaches a loopback server only when private network access is allowed, and an explicit denial sends no HTTP request.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS Darwin 27.0.0 arm64, Node v26.12.1, worktree `/tmp/oc-f080` at `008522d58e56d9` on `fix/lmstudio-discovery-ssrf`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/lmstudio/src/models.discovery-transport.test.ts extensions/lmstudio/src/models.test.ts`
- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output copied below.
```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/lmstudio/src/models.discovery-transport.test.ts
 ✓ reaches a loopback server only when private network access is allowed 157ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  40 passed (40)
   Start at  16:01:40
   Duration  29.60s
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 32.39s
```
- **Observed result after fix:** With `allowPrivateNetwork: false`, the loopback server saw 0 requests and discovery returned no models. With `allowPrivateNetwork: true`, the server saw 1 request. Dynamic model discovery forwards the configured setting.
- **What was not tested:** A live LM Studio server and a live metadata address. The guard is the same one embeddings already use.

## Summary

`discoverLmstudioModels` passes `resolveEmbeddingProviderSsrFPolicy` into `fetchLmstudioModels`. When that resolution is empty, discovery still uses a restrictive policy object instead of platform fetch. Catalog and dynamic model discovery forward the configured `allowPrivateNetwork` flag. When that flag is omitted, discovery keeps the local private-network default.

prs.title: fix(read): avoid long pauses on missing-file suggestions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes long Gateway pauses when a missing-file read searches a large directory for similar filenames.

## User Impact

Missing-file errors keep exactly the same top three suggestions, distance cutoff, and alphabetical tie ordering while using less main-thread CPU and allocation. No configuration or migration is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The read tool calculated unrestricted edit distances before applying a cutoff. It now passes that cutoff to the shared owner, computes the requested basename once, and allocates score records only for matches. The shared helper removes provably redundant per-cell guards, carries the current cell locally, and computes the early-exit row minimum during scoring instead of scanning each row again. Full-distance callers and the existing bounded empty-string contract are preserved.

Directories remain exhaustive: a cap or skip could hide the best match. Production code is three lines smaller. The 65 added test lines protect exact ranking, zero scoring for impossible lengths, and UTF-16/cutoff equivalence; a separate test-line allocation records that cost.

## Evidence

Acceptance: identical errors/results; at least five counterbalanced A/A and A/B pairs per workload, with CPU/wall timing separated from sampled allocations; remove the observed 300–600 ms class of main-thread work without a material regression in other callers. Real `createReadTool.execute` calls use synthetic directories containing 1k, 10k and 50k filenames, with short document and long session-like typos. Baseline is `7f2aaee19ffcfbf069d4ae1135a9482287020e41`.

| Directory / typo | Main-thread CPU median ms before → after | CPU p95 ms before → after | Wall median ms before → after | Sampled heap MB before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 / short | 2.000 → 0.532 | 2.135 → 0.591 | 2.665 → 1.159 | 0.488 → 0.260 |
| 1,000 / long | 7.663 → 4.555 | 7.737 → 4.651 | 8.283 → 5.218 | 0.500 → 0.434 |
| 10,000 / short | 16.406 → 1.201 | 16.799 → 1.391 | 22.723 → 7.409 | 4.457 → 1.959 |
| 10,000 / long | 73.047 → 40.208 | 73.987 → 40.531 | 80.803 → 47.387 | 4.570 → 3.586 |
| 50,000 / short | 79.212 → 3.648 | 80.039 → 4.448 | 115.123 → 39.066 | 21.703 → 7.885 |
| 50,000 / long | 360.769 → 158.480 | 362.823 → 159.481 | 397.505 → 192.991 | 21.804 → 15.710 |

The 50k long-name A/A CPU medians were 362.655/362.186 ms; short-name A/A medians were 79.338/79.152 ms. Full-distance microbenchmark (12,000 calls): 15.986→15.748 ms CPU; bounded: 5.943→2.537 ms. At n=5, nearest-rank p95 is the maximum. Allocation uses V8 4 KiB sampling including collected objects, excludes ArrayBuffer backing stores, and is not retained-heap size. No timing claim uses the allocation-instrumented pass.

The benchmark loads the exact old and new read/distance modules with shared unchanged dependencies and compares complete errors. It additionally compares 1,992 old/new distance results across tracked filenames, seeded random UTF-16 strings and empty/equal cases. A separate independent full-matrix unit test checks 344 pairs with full and six bounded queries. The real-read regression fails on the baseline (400 scoring cells for a length-impossible filename versus expected zero) and passes with the fix.

162 focused tests passed across all seven distance consumers and the shared helper; Chromium tool-card and production-bundled output-fidelity tests passed (four tests). Focused suites completed in 88.61 seconds total; the shared distance file took 15 ms of test time in the first equivalence run. No direct UI import path to the helper or its callers was found. Codex autoreview completed scoped-clean through P2. The requested `pnpm check:changed` completed: format, ratchets, core/test/script typechecks, scripts lint and remaining guards passed. Its two new test-lint findings were repaired; targeted lint and both changed test files then passed (49 tests in 15.73 seconds). The dead-export gate is red on unchanged CI scripts, reproduced with the same three findings on the exact base: `ci-test-observations.mjs: main` introduced by #191226 (`586f57665699`), `ci-adaptive-select.mjs: main` by #191228 (`1e964bb21464`), and `ci-adaptive-costs.mjs: main` by #191229 (`8f8ffc232db9`). This was an inherited main regression on the original base. It has since been repaired by #191663 (`cde38490e291`), which is the exact main parent used by this PR CI run. The script-only export scan passes on that parent, so those exports require no exception. Those owners are unchanged here.

Reproduce timing and allocation separately:

```sh
node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/read-path-suggestions-measure.ts --baseline 7f2aaee19ffc --pairs 5 --mode timing
node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/read-path-suggestions-measure.ts --baseline 7f2aaee19ffc --pairs 5 --mode allocation
```

Measured on macOS arm64 / Node 26.12.1, shared external volume, load average 19.5–22.5. This proves the real missing-file tool boundary, not whole-Gateway/model latency or Linux/btrfs behavior. File contents and the agent database are not read on this path. The longest measured miss still consumes about 158 ms CPU; the scan remains linear. No production data or live runtime was changed.


The exact-head CI run [41577819797](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41577819797) passed every executed job except the test-line ratchet and its aggregate gate. This is a different inherited main regression: #191638 added 48 unallocated test lines, #191548 added 7, and #191604 added 170, consuming the original two-line margin and leaving **223 lines of debt**. The exact CI parent reproduces that 223-line failure against the original main baseline. A same-parent comparison passes with a notice because the checker exempts zero test growth; this is not being represented as a failing self-comparison.

This PR's 65 new test lines and 65-line allocation leave the debt unchanged, and its local test-line check against the original base passes with two lines of slack. The failed source inputs are identical between the CI parent and tested merge. Landing uses the explicitly authorized, pinned inherited-failure route with this evidence; CI is **not** reported as green. No extra allocation, test deletion, guard change, or rerun was used to hide the deficit.

prs.title: fix(cli): explain unknown ids in devices reject and remove
prs.body:
Fixes #190293

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw devices reject <id>` and `openclaw devices remove <id>` with an id the Gateway does not know printed only `The CLI command failed.` (exit 1). The Gateway's `INVALID_REQUEST unknown requestId` / `unknown deviceId` reason was lost in text mode, and the JSON envelope carried the bare Gateway string.

## User Impact

Text and `--json` callers now get `No pending device request matches <id>` / `No paired device matches <id>` plus a `openclaw devices list` hint, the same wording `devices approve` already uses. Exit code stays 1. Other Gateway failures still go to the root failure handler unchanged.

## Why

`runDevicesDeleteCommand` called `device.pair.reject|remove` without the unknown-id handling `devices approve` has. The fix catches only the unknown-id refusal for the requested field and routes it through the existing `failDevicesCommand`. The `isUnknownRequestIdError` helper moves to `src/cli/devices-cli.unknown-id.ts` and takes the field, so `devices-cli.runtime.ts` does not grow past the line-cap ratchet. The moved helper now narrows with `in` checks instead of a type assertion, so the runtime file's assertion-safety baseline shrinks from 9 to 8.

## Evidence

Linux, isolated HOME, a real local Gateway from this tree (`gateway run --auth token --bind loopback`), the same Gateway for both runs.

Before (main `devices-cli.runtime.ts`):
```
$ openclaw devices reject does-not-exist --token <local>
[openclaw] The CLI command failed.
[openclaw] For help, run `openclaw doctor`.
$ openclaw devices remove does-not-exist --token <local>
[openclaw] The CLI command failed.
[openclaw] For help, run `openclaw doctor`.
$ openclaw devices reject does-not-exist --json --token <local>
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "type": "cli_error",
    "message": "unknown requestId"
```

After (head 56ea4f08156):
```
$ openclaw devices reject does-not-exist --token <local>
No pending device request matches does-not-exist. Run openclaw devices list and retry with the current requestId.
# exit=1
$ openclaw devices remove does-not-exist --token <local>
No paired device matches does-not-exist. Run openclaw devices list and retry with the current deviceId.
# exit=1
$ openclaw devices reject does-not-exist --json --token <local>
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "type": "cli_error",
    "message": "No pending device request matches does-not-exist. Run openclaw devices list and retry with the current requestId."
  }
}
No pending device request matches does-not-exist. Run openclaw devices list and retry with the current requestId.
# exit=1
```

Scoped tests: `vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts src/cli/devices-cli.test.ts`: 43 passed. The two new unknown-id text cases fail on the main runtime (2 failed | 41 passed). New coverage: text and JSON for both commands, and a non-unknown-id failure that still reaches the root handler.

prs.title: fix(infra): name the lock path in gateway lock errors (companion to #159614)
prs.body:
Companion to #159614 by @carlosjarenom, which went stale waiting on proof. This branch keeps his commit (authorship intact), applies it to current `main`, adds one follow-up commit, and supplies the missing real-run evidence. Related issue: #135133.

## What Problem This Solves

When Gateway startup cannot acquire state ownership, the error says `failed to acquire gateway state ownership` without naming the lock file that blocked it. The operator has to guess between the process owner sidecar (`state.<hash>.lock`), the historical state lock (`gateway.state.lock`) and the config lock (`gateway.<hash>.lock`). This is worst when the holder sits in another PID namespace, e.g. a containerized Gateway sharing `~/.openclaw`, because nothing on the host can verify or reclaim it.

## User Impact

The startup error now ends with `at <lock path>`, naming the exact file that refused ownership, so the operator knows what to inspect (or hand to `openclaw gateway recover-lock`). There is no behavior change to locking, reclaiming or timeouts; only the error text changes. When the failure is a database error rather than a lock, the message keeps pointing at the database, as on `main`.

## Why

- `4418884` (@carlosjarenom, from #159614): tracks the lock file that blocked each poll attempt, resets it every attempt so a stale path is never reported, and falls back to the owner sidecar. Conflicts with current `main`'s acquire loop were resolved by keeping `main`'s structure and adding only his tracking.
- `df683a6` (follow-up): on current `main`, an unverifiable or unreadable historical lock payload throws before live contention, so his hook never fired for those cases (his own "recorded owner cannot be verified" tests failed after rebasing). The follow-up attributes any refusal from a historical lock check to that file, includes the lock path in `GatewayLockNamespaceError` when it is known, and skips the lock suffix for database failures (which `backup-sqlite.test.ts` covers). It adds a regression test for the foreign-PID-namespace state lock. `gateway-lock.ts` stays under the 700 code-line limit.

## Evidence

Real Gateway startup on Linux from the source CLI (`node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs src/entry.ts`), isolated `HOME`, port 19462. A `gateway.state.lock` is left by a Gateway in another PID namespace (live PID, foreign `processNamespace`), then a second Gateway starts on the same state dir.

Before (`origin/main` 2c0ab86):
```
# source tree 2c0ab86fa41 (origin/main); isolated HOME=/tmp/h159614.8Shj
$ cat /tmp/h159614.8Shj/.openclaw/tmp/openclaw-1000/gateway.state.lock
{"pid":3662774,"createdAt":"2026-11-01T11:11:58.000Z","configPath":"/tmp/h159614.8Shj/.openclaw/openclaw.json","stateDir":"/tmp/h159614.8Shj/.openclaw","role":"gateway","processNamespace":{"platform":"linux","host":"gateway-container","pidNsInode":"4026532999"}}
$ openclaw gateway run --allow-unconfigured --port 19462
Run "openclaw doctor --fix" against the same state/config, then restart the gateway.
2026-11-01T19:12:18.525+08:00 [gateway] loading configuration…
2026-11-01T19:12:18.534+08:00 [gateway] resolving authentication…
2026-11-01T19:12:18.536+08:00 [gateway] starting...
2026-11-01T19:12:19.256+08:00 Gateway failed to start: failed to acquire gateway state ownership | Gateway lock inspection is unavailable | Gateway lock payload could not be verified
If the gateway is supervised, stop it with: openclaw gateway stop
# exit=1
```

After (this branch, df683a6):
```
# source tree df683a6449e (branch); isolated HOME=/tmp/h159614.fFAO
$ cat /tmp/h159614.fFAO/.openclaw/tmp/openclaw-1000/gateway.state.lock
{"pid":3688236,"createdAt":"2026-11-01T11:27:22.000Z","configPath":"/tmp/h159614.fFAO/.openclaw/openclaw.json","stateDir":"/tmp/h159614.fFAO/.openclaw","role":"gateway","processNamespace":{"platform":"linux","host":"gateway-container","pidNsInode":"4026532999"}}
$ openclaw gateway run --allow-unconfigured --port 19462
Run "openclaw doctor --fix" against the same state/config, then restart the gateway.
2026-11-01T19:27:41.965+08:00 [gateway] loading configuration…
2026-11-01T19:27:41.975+08:00 [gateway] resolving authentication…
2026-11-01T19:27:41.977+08:00 [gateway] starting...
2026-11-01T19:27:42.700+08:00 Gateway failed to start: failed to acquire gateway state ownership at /tmp/h159614.fFAO/.openclaw/tmp/openclaw-1000/gateway.state.lock | Gateway lock inspection is unavailable | Gateway lock payload could not be verified
If the gateway is supervised, stop it with: openclaw gateway stop
# exit=1
```

Tests (Linux, vitest infra config, `--maxWorkers=1`):
- `src/infra/gateway-lock*.test.ts`: 7 files passed, 1 skipped (Windows-only), 102 tests passed.
- Red/green for `src/infra/gateway-lock.unactionable-timeout.test.ts`: against `main`'s `gateway-lock.ts`/`gateway-lock-payload.ts`, 5/5 fail. Against #159614's commit alone on current `main`, 3/5 fail (the unverifiable-owner and foreign-namespace cases). On this branch, 5/5 pass.
- Callers that assert on these messages: `backup-sqlite`, `doctor-sqlite-maintenance-lock`, `run.supervised-lock`, `daemon/diagnostics`, `update-database-restore`, `sqlite-readonly-location`, `startup-plugin-source-captures`, `update-command-invalid-config` all pass. `run-loop.test.ts` has timeouts locally that reproduce identically on `main`, so they are unrelated.
- `checks-node-changed-compact-large-36` on #159614 failed in `src/agents/sandbox/sdk-state-owner.process.test.ts` (filesystem snapshot `.bun` entry count 1645 vs 1639), which does not touch the lock code. Locally that test passes on both `main` and this branch (1/1 each), so it looks like a runner-environment snapshot flake, not this patch.

If @carlosjarenom prefers to fold `df683a6` into #159614, I'll close this one.


CI attribution: `check-lint-core-5` (and the `ci-gate` that follows it) fails on `src/skills/workshop/experience-review.test.ts:167-168` (`typescript(no-unnecessary-type-arguments)`). This PR does not touch that file; the same failure shows on other open PRs against current main (for example #190299). Head a0669ece542 merges current main; all checks for the files this PR changes pass.

prs.title: fix: observer fallback models get time after a primary timeout
prs.body:
Closes #191600

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a utility-model primary that uses the session observer's full 30-second budget leaves no time for its configured fallback, so assessments stop even though a usable fallback is configured.

## User Impact

User impact: a timed-out primary can now hand the assessment to a configured fallback with its own bounded execution budget instead of cancelling the whole chain. If the chain is exhausted, the warning says the configured fallbacks failed rather than telling the user to add fallbacks that already exist. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The observer's abort timer covered model preparation and every candidate in the fallback chain. Isolated completion already creates a fresh timeout for each candidate while preserving caller cancellation and cleanup ownership. The observer now keeps its 30-second bound only through preparation, then lets that per-candidate boundary handle completion. Existing caller cancellation remains in place.

## Evidence

- New composed regression uses `createSessionObserverCompletion` with the real `runUtilityCompletion` fallback path. On the unfixed observer it rejects with `session observer model call timed out or was cancelled`; after the change, the primary times out, the fallback returns a digest, and both candidates are observed in order.
- `session-observer-completion.test.ts`, `session-observer-settlement.test.ts`, and `utility-completion.runtime.test.ts`: **32 passed**. The local run uses a minimal Vitest config with source aliases because the existing dependency install is missing current-main workspace links. No live provider was contacted.
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` pass on all three changed files. `git diff --check` is clean.
- The standard full Vitest config and tsgo were attempted but could not complete in this existing install: missing `@openclaw/proc-safe/windows-job`, `micromark`, and other pre-existing dependency/type errors stop those lanes outside this diff. I am not claiming a full local suite or typecheck pass; PR CI remains the authoritative full lane.

prs.title: fix: preserve command output with long temporary paths
prs.body:
Related: #190843, #190845.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes buffered commands failing with EINVAL when a long temporary directory makes their Unix-socket path exceed the platform limit. This also prevented private repository history from reaching native child sessions, despite file reconciliation succeeding.

## User Impact

Commands can complete under long temporary roots, and repository operations can preserve private Git history instead of falling back to files-only recovery. Missing or unwritable temporary directories still fail normally. No configuration, authentication, execution-permission or cancellation behavior changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The native-resource broker already uses a portable socket-path budget and a private short fallback. Buffered command output now shares that decision. It checks the actual created path, removes an oversized rendezvous directory, and preserves private permissions, current launch authority and cleanup.

The two regressions use real sockets and subprocesses, covering absolute and UTF-8-byte-overlong paths, output, cleanup, refusal and ordinary temporary-directory errors. The exact 122-line test allocation covers these distinct owner-boundary contracts.

## Evidence

- Frozen source: **2 intended regression failures** from native EINVAL. Qualified repair: **2 passed**.
- **44 process/broker cases + 5 native-resource cases passed**, including output transfer, cancellation and cleanup.
- **3 real broker/Git diagnostic cases passed:** private history exported/imported/adopted under long and short paths; revoked authority refused import and preserved the base.
- [Real-Gateway qualification run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41571285323): **2/2 tests passed**, including complete mirrored and retained native-child flows, four authenticated nodes, private ancestry/current bytes and parent authority/filesystem preservation. Model and provisioning transports were deterministic fixtures; this is not live frontier inference or commercial volume provisioning.
- Targeted types, lint and formatting passed on the qualified source. The original five-file socket repair is byte-identical to that source; the follow-up adds only the missing helper to the extracted-wrapper inventory. On observed main c86fbe68e5a1ae494e49ac6ad41aef9585210ab6, format, whitespace and the test-line ratchet passed. Main’s changed execution-scope/cleanup callers were reviewed; the socket owners, remaining broker transport inputs and Execa dependency closure are unchanged.
- Fresh independent full-context review: **no actionable P0–P2 findings**. Canonical committed-range autoreview of `c86fbe68e5a1ae494e49ac6ad41aef9585210ab6` → `61b12733e4b6c7bfa83c2e756d88c9e54ca1c680`: **scoped-clean P0–P2, complete, exit 0**, including complete socket owners, extraction contracts and the inventory correction. Static review did not execute tests. Local ClawSweeper was unavailable; the documented autoreview fallback was used. The original e704 hosted review identified the inventory omission addressed below. The completed [fresh hosted review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191659#issuecomment-6595387495) on `61b12733e4b6c7bfa83c2e756d88c9e54ca1c680` rates overall/proof Platinum and patch Diamond, with zero actionable findings. Current-head CI remains blocked by the separate budget result below.

The remote driver returned **2 after its passing tests** because two configured reporters rendered the same complete ledger twice. Raw receipts remain unchanged. The collector-only proposal was separately qualified against that retained log and empty/incomplete/conflicting-output controls; it is not part of this production PR.

Proof reuse is component-specific: prior-tree execution is not current-candidate CI or whole merge-tree equivalence. Linux Node24.22.1/Node26.12.1 were exercised; no Darwin/Windows runtime claim. Current-head CI and overall Platinum-or-higher hosted review remain landing gates.


### CI follow-up: extracted PR-wrapper source closure

The first CI run on e704 exposed a packaging omission: the new shared socket-directory helper was missing from the maintained PR-wrapper source inventory. Extracted wrappers could not load resource-authority, which also prevented the cold provisioner's private handoff preload from completing. The repair adds that single source path; authority guards, implementation behavior and test assertions are unchanged.

Local proof: the three existing source-inventory regressions failed on e704 and identified exactly the missing module. With the entry added, both complete wrapper tooling files passed **39/39**, including extracted lease/template bootstrap. A separate real extracted-wrapper/private-preload witness reproduced the hidden missing-module error before the fix and verified private-store injection/preflight afterward; it intentionally stopped at ordinary CLI argument validation, not complete provisioning.

The full cold-provision file could not be replayed locally because compiled-worker setup required a dependency version absent from the prepared installation; no install, older-version substitution or preparation bypass was used. The new-head provisioning CI lane subsequently passed, as recorded below. These are PR-caused failures, not an inherited-failure waiver. No runtime qualification rerun or CI rerun was performed merely to obtain green.

### Exact-head CI result: inherited test-budget debt

[CI 41578015635](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41578015635) on `61b12733` passed the previously failing extracted-wrapper and provisioning lanes. Its sole failed leaf is [checks-fast-baseline-ratchets](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41578015635/job/125726365304); the CI gate aggregates that failure.

The unchanged owning checker was replayed on exact Git-index snapshots:

| Snapshot | Counted test lines | Effective ceiling | Debt | Compared growth | Result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Tested main parent `cde38490` | 6,419,861 | 6,419,638 | 223 | 0 | Exit 0 with over-budget notice |
| Tested merge `57f5bffc` | 6,419,983 | 6,419,760 | 223 | +122 | Exit 1, same CI failure |
| Later observed main `bb10c4ba` | 6,419,857 | 6,419,638 | 219 | 0 | Exit 0 with over-budget notice |

This PR adds exactly 122 counted regression-test lines and exactly 122 allocation lines of credit: **zero added debt**. The checker intentionally rejects positive growth on an already-over-budget tree even when this change fully allocates its own growth. Its existing regression preserves that policy. The native CI classifier's `new` verdict is retained: inherited numeric debt is not an inherited failed-CI verdict or a waiver.

History attributes 225 uncovered lines to #191638 (+48), #191548 (+7), and #191604 (+170), consuming the prior two-line slack. #191635 later removed four lines. These measurements are pinned snapshots, not a claim about continuously advancing main.

No test removal, baseline/allocation increase, policy change, bypass, or CI rerun was made. Increasing this PR's allocation to absorb shared debt would violate the credit-versus-growth check. Landing still requires green exact-head CI and the required rating.

## Credits

Requested by @galiniliev. The commit retains `Co-authored-by: galiniliev <5711535+galiniliev@users.noreply.github.com>`.
