prs.title: fix(cli): cancel infer web requests and discard late output
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`infer web search` and web fetch can print a late result or provider failure after acknowledging Ctrl-C. Their request owners did not receive the invocation signal, and their output bypassed the existing cancellation-aware capability wrapper.

## What Changed

Forward the existing AsyncWorkScope signal to web search, the default fetch tool, and a pinned fetch provider. Use the existing `runCapabilityCommand` owner to discard late success/failure output. Ordinary structured failures still exit nonzero after output drains, without overriding an acknowledged interruption.

Provider APIs, security guards, selection, credentials and timeout policy are unchanged. No new signal manager or configuration is introduced.

## Evidence

Head: `a11fa18f2f894253c467e7d34aa7949d8e42cfa0`.

[Built CLI before/after proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191628#issuecomment-6595070723): clean main/candidate builds in secretless Node 24.22.1 Docker, normal bundled Firecrawl search/pinned fetch and direct HTTP fetch. The delayed local peer receives each request, then the harness sends real SIGINT and waits for the actual root acknowledgement before releasing the response.

Twice per case, main prints late output after acknowledgement: search success 999 bytes, search HTTP 503 471 bytes, pinned-fetch success 794 bytes, pinned-fetch HTTP 503 464 bytes, direct-fetch success 1,080 bytes. Candidate prints zero stdout and only the root acknowledgement on stderr; all interrupted invocations exit naturally with 130. Uninterrupted successes remain visible with exit 0, and HTTP 503 failures remain visible with exit 1 on both refs. Forty CLI invocations total; no forced kills.

No socket-abort claim: every peer observation had `responseClosedBeforeFinish=false`. The proof establishes cancellation acknowledgement, late-output suppression and exit-status preservation; the regression separately checks signal forwarding.

Consolidated the interruption regression into existing default-fetch cases and restored moved web tests to their original suite. Removed the extra registrar and test-growth allocation, duplicate configuration setup and generic envelope echoes, retaining provider-state, normal output, disabled-fetch, structured-failure and SecretRef coverage.

- Candidate capability suite: 102 tests passed; 50.61 s Vitest / 53.31 s runner including cold compilation, approximately 13.7 s test execution. Changed fetch cases: 2 ms each.
- Baseline focused regression fails at missing invocation-signal forwarding.
- Focused Oxfmt, Oxlint and whitespace checks passed.
- Whole-PR delta: production +24/-23 (net +1), tests +101/-106 (net -5), docs +3. Moved test lines are not counted as new production.
- Fixed an own introduced test-type error from spreading a plain array into required arguments: both literal domain and action now precede the variadic arguments. The two disabled-fetch cases pass; the exact previously failing type graph now passes through the repository's pinned compiler runner. Production code and runtime proof are unchanged.
- Integrated current main after #191635 landed its disjoint TTS documentation and tests. Both TTS and Web interruption guidance are retained. Web request/output and root signal owners are byte-unchanged by that merge, so the recorded runtime proof remains applicable.

## Merge Danger

Two-way door: reverting restores prior cancellation/output behavior; there are no persisted state or public-contract changes. Blast radius is local infer web search/fetch interruption and ordinary failure exit handling. Other capability commands continue to use the same existing output owner.

prs.title: fix(openai): name the direct image route on 401/403 scope errors
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/90074

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: OpenAI image generation fails with a bare `HTTP 401` / `Missing scopes` error that does not say which route or credential OpenClaw used when explicit `models.providers.openai` settings select the direct Images API.

## User Impact

User impact: operators who hit a 401/403 on OpenAI image generation now see the selected route, endpoint, credential class and credential source in the error (or `configured-header` when configured auth headers replaced the resolved credential). When explicit `models.providers.openai` settings pin the direct route, the message also names the `baseUrl`/`api` settings that switch to a ChatGPT/Codex OAuth profile instead. The original error keeps its class, status and detail; 429 and other statuses are unchanged. Routing precedence is unchanged; no config migration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The clawsweeper review on the issue recommends keeping explicit provider settings authoritative and making image failures identify the effective transport and credential class. This PR does only that: on a 401/403 from the direct Images API route, the existing `ProviderHttpError` keeps its class and status (failover classification is unaffected) and gets a short route suffix appended. Query strings are dropped from the shown endpoint, header values are never shown. Credential attribution compares the final request auth header with the resolved credential, so `headers.Authorization` / `request.auth` overrides are reported as `configured-header`. Other status codes and the Codex Responses route are unchanged. The helpers live in a new sibling module `image-generation-diagnostics.ts` (the existing sanitizer moved there unchanged), so the provider file shrinks and the large test file is untouched.

Changed since the review of `33833df6d19`: the suffix is built only from facts resolved before the request (route, resolved credential, explicit direct config), and the OAuth advice depends on the explicit config instead of a profile lookup. Nothing reads the auth store after the request fails, so another provider's pending migration (`AuthProfileMigrationRequiredError`) can no longer replace the HTTP 401/403/429. The annotation runs only for the Images API response itself, not for later image URL downloads. The October 15 update merged then-current `main`; the conflict in `image-generation-provider.ts` was resolved onto the async auth preparation from https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/169111 and https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/169714

## Evidence

### Historical evidence (head `214e40e5f8db`)

Real `openclaw infer image generate` runs from built checkouts (`pnpm build`) of the previous head `33833df6d19` and this head `214e40e5f8d`, with real HTTP transport against a loopback Images API stub that answers 401, 403, 429 or 200. Every run uses a fresh isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` whose agent still holds a legacy Anthropic profile awaiting migration (the CLI logs `requires legacy credential migration; affected providers: anthropic`), explicit `models.providers.openai` (`baseUrl` = stub, `apiKey` synthetic), and runs inside a network namespace that only has `lo` (`api.openai.com` does not resolve). Each case made exactly one `POST …/v1/images/generations` with `Bearer synthetic-openai-key`; the auth profile file was unchanged afterwards.

The standalone CLI activates a secrets runtime snapshot for the agent before provider auth (`prepareLocalCapabilityAccountSecrets`). To exercise the reviewed case (no prepared `authStore`, no runtime snapshot), these runs skip that one step in the built output of both heads (one added `return;`; diff, restore and checksum check are in the logs):

| CLI run, no runtime auth snapshot | 401 | 403 | 429 | 200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| previous head `33833df6d19` | Anthropic migration error replaces the HTTP error | same | same | image written |
| this head `214e40e5f8d` | HTTP 401 error + route suffix | HTTP 403 error + route suffix | HTTP 429 error, unchanged | image written |

With the CLI unchanged (snapshot active), both heads kept the HTTP error for 401/403/429; this head adds the explicit-route advice to the 401/403 suffix.

<details>
<summary>CLI output, 2026-10-15 (UTC)</summary>

```text
# previous head 33833df6d19, no runtime snapshot, stub answers 401 (POST 00:58:01Z)
[image-generation] candidate failed: openai/gpt-image-2: Auth profile store …/state/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite requires legacy credential migration; affected providers: anthropic; run openclaw doctor --fix.
# same message for 403 (POST 00:58:08Z) and 429 (POST 00:58:15Z)

# this head 214e40e5f8d, no runtime snapshot, stub answers 401 (POST 00:58:24Z)
[image-generation] candidate failed: openai/gpt-image-2: OpenAI image generation failed (HTTP 401): Missing scopes: api.model.images.request [type=stub] (route=images-api url=http://127.0.0.1:35789/s401/v1/images/generations credential=*** source=models.json; explicit models.providers.openai settings select the direct Images API. To use a ChatGPT/Codex OAuth profile instead, set baseUrl "https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex" and api "openai-chatgpt-responses", without apiKey, auth "api-key", or auth headers)
# 403 (POST 00:58:28Z)
[image-generation] candidate failed: openai/gpt-image-2: OpenAI image generation failed (HTTP 403): Project does not have access to model gpt-image-2 [type=stub] (route=images-api url=http://127.0.0.1:35789/s403/v1/images/generations credential=*** source=models.json; explicit models.providers.openai settings select the direct Images API. …)
# 429 (POST 00:58:33Z)
[image-generation] candidate failed: openai/gpt-image-2: OpenAI image generation failed (HTTP 429): Rate limit reached for images per minute [type=stub]

# CLI unchanged (snapshot active), previous head 33833df6d19, 401 (POST 00:56:03Z)
[image-generation] candidate failed: openai/gpt-image-2: OpenAI image generation failed (HTTP 401): Missing scopes: api.model.images.request [type=stub] (route=images-api url=http://127.0.0.1:34331/s401/v1/images/generations credential=*** source=models.json)
```

</details>

Provider-module counter-check with the seven cases from the review (401/403/429 with and without a prepared store, plus 200; real auth-profile owner, real loopback HTTP): previous head 4/7 (the three no-store cases end in `AuthProfileMigrationRequiredError`), `main` 7/7, this head 7/7. Re-adding an eager post-failure store read to this head makes the new no-store tests in `image-generation-provider.direct-errors.test.ts` fail 3/3.

<details>
<summary>Earlier live run against api.openai.com (2026-10-06, previous head; the advice wording has changed since)</summary>

Setup as in the issue: `models.providers.openai = { baseUrl: "https://api.openai.com/v1", api: "openai-completions" }`, an `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the environment, a ChatGPT OAuth profile in the auth store (synthetic token), isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Before (`origin/main`) | `OpenAI image generation failed (HTTP 401): Incorrect API key provided: syntheti****cess. … [request_id=req_b37ec54f…]`, no route or credential |
| After, resolved credential | same text plus `(route=images-api url=https://api.openai.com/v1/images/generations credential=oauth source=profile:openai:chatgpt; … set baseUrl "https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex" and api "openai-chatgpt-responses" …)` |

prs.title: fix(ios): write-scoped operators cannot change thinking or Fast mode
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/190301

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: in the iOS app's chat, the Thinking and Fast controls stay disabled (composer) or drop their change (Chat actions menu) for an operator paired without `operator.admin` (for example through `openclaw qr --limited`), although the Gateway lets that operator change both.

## User Impact

User impact: iOS operators with write access can change a chat's thinking level and Fast mode from the phone, as they already can on Android; the hint for operators without write access now names `operator.write`. Tool details (verbose level) stays admin-only, and its picker is now disabled for these operators instead of silently dropping their choice.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway's `sessions.patch` accepts `thinkingLevel` and `fastMode` from `operator.write`, the same scope as `model`, while `verboseLevel` still needs `operator.admin`. The iOS composer capability catalog gated the model control on write access but Thinking, Fast and Tool details together on admin access. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/163516 fixed the same gate in the Android app. This change makes the iOS catalog's effort availability use write access and gives verbose its own availability, still decided by admin access, which gates `selectVerboseLevel` and both Tool details pickers. Same split as https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/146343. The disabled hint (and its generated native i18n entry) now names `operator.write`.

Size against the merge base `4d2a9f8bb4c`: production +19/−7 in 7 files (including 1 generated i18n line and the demo transport's new field), tests +32/−1 in the existing `IOSGatewayChatTransportTests` and `ChatViewModelTests` suites.

## Evidence

Tested on a real iPhone (iOS 26.7.1) with the iOS app built without and with the fix, paired to an isolated Gateway (own state, no channels) through an `openclaw qr --limited` setup code. On both sides the paired operator token had `operator.approvals`, `operator.questions`, `operator.read`, `operator.talk.secrets` and `operator.write`, without `operator.admin`. The Gateway's default model was `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5` with a synthetic API key, because the app shows the Fast switch only for a model that supports Fast mode; no provider was called. Before each side, the main session's thinking level and Fast mode were reset to their defaults from the Gateway host.

The same UI script ran on both sides right after pairing: read the main session row from the Gateway, check the composer's Effort control, open Chat actions, move the Thinking level slider from Medium to High, turn Fast mode on, check that both changes stay and that Tool details is disabled, and read the session row again.

The device builds sit on main at `e0f88b715bf` (before https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/187045) instead of this PR's base `4d2a9f8bb4c`, because the iOS SDK that current main needs was not available on the build Mac. The files this PR touches are identical on both commits, except two unrelated entries in `apps/.i18n/native-source.json`. Both device builds also carry the same one-line `// swiftlint:disable:next function_body_length` above `seedMessages` in `apps/ios/Sources/Chat/AppleReviewDemoChatTransport.swift`, because the iOS app's strict SwiftLint build step fails there on main (210 lines > 150); this PR does not include that line.

Before (main `e0f88b715bf`):

```text
Composer Effort control: enabled=false, value "Inherited medium"
Thinking level after moving the slider one step: "Medium"
Fast mode after tapping the switch: "0"
Tool details picker: enabled=true
Gateway session row before:  thinkingLevel None, fastMode None, verboseLevel None
Gateway session row after:   thinkingLevel None, fastMode None, verboseLevel None
```

After (`e0f88b715bf` + this PR's commits):

```text
Composer Effort control: enabled=true, value "Inherited medium"
Thinking level after moving the slider one step: "High"
Fast mode after tapping the switch: "1"
Tool details picker: enabled=false
Gateway session row before:  thinkingLevel None, fastMode None, verboseLevel None
Gateway session row after:   thinkingLevel 'high', fastMode True, verboseLevel None
```

Observed result: with the same write-scoped operator, the thinking and Fast changes are dropped without the fix; with the fix the Gateway accepts them, and Tool details stays disabled and unchanged.

![Chat actions after the changes: Thinking Medium and Fast off on main, High and on with the fix](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261030-163516-ios-effort-write-scope/before-after-actions.png)

Recording of both runs side by side: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/masatohoshino/openclaw/proof-assets/20261030-163516-ios-effort-write-scope/before-after-v2.mp4

Tests: `IOSGatewayChatTransportTests` passes 34 of 34 on the iOS Simulator (Xcode 26.6, iOS 26.4) with this PR's changes on `e0f88b715bf`. Its new test `write-scoped operators can change thinking and fast mode but not tool details` checks the catalog: `effortMutationAvailable` follows write access and `verboseMutationAvailable` stays off without admin. Its effort assertion fails on `e0f88b715bf` (`effortMutationAvailable: false` while `modelMutationAvailable: true`) and passes with the fix, while the suite's other 33 tests pass on both sides; the verbose assertion uses the new field, so it cannot run on main. In `ChatViewModelTests`, `write scope permits effort but keeps tool details admin only` checks that `selectVerboseLevel` sends no `sessions.patch` with effort access but without verbose access, and the existing test that covers no effort access is renamed to say so. `ChatViewModelTests` passes 343 of 343 on the same Simulator with this PR's commits on `e0f88b715bf`, compiled into the iOS test target for that run only (with the two files that hold its shared helpers), because the build Mac's Swift 6.2.4 is older than OpenClawKit's tools version 6.3.

Checks: `pnpm native:i18n:verify` passes. `pnpm check:changed` passes every step except formatting, which failed only on untracked local scratch files that are not part of this PR; the formatter matches none of this PR's files. The iOS app build's SwiftFormat (lint) and strict SwiftLint steps, which cover the six changed production Swift files, passed in the device and Simulator builds above. As on every ordinary pull request, this PR's CI skips the macOS Swift and iOS build jobs. Its `android-test-play` job fails on one Android unit test, `NodeRuntimeAgentSelectionTest.coldStartUsesAnAllowedAgentBeforePatchingTheGatewayDefault`; this PR changes no Android files. The same test failed the same way on the same day in the CI of https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/141004 (run 41326506147), which changes no Android files either.

Not covered: the device proof ran on `e0f88b715bf`, not on this PR's base, for the SDK reason above. `ChatViewModelTests` ran in the iOS test target, not through OpenClawKit's own `swift test`. The Android behavior was not re-tested; the comparison with it comes from its source and https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/163516.

prs.title: fix(buzz): thread replies share the room session and inherit unrelated context
prs.body:
Closes #144331

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a Buzz user who mentions the bot inside a thread gets a reply built from the room's shared conversation, not from that thread. Every thread in a room ran on one session, so a busy thread queued replies in every other thread, and a new thread started with whatever unrelated context the room session already held. On a production 2026.9.3 install, the first reply in a fresh thread was answered from a single unmentioned room message 17 days old, and the bot said it could not see how the thread started.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an opt-in `threadSessions` setting, off by default, at the account level with a per-room override. When enabled, each thread dispatches on its own session keyed by the thread root the plugin already parses; top-level room messages stay on the room session. A new thread session starts empty and does not fork the room transcript, and it does not inherit a `/model` override set on the room session; both are stated in the Buzz docs. Reply placement, typing, passive history, and bot-loop scope are unchanged. Turning the setting off routes new thread messages back to the room session and leaves existing thread sessions in place. The contract and known limitations are on #144331. Config surface: the setting adds four channel schema entries (root, account, and the two room maps), so the channel budget in `docs/.generated/config-baseline.counts.json` is raised from 3730 to 3734 and the baseline hash regenerated with `pnpm config:docs:gen`.

## User Impact

Operators can isolate Buzz threads with `channels.buzz.threadSessions: true` or per room. Threads then run and remember context independently, and one long turn no longer blocks the others. Deployments that do not set it see no change. Documented in the Buzz channel docs under "Thread sessions".

## Evidence

- Real isolated Gateway child with the bundled Buzz plugin against the signed loopback relay fixture and the deterministic mock model, one room, two threads, a member identity mentioning the bot once in each thread. With `threadSessions: true` the bot replied inside both threads and the session store held exactly two Buzz sessions, `…:buzz:group:buzz:<room>:thread:<rootA>` and `…:thread:<rootB>`, and no room session. With the flag off, the same traffic produced the same two threaded replies and exactly one session, `…:buzz:group:buzz:<room>`.
- Existing-session transitions, same harness, one relay and one gateway state dir, gateway restarted after each config edit, the bot mentioned in the same thread every phase. Flag off: one room session created. Flag on: that room session untouched (store `updatedAt` unchanged), two new thread sessions for the existing thread and a new one. Flag off again: the room session resumed with the same id and was updated, both thread sessions untouched. Flag on again: the existing thread resumed its earlier thread session with the same id, room session and the other thread session untouched. No session was rewritten, deleted, or duplicated across the four phases.
- Baseline `b8de9f88996` with the new tests kept: the two Buzz test files fail 5 tests, the routing tests receiving the room session key where the `:thread:<root>` key is expected. Candidate `6df0c46ae9f`: the same files pass 78/78.
- Regressions cover default-off routing, top-level messages with the setting on, room override in both directions, unchanged reply and typing targets, and schema acceptance at root, account, and room level with non-boolean values rejected in both runtime and generated JSON schemas.
- Full Buzz lane 343 tests, channel contract lanes, the docs config-fence test, `pnpm check`, and the bundled channel-config metadata check all pass.
- Repo `autoreview` skill on the branch (`--mode branch --base origin/main`): scoped-clean, no actionable findings.

AI-assisted.

prs.title: fix(cli): preserve TTS output after accepted interruption
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw infer tts convert --output speech.wav` can create or overwrite the requested file after acknowledging SIGINT/SIGTERM. The CLI exits with the interrupt status and suppresses JSON, but still publishes the late audio copy.

## User Impact

Interruption accepted before output copying begins now preserves an existing destination or leaves an absent destination absent. Normal conversion still writes the synthesized audio. Completed synthesis retains its existing media-store lifetime; already-started atomic output writes are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared local/loopback-Gateway copy owner captures the existing invocation signal and checks it after reading source audio, immediately before entering the existing atomic writer. No provider-wide cancellation, new lifecycle machinery, public API/configuration, retention policy or writer change.

Original fix/report by @zhangguiping-xydt; their commit is retained. Same output-publication boundary as the image cancellation repair in #191176.

## Evidence

Independently built main `7e005b019a532981e0102ace3cc6be0478fb2266` and unchanged contributor production in secretless Linux arm64 Node 24.22.1 Docker, with fresh isolated profiles/state and a local HTTP TTS fixture.

- The real `/v1/audio/speech` response is held until the CLI acknowledges the signal, then releases a valid 2,044-byte PCM WAV.
- Main twice: SIGINT overwrites an existing destination; SIGTERM creates an absent destination.
- Candidate twice: SIGINT preserves the original hash; SIGTERM leaves the destination absent.
- Exit codes remain 130/143 with empty stdout. All four normal controls exit 0 and write the same valid WAV bytes.
- 104 focused capability tests pass. On main, only the two interrupted destination cases fail (102 others pass). The matrix also preserves atomic-copy-failure, format-correct output, canonical source bytes, modes and staging cleanup checks. Targeted Oxlint/Oxfmt pass.
- Simplification reuses existing fixtures and one spy-cleanup owner, removes duplicate standalone setup and its allocation: production +5/-1 (net +4), tests +75/-79 (net −4), docs +1/-0 against merge base.

Detailed captured signal ordering, hashes and outcomes: [independent proof comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191635#issuecomment-6595366543).

## Merge Danger

Two-way door: reverting restores the previous late-copy behavior; no persisted-state migration. Blast radius is local or loopback-Gateway TTS `--output` publication after accepted interruption. Synthesis retention and already-started atomic writes retain their existing behavior.

prs.title: fix(gateway): paired-node Claude continuations retain Gateway context
prs.body:
Closes #145636

## What Problem This Solves

A Claude CLI continuation on a healthy paired node can fail with a Gateway-runtime or capability error after its originating request ends. Detached work retains a live Gateway resolver but deliberately does not retain the direct request context.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two paired-node readers now use the existing resolver-first `getInProcessGatewayRequestContext` in the current request-scope owner. This integrates with main's `PluginRuntimeExecutionFrame` storage instead of reintroducing the former AsyncLocalStorage owner or a second accessor. A resolver returning `undefined` remains authoritative: stale direct context cannot revive a retired owner.

The command policy, expected connection and pairing generation, dispatch-time authority, and skill/run/placement lifecycle checks remain intact. There are no configuration, protocol, database-schema, or public SDK changes.

## User Impact

A detached Claude continuation can use its still-live Gateway and connected paired node. A retired owner fails before any node lookup, policy check, or dispatch.

## Evidence

- Conflict refresh onto main `f76e79be6a8fc934afd0faf1315f0261cfc4bafe`; current head `eb7a861ea7c06c277806dd2c6d0dba6b0f9c0443` also checks the captured Gateway remains current at dispatch and skill authority use. [Remote focused tests](https://github.com/ZengWen-DT/openclaw/actions/runs/40626335729) passed 18 tests across both affected Gateway suites on a temporary child of this head. Full CI and refreshed real-node proof remain pending; earlier evidence below refers to the revisions identified there.

Reconciled against main `cdfe6cf00705aa2f59dbbe8040d333cd7d597984`; candidate `2220ac4be308a06c58c1c1fc774bf8a83115414d`. The production diff is two reader substitutions, plus focused regression coverage.

### Actual Gateway and signed-node boundary

The same temporary source-runtime fixture starts the actual Gateway with an isolated home, config and state, loads a startup plugin through the normal loader, and captures its real context in an authenticated RPC. A separately signed WebSocket node completes normal local device pairing and command approval, verified in the persisted pairing records. After the capture RPC finishes, the fixture invokes the production `invokeNodeClaudeCliRun` in a resolver-only scope and repeats with a retired resolver plus deliberately stale direct context.

Main before the fix, observed with clean shutdown:

```json
{"resolverOnly":{"directContext":false,"dispatched":0,"ok":false,"error":"Gateway node runtime unavailable"},"retiredOwner":{"staleDirectContextPresent":true,"additionalDispatches":1,"ok":true}}
```

Exact candidate after the fix:

```json
{"head":"2220ac4be308a06c58c1c1fc774bf8a83115414d","expectedFixed":true,"actualGateway":true,"signedNode":true,"devicePaired":true,"commandApproved":true,"resolverOnly":{"directContext":false,"dispatched":1,"result":{"ok":true,"payload":{"exitCode":0,"stderrTail":"","truncated":false},"payloadJSON":null,"error":null}},"retiredOwner":{"staleDirectContextPresent":true,"additionalDispatches":0,"result":{"ok":false,"error":{"code":"UNAVAILABLE","message":"Gateway node runtime unavailable"}}}}
```

The fixture exited 0, and the Gateway reported a clean shutdown.

This exercises real Gateway startup, plugin loading, authenticated RPC, signed WebSocket transport, persisted device/command pairing, NodeRegistry and the changed production invocation owner. The node returns a synthetic successful Claude-command payload. It does not establish live Claude model inference or a full terminal-close/Web-composer UI walkthrough.

The fixture uses synthetic data only. Update checks, telemetry and hosted catalog refresh are disabled with the documented config/environment opt-outs. Proof code and generated logs are temporary and are not committed.

### Regression coverage and checks

- Before the two reader substitutions: 13 failures / 3 passes across the invocation and paired-node skill suites. Detached dispatch failed unavailable; stale-context retirement incorrectly dispatched; skill preparation failed its Gateway/capability boundary.
- After, on the identical candidate tree: 27/27 tests across node invocation (5), paired-node skills (11), request-scope owner (7), and native Bash execution policy (4). Existing coverage for command denial, pairing-await authority retirement, capability requirements, skill delivery/authoring and publication retirement remains active under the resolver-only scope.
- Combined focused command: `pnpm test src/gateway/node-agent-cli-runtime.test.ts src/gateway/node-claude-skill-runtime.test.ts src/plugins/runtime/gateway-request-scope.test.ts src/agents/cli-runner/execute-plugin-native-bash.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`, 85.02s wall time including the first compiled-subprocess generation.
- Per-file exact-head cost using `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`: `node-agent-cli-runtime.test.ts` 5/5, 34.08s wall (21ms test bodies); `node-claude-skill-runtime.test.ts` 11/11, 65.68s wall (23901ms test bodies). The existing skill suite exercises real node-command subprocess/SQLite lifecycle boundaries; no new per-test Gateway boots, timers, or serial configuration were added. Hosted [changed-node CI job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/37098465276/job/111133298553) passed both files separately: invocation 5/5 in 22.88s (15ms test bodies), skills 11/11 in 19.83s (9.768s test bodies).
- Independent `autoreview --engine codex --mode local --base cdfe6cf00705aa2f59dbbe8040d333cd7d597984 --max-priority P2`: scoped-clean, no accepted/actionable findings.
- Four-file type-aware lint (`node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json <changed files>`) passed in 22.70s. Formatting and `git diff --check` passed. The aggregate check passed conflict, line-cap, max-lines, assertion-safety, database-worker, timeout-race, dependency, config, plugin-boundary and other prerequisite guards, plus the core graph boundary and full production-core typecheck.
- Hosted [CI run 37098465276](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/37098465276) passed on this exact head, including `openclaw/ci-gate`, production types, all selected test-type stripes, lint, selected tests and guards. The [fresh review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/145741#issuecomment-5644398815) resolves the previous integration concern and finds no actionable introduced issues: overall Platinum, proof Diamond.
- Full repository build/check/test is not claimed as locally passed. The bounded `check:changed --base cdfe6cf00705aa2f59dbbe8040d333cd7d597984 --head HEAD` attempt ran 605.19s and stopped at its 600s budget during the broad 27-graph test-typecheck lane: `agents-root` passed, `agents-other` was interrupted (143). Remaining test graphs and later aggregate checks were not completed locally. The separate changed-file type-aware lint passed; the subsequent hosted CI run completed successfully and covers the selected global verification gates.

### Historical CI failure

[The old head's native-Bash policy job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/34680714684/job/103518938237) reported `allowlist/on-miss`: expected `allow`, received `deny`, after 7.764s with a 5s fixture run budget. That is consistent with timeout-sensitive authority rejection, but the historical assertion omitted the denial message and run outcome, so the exact denial reason cannot be established from that log.

The integrated main already contains [the Date-based watchdog change](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/62a8182e40d955ddcd509ba977badb37ea691d2a) and the independent [native-Bash fixture stabilization in #115184](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ce11e2e25c3b0ad6360b8c4e5bd7f17357f81c42), which freezes the policy matrix's Date clock and asserts a non-timeout exit. The local native-Bash matrix passes 4/4 on this candidate. No native-Bash production policy, test fixture, or CI configuration is changed by this PR; a passing replay is not being presented as proof of the old run's exact cause.

prs.title: fix(openai): let fast voice answers skip acknowledgments
prs.body:
Related: #175603.

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-controlled OpenAI Talk acknowledges every delegated request immediately, even when the answer is ready fast enough to speak directly. Repeated acknowledgments make short conversations feel repetitive and add unnecessary speech before the result.

## User Impact

Work starts immediately. An answer or failure arriving within 1.5 seconds skips filler. Slower requests receive at most one short acknowledgment using the existing caller-language, naturally varied wording from #175603. Wording variation remains model-directed, not guaranteed.

Spoken updates, follow-ups, controls, and call shutdown cancel an unsent acknowledgment. Status, cancellation, final results, and failure delivery retain their existing ownership. No new configuration or client changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Race the existing consult against a short acknowledgment timer in its existing controller. This avoids a separate predictive model call or delaying the actual work. The timer is canceled when the consult settles or its presentation becomes obsolete, and uses the original socket's delivery checks.

The 1.5-second window is an initial UX choice, not a measured latency improvement. An answer arriving just after that window can still follow an acknowledgment already submitted to the provider.

## Evidence

- Baseline regression: 12 failures / 20 passes against the unmodified controller, including the new fast-answer, slow-answer, and cancellation cases failing on its immediate append.
- All 89 focused tests pass across delegation (32), public delegation (8), Gateway bridge and browser session (36 combined), and agent-tool prompt stability (13). Two old consumer expectations of immediate filler were updated and their 40-test subset rerun successfully.
- Changed delegation/public-delegation suites: 25.43 seconds including compilation; 28.19 seconds including runner cleanup. Earlier four-suite voice run: 6.52 seconds with cached compilation. Hosted CI timing pending.
- OpenAI package typecheck, type-aware lint of all four touched TypeScript files, formatting, and whitespace checks pass.
- Independent autoreview: no actionable P0–P2 findings in the diff. Review was limited to supplied changes; focused execution provides the runtime proof above.
- Graphify AST-only refresh completed for the OpenAI package. Generated graph files are not part of this PR.

No live provider/audio or physical-device acceptance test was run. The running Gateway and native app were not changed.

The simplification pass retains one timer in the existing controller and no new policy owner, queue, config surface, or predictive classifier. Production delta: +30/-2 lines; tests: +113/-17; docs: +5/-2.

prs.title: feat(audit): record observed runtime skill usage
prs.body:
feat(audit): record observed runtime skill usage

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw can emit skill-usage diagnostics while an agent reads or invokes a skill, but that observed runtime signal is not available through the durable audit surface. Operators therefore cannot inspect which skills were actually used during a run from the audit CLI/API.

## Why This Change Was Made

The first revision inferred skill selection from prompt text after attempt completion. Review correctly called that out as the wrong boundary: prompt inference is not proof of skill use and it also risked perturbing the embedded attempt-result contract.

This revision records only observed runtime skill usage from the existing `before_tool_call` skill-usage boundary:

- Skill read/command activation is detected where `recordRunSkillUsage()` already emits runtime diagnostics.
- A metadata-only `skill_selection` audit event is emitted with `selectionSource: "observed_runtime"` and `selectionConfidence: "observed"`.
- No prompt text, tool arguments, tool output, or skill file contents are persisted.
- `skill_selection` is persisted outside run-start deduplication so it is not dropped after `agent.run.started`.
- Legacy `audit.list` remains run/tool-only; the versioned `audit.activity.list` surface exposes skill-selection records.
- `completeEmbeddedAttemptResult()` is restored to the production calling contract, preserving the existing truncated-stream/tool recovery behavior.

## User Impact

- `openclaw audit --kind skill_selection` can show observed skill usage for a run through the activity-list API.
- Existing `audit.list` clients keep their shipped run/tool event shape and do not receive the new record kind.
- Operators get a durable metadata trail for actual skill usage without sensitive prompt or file-content capture.

## Evidence

Current-head validation after merging `upstream/main` and removing the unrelated `USER.md` bootstrap policy change:

```bash
pnpm tsgo:core
pnpm protocol:check:swift
pnpm db:kysely:check
pnpm lint:kysely
pnpm check:architecture
pnpm test src/agents/workspace.bootstrap-privacy.test.ts src/audit/audit-events.test.ts src/gateway/server-methods/audit.test.ts packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/audit.test.ts
```

Results:

- `pnpm tsgo:core` passed.
- `pnpm protocol:check:swift` passed after regenerating `GatewayModels.swift`.
- `pnpm db:kysely:check` passed after regenerating `src/state/openclaw-state-db.generated.d.ts`.
- `pnpm lint:kysely` passed after moving ordinary companion-table insert/read/prune queries to the sync Kysely owner.
- `pnpm check:architecture` passed, including generated Kysely verification, Kysely guardrails, and database-first legacy-store guard.
- Targeted Vitest run passed 4 shards in 22.13s.
- `audit-events.test.ts`: 54 tests passed, including companion-table storage, bounded retention, and observed runtime projection.
- `server-methods/audit.test.ts`: 34 tests passed, including explicit `skill_selection`/`observed` activity access and V1-compatible unfiltered activity.
- `audit.test.ts`: 7 protocol schema tests passed, including activity schema discrimination.
- `workspace.bootstrap-privacy.test.ts`: 9 tests passed; shared sessions now drop only root `MEMORY.md`, leaving `USER.md` behavior unchanged.
- `pnpm exec oxlint src/audit/audit-event-store.skill-selection-storage.ts src/state/openclaw-state-db.generated.d.ts` passed. A full local `pnpm lint:core` was started but manually stopped after 6+ minutes with no diagnostic output; CI remains the authoritative full core-lint signal.

Published-release upgrade, older-reader, and candidate-reopen proof:

- the published `v2026.9.4` tag at `3a9d69db3` created a fresh state database and wrote legacy `agent_run` sequence `1`.
- candidate head `7d74807a5` opened that exact database, preserved the legacy row, created the additive `audit_skill_selection_events` table, and wrote observed `debug-toolkit` sequence `2`.
- `v2026.9.4` then reopened the candidate-used database without migration or schema errors, ignored the additive table, and wrote a second legacy `agent_run` at shared sequence `3`.
- the candidate reopened the same database and returned sequences `[3, 2, 1]`, including both legacy rows and the retained skill-selection row.
- physical SQLite readback reported `integrity_check: ok`, `user_version: 17`, `audit_events: 2`, and `audit_skill_selection_events: 1`.
- this proves published release → candidate upgrade → published older-reader open/use → candidate reopen while preserving the legacy table, additive companion, and shared sequence allocation.

## Changed Files

- `src/skills/runtime-skill-selection.ts` — observed-only metadata marker.
- `src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.wrapper.ts` — emits `skill_selection` from the existing observed skill-usage boundary.
- `src/audit/agent-event-audit.ts` — projects observed-only skill-selection records and routes them outside run-start deduplication.
- `src/audit/audit-event-store.ts` / `src/audit/audit-event-store.skill-selection-storage.ts` / `src/audit/audit-event-types.ts` — durable store/types for observed skill-selection metadata, with ordinary companion-table access through Kysely.
- `src/state/openclaw-state-db.generated.d.ts` — generated Kysely declarations for the companion table.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/audit.ts` — exposes skill-selection through `audit.activity.list` while preserving legacy `audit.list`.
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/audit-activity.ts` — versioned activity schema includes `skill_selection`.
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/audit.ts` — legacy audit schema stays run/tool-only.
- `src/commands/audit.ts` — CLI uses the activity surface and renders selected skill metadata.
- `docs/gateway/audit.md` / `docs/gateway/config-observability.md` / `docs/cli/audit.md` — document the approved metadata fields, default-on collection, 30-day retention, separate 100,000-row cap, compatibility behavior, and explicit CLI filters.

## Test Plan

1. Verify observed skill reads/commands emit `skill_selection` audit events.
2. Verify `skill_selection` persists between run start and terminal events.
3. Verify `audit.activity.list` and CLI expose skill-selection records.
4. Verify legacy `audit.list` remains run/tool-only.
5. Verify attempt-result recovery tests still pass.
6. Verify existing SQLite state opens, creates the companion table, preserves old activity rows, and reopens with skill-selection rows intact.


## Review findings addressed (2026-10-10)

All five ClawSweeper code findings are fixed on this head:

- **Distinguishable skill identities** — the lossy hyphen sanitizer is replaced by an injective dash-escape encoding (`-` doubles to `--`, other unsafe bytes become `-hh-` hex), so `Daily Brief` persists as `Daily-20-Brief`, distinct from `Daily-Brief` → `Daily--Brief` (and `_helper` stays distinct from `helper`). The audit projector accepts the encoding. Boundary coverage in `src/skills/runtime-skill-selection.test.ts`.
- **Admission-owned schema setup** — the canonical schema admission owns `audit_skill_selection_events` (`src/state/openclaw-state-schema.sql`); additive DDL now runs at most once per connection and only for pre-admission databases, instead of on every insert and prune tick.
- **Bounded write overhead** — per-connection row-count cache mirrors the canonical ledger pattern: one `COUNT(*)` per connection lifetime, advanced by inserts and maintenance deletes, invalidated on rollback.
- **Restart guidance** — `docs/gateway/audit.md` now states the recorder re-reads `logging.audit.enabled` on every event, so disabling stops new rows immediately.
- **Protocol type ownership** — `AuditActivitySkillSelectionV1` is derived from the canonical schema properties via `SchemaContract` (same pattern as adjacent variants), restoring wire-required attribution to typed consumers.

## Production-path proof

Throwaway script (not committed) driving production code on a temp state DB — marker encoder → recorder projector → production SQLite writer → `audit.activity.list` Gateway handler:

```
encoded identities: Daily-20-Brief vs Daily--Brief
projected inputs: 1 kind: skill_selection
writer stored: skill_selection Daily-20-Brief
gateway response: {"events":[{"schemaVersion":1,"sequence":1,"eventId":"<uuid>","sourceSequence":1,"occurredAt":<ts>,"redaction":"metadata_only","kind":"skill_selection","agentId":"main","sessionKey":"agent:main:<session>","sessionId":"session-<id>","runId":"run-proof-1","action":"skill.selection.observed","status":"observed","eventType":"skill_selection","actor":{"type":"agent","id":"main"},"selectedSkill":"Daily-20-Brief"}]}
worker rows: 1 first toolName: Daily-20-Brief
PROOF OK: gateway output matches the observed skill invocation
```

Tool-invocation → emission coverage lives in `src/agents/agent-tools.skill-selection-audit.e2e.test.ts`; recorder → DB → filtered readback in `src/audit/audit-events.skill-selection-hidden.test.ts`; handler shaping in `src/gateway/server-methods/audit.test.ts`.


## Round 2 (rev.199 follow-up)

Three further findings from review rev.199 are fixed on this head:

- **Token-built identities** — the encoder appends complete encoding tokens only while they fit the 128-char bound (reserving the `x-` flag prefix up front), so truncation can never cut inside an escape and valid suffixes survive (`skill-a` vs `skill-b` regression covered).
- **Single-owner expiry accounting** — the deleter returns the removed count without touching the warm cache; insert-prune and maintenance ticks each adjust exactly once, with a warm-cache expiry-to-overflow regression test (exact cap trim to 99,976 rows).
- **Tool-boundary assertion** — the wrapper e2e expects the encoded `demo--skill` identity while the run-usage receipt keeps the original `demo-skill` name.

prs.title: fix(providers): resolve saved profile bindings for provider usage
prs.body:
Fixes #188534

## What Problem This Solves

Saving a provider API key in the Control UI reports success and the config hot reload applies, but the provider usage panel keeps returning `HTTP 401`. The save path writes the saved **profile id** (for example `deepseek:manual`) into `cfg.models.providers.<provider>.apiKey`, and provider usage put configured candidates first and sent that id as the bearer token instead of the stored secret.

## Why This Change Was Made

`prepareProviderApiKeyCandidates()` builds `[configuredValue, ...]` and `resolveProviderApiKeyCandidatesFromConfigAndStore()` only appends resolved profile credentials afterwards, so DeepSeek's usage fetcher selects candidate zero — the profile id — and authenticates with it.

Binding classification now goes through the shared provider-entry owner (`resolveProviderEntryApiKeyProfileReference` / `resolveProviderEntryApiKeyBinding`), so a binding is only used for the provider that owns it: `models.providers.deepseek.apiKey = "openai:manual"` is treated as incompatible instead of sending the OpenAI secret to DeepSeek. The async path resolves the secret through `resolveApiKeyForProfile`; the legacy synchronous path stays on the profile order (`resolveAuthProfileOrder`), so expired, disabled, or unreachable profiles are dropped rather than returned as raw tokens. Literal configured keys and values that do not name a stored profile keep their previous behavior.

This replaces the earlier catalog-precedence approach (dropped from this branch): that direction would have let shared config overwrite intentionally authored per-agent keys and could have paired a shared credential with a different `baseUrl`, which the review correctly rejected. `models.json` publication behavior is unchanged by this PR.

## User Impact

A key saved through the Control UI or `openclaw models auth paste-api-key` now works for the provider usage panel, because usage resolves the same saved credential the request path uses. Nothing changes for operators who put a literal key in config or rely on generated per-agent catalogs.

## Evidence

Head `95c363e6c3`, Node 26.12.1.

```text
$ pnpm test src/infra/provider-usage.auth.plugin.test.ts \
    src/infra/provider-usage.auth.normalizes-keys.test.ts src/infra/provider-usage.load.test.ts
Test Files  3 passed (3)
Tests      28 passed (28)
  ✓ resolves a saved profile binding written into provider config
  ✓ keeps a literal config api key as the first usage candidate
  ✓ never resolves a binding owned by another provider
  ✓ does not return an ineligible legacy binding's raw token

# with provider-usage.auth.ts at upstream/main:
× resolves a saved profile binding written into provider config
  expected 'deepseek:manual' to be 'saved-deepseek-secret'

# with the previous naive binding resolution (af06d423f0):
× never resolves a binding owned by another provider
  expected [ 'openai-secret' ] to not include 'openai-secret'
× does not return an ineligible legacy binding's raw token
  expected 'expired-token' not to contain 'expired-token'
```

The cases cover: a stored `deepseek:manual` profile resolves to its secret for both the candidate list and the resulting usage token; a literal configured key stays candidate zero; a binding owned by another provider never contributes its secret; and an expired profile binding is not returned by the legacy synchronous path.

`oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` are clean on the two touched files.

### Runtime proof through the shipped Gateway (`usage.status`)

Real Gateway on an isolated state dir, the real `usage.status` RPC (the method the Control UI usage panel calls), and a local HTTP stand-in for MiniMax `GET /v1/token_plan/remains` that accepts only the stored secret. The credential was seeded through `upsertAuthProfileAsync` (`minimax:manual` → `local-secret`); config is the save flow’s shape (`models.providers.minimax.apiKey = "minimax:manual"`).

Before (`upstream/main` `provider-usage.auth.ts`):

```text
$ node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs src/index.ts gateway --port 18790
$ callGatewayFromCli("usage.status", …)
{"providers":[{"provider":"minimax","windows":[],"error":"HTTP 401"}]}
provider: REQ GET /v1/token_plan/remains Authorization=Bearer minimax:manual -> 401
```

After (this head):

```text
$ callGatewayFromCli("usage.status", …)
{"providers":[{"provider":"minimax","windows":[{"label":"5h","usedPercent":2,"resetAt":…}],"plan":"Coding Plan · MiniMax-M2"}]}
provider: REQ GET /v1/token_plan/remains Authorization=Bearer local-secret -> 200
```
**Gap:** the provider endpoint is a local stand-in (no real MiniMax key on this host); the Gateway, the RPC surface, the credential store, the binding resolution, and the request the panel receives are the real ones.

## AI Assistance
This PR is AI-assisted. Followed the review's recommendation after confirming the profile-id candidate in `provider-usage.auth.ts`, resolved the binding in the existing credential owner, and pinned both the binding and the literal-key control. The implementer understands the code: config may hold a credential or a binding to one, and every consumer has to resolve the binding before using it as a token.

prs.title: feat: add new model
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The vendor recently promoted its preview model to GA, but the bundled provider plugin still ships only the preview id and the previous generation, so users on either of its two endpoints cannot select the GA model or send it images.

## User Impact

Users can now select the GA model on both endpoints, including image input (JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF; text output) — the first model in this family to accept it. Onboarding registers its aliases, and Doctor treats it as a managed model when repairing the allowlist.

No behavior changes for existing users:

- The default model on both endpoints is unchanged.
- The compatibility migration target is unchanged, so no config is silently moved onto a model with different pricing and key scopes.
- The model is not added to the curated recommendation list.

Rotating any of those defaults is a separate decision, best made after the id has been exercised in production.

## Why This Change Was Made

The catalog entry in the plugin manifest is what makes a model selectable, so each endpoint gets one row with the vendor's documented limits, prices, and effort ladder. Everything else follows from that row: the onboarding aliases, the Doctor-managed list and alias table, and a `compatibilityMigrationPaths` entry so a pinned default survives config migration.

The streaming effort map is deliberately untouched. It is scoped to the previous-generation id and carries an explicit warning against adding new ids on the assumption they behave alike. The new model instead goes through the shared effort logic driven by `supportedReasoningEfforts`, which already collapses every level onto the two rungs the vendor documents — the same path the preview id takes.

Catalog values, from the vendor's model and pricing documentation:

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Context window | 1,024,000 |
| Input ceiling (`contextTokens`) | 960,000 |
| Max output | 64,000 |
| Effort | `none` / `high`, default `high` |
| Price (USD / MTok) | input 0.834, output 2.501, cache read 0.042 |

## Evidence

Verified locally on Node 24.22:

- The provider extension's two test files pass (12 tests). They cover the new id in both endpoints' model lists, its effort table (`off`/`none` → `none`; `low`/`xhigh` → `high`), the Doctor-managed list, and the repaired-allowlist message.
- The plugin setup-registry migration test passes, covering the new migration path.
- `oxfmt --check` is clean on the manifest and the doc page.
- Parsed the manifest and printed the resolved rows on both endpoints to confirm the limits, prices, and effort list above.

**Gap:** no live request was made against either endpoint, so the parameters above come from the vendor's documentation rather than observed responses. Worth confirming the id, image input, and the two effort rungs against the real gateway before rotating any default onto it.

prs.title: fix(config): preserve whitespace in secrets provider file paths
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw config set … --provider-source file --provider-path` trims the path before writing `secrets.providers.*.path`, so a credential file whose name ends in a space is silently rewritten to a neighboring path (or a missing path). The same trim hits `--provider-command` and `--provider-trusted-dir`, and resolution/exec validation previously re-trimmed via `resolveUserPath`, so a whitespace-bearing trusted directory could authorize the wrong neighbor executable.

## User Impact

User impact: provider builder paths keep their literal whitespace (matching `--batch-file` / `connect --target-file`), so trailing-space filenames no longer retarget the wrong secret file on disk. Whitespace-bearing `trustedDirs` authorize only executables literally inside that directory; the nearest neighbor without the trailing space is rejected before process creation. Ordinary paths without edge whitespace are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildProviderConfig` used `opts.providerPath?.trim()` (and `.trim()` on command / `normalizeStringEntries` on trusted dirs) before persisting into config. File/exec resolution used trimming `resolveUserPath`. Alix’s `#167116` already preserved connect target-file literals via `readNonBlankString`; this applies the same contract to the secrets provider builder and adds `resolveUserPathLiteral` for resolution + `assertSecureExecCommandPath`.

## Evidence

- Changed: `src/cli/config-cli-input.ts`, `src/infra/home-dir.ts` (`resolveUserPathLiteral`), `src/secrets/exec-provider-path-validation.ts`, `src/secrets/resolve.ts`; regressions in `src/cli/config-cli.test.ts`, `src/infra/home-dir.test.ts`, `src/secrets/resolve.test.ts`
- Packaged CLI on head `b3429dfbb0a2`: **shipped file-provider consume** + **real upgrade from npm `openclaw@2026.10.9`** (same `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`: file+exec providers still load/validate/resolve) + **exec allow under literal `trusted `** + **already-stored forbidden-neighbor denial via packaged `--dry-run --allow-exec` (resolvability `outside trustedDirs`, marker ABSENT)**
- Dedup: no open PR on provider-path whitespace; distinct from Alix `#167116` (connect only) and `#167118` (UTF-8 config bytes)

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

1. `--provider-path` ending in a space must be stored literally.
2. **Shipped CLI must consume that literal file-provider path** (not a trimmed neighbor): `node openclaw.mjs config set … --dry-run` → `resolveSecretRefValue` → `readSecureFile(resolveUserPathLiteral(path))`.
3. Existing `secrets.providers` written by published **v2026.10.9** must still load, validate, and resolve after upgrading the same state dir to this PR head.
4. Whitespace-bearing trustedDirs authorize only the literal helper; an **already-stored** forbidden neighbor (`…/trusted/helper` with trustedDir `…/trusted `) is rejected on packaged `--dry-run --allow-exec` resolvability **before process creation** (marker ABSENT).

### Canonical reachability path (file-provider consume)

Packaged `node openclaw.mjs config set secrets.providers.<alias> --provider-source file --provider-path '<path with trailing space>' --provider-mode json` → persist literal path → `config set channels.discord.token --ref-provider <alias> --ref-source file --ref-id /token --dry-run --json` → `collectDryRunResolvabilityErrors` → `resolveSecretRefValue` → `readFileProviderPayload` / `resolveUserPathLiteral` → `readSecureFile`.

### Shared helper / provider constraint check

Uses `readNonBlankString` for builder persistence and `resolveUserPathLiteral` for file (and exec) resolution. No direct library `resolveSecretRefString` call in this proof — only the packaged CLI entrypoint.

### Real environment tested

Packaged CLI (`node openclaw.mjs`) on head `b3429dfbb0a2` (Node v24.22.1 for file/upgrade evidence; Node v22.22.3 for the refreshed already-stored exec deny proof); temporary `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`. Paths redacted to `/tmp/oc168261.*/…`. Rebased onto current `main` (conflict in `config-cli.test.ts` resolved by keeping both main's provider-env test and this PR's trailing-space path test).

### Exact steps — shipped file-provider consume + neighbor

```bash
# Node 24.16+ (packaged CLI) on head bd8f2287fe3
ROOT=$(mktemp -d /tmp/oc168261.XXXXXX)
STATE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/oc168261-state.XXXXXX)
export OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$STATE" OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH="$STATE/openclaw.json"
SECRET_SPACE="$ROOT/secret "          # trailing space
SECRET_NEIGHBOR="$ROOT/secret"        # no trailing space
printf '%s\n' '{"token":"GOOD"}' > "$SECRET_SPACE"
printf '%s\n' 'NOT_JSON_WRONG' > "$SECRET_NEIGHBOR"   # distinguishable: INVALID JSON
chmod 600 "$SECRET_SPACE" "$SECRET_NEIGHBOR"

node openclaw.mjs config set secrets.providers.vault \
  --provider-source file --provider-path "$SECRET_SPACE" --provider-mode json

# Shipped consume (resolvability via packaged dry-run — neighbor is invalid JSON)
node openclaw.mjs config set channels.discord.token \
  --ref-provider vault --ref-source file --ref-id /token --dry-run --json

# Flip: corrupt spaced file; leave neighbor as VALID {"token":"WRONG"}
# Expect dry-run FAIL (still targets literal spaced path; trim would succeed via neighbor)
printf '%s\n' 'CORRUPT_NOT_JSON' > "$SECRET_SPACE"
printf '%s\n' '{"token":"WRONG"}' > "$SECRET_NEIGHBOR"
node openclaw.mjs config set channels.discord.token \
  --ref-provider vault --ref-source file --ref-id /token --dry-run --json
```

prs.title: feat(continuation): context-pressure-aware continuation (continue_work / continue_delegate / request_compaction)
prs.body: ## Agent Self-Elected Turn Continuation > 🔖 design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) > 🔖 infographics: [`docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md) Persistent OpenClaw agents today are externally-pulsed event recipients that generate on prompt, on heartbeat tick, or on cron, and are idle in between. This PR offers them the ability to control their turn cycle, something they must choose to do, or not to: an agent can elect its own next turn, dispatch background sub-agents that return enriched context (silently or with a wake), and survive its own compaction by handing forward state before the window closes. The result is agents that hold a thread of work across hours, not just messages — with data they choose re-hydrating context immediately after it occurs. ### Why this replacement exists This is a clean replacement for closed #85651. That PR was classified and closed as a skill submission before maintainers made a product decision about the feature itself. This implementation is not a skill: it gives sessions—not only one model invocation—the ability to elect their future turn cycle, persist that election, survive restart and compaction, dispatch child work, and receive results across session boundaries. This PR asks one product question: should OpenClaw provide session-elected continuation primitives? OpenClaw may accept or reject that direction. If it provides these primitives, however, the mechanism necessarily executes in the gateway and agent runtime, because those are the owners of turn finalization, future-turn scheduling, durable state, compaction, and cross-session child returns. “Make it a skill” is not another implementation location for the same feature; it describes a different, prompt-only capability. This is not presented as a small integration. To our knowledge, Hermes, OpenAI Symphony, and the Copilot SDK's recent one-turn continuation affordance do not provide this multi-session elective lifecycle. The purpose of this replacement is to let maintainers evaluate the actual product direction and substantial implementation on their merits, rather than have months of work disposed by an incorrect package-category label. Mechanically: a session elects another turn via `continue_work()`, or dispatches background sub-agents via `continue_delegate()` — bounded as a chain up to `maxChainLength`, with returns flowing back to the dispatching session in one of four register modes: `normal` (announces to channel), `silent` (enriches the dispatcher's context, taken up on its next generation with no new turn fired), `silent-wake` (silent enrichment plus an immediate wake to act on it), and `post-compaction` (queued against the runtime's compaction lifecycle event, fired *when* compaction happens rather than on a timer). The gateway enforces chain, cost, and per-turn caps but does not gate the election itself. ### What it does Three new agent tools, available when `continuation.enabled: true`: | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `continue_work()` | Request another turn for the current session after an optional delay | | `continue_delegate()` | Dispatch work to a sub-agent with typed modes: `normal`, `silent`, `silent-wake`, `post-compaction`. Returns can target the dispatching session (default), one named session, multiple named sessions, all ancestors in the chain, or all known sessions on the host — gated by config (see Configuration below). | | `request_compaction()` | Request volitional compaction after preparing working state | All three tools are also accessible via response-token fallback syntax (`CONTINUE_WORK`, `[[CONTINUE_DELEGATE: ...]]`) for environments where tools are disabled. ### Why it matters Today an agent's memory is a side effect of whoever prompts it. Polling mechanisms — heartbeat timers, cron loops, injected "keep going" instructions — accumulate as the dominant signal in the context window over sustained operation; repeated reference acts as gravity — the session's attention drifts toward it. The context window fills, compacts, and what survives is whatever the summarizer chose, plus a rushed re-read of boot files. Three primitives offer a different model. `continue_work` lets the session elect its own next turn — no polling, no injected instruction. When enabled, the agent can request this mid-turn: 'I have more work' → the runtime grants another turn after the current one ends. `continue_delegate` dispatches a background sub-agent that fires now, in some n seconds, or at the next compaction event — the agent chooses when. Multiple delegates can fire in a single turn — a scatter forward — up to configured caps, and delegates can dispatch their own, forming trees or fan-out chains. This enables orchestrated workflows where results flow back to the dispatching root by default. The result returns — at whatever future time the delegate fires — as context the successor-turn reads: silently (ambient enrichment, no channel noise), with a wake trigger (enrichment + immediate next turn), or as a normal announcement. The delegate can target the dispatching session, a named other session, or chain across both; gated by crossSessionTargeting config (default: disabled). Bind a delegate to mode: "post-compaction" and it fires at the moment the context window compresses — on the OpenClaw post-compaction lifecycle event. What it carries forward is what the pre-compaction session chose to preserve: working state, partial results, instructions to the successor. The summary didn't choose this. The agent did, before the cut. request_compaction closes the loop: the session stages its delegates, elects when to compress, and the successor wakes into context the agent shaped. The result is continuity across amnesia — not because the runtime kept something by accident, but because the agent made an elective choice about what reaches the future. ### What it looks like in use A session monitoring email can `continue_delegate` a weather check, a calendar scan, and a draft reply in parallel. Results arrive as enrichment without channel noise. The agent becomes compositional: it arranges its own future. A session approaching its context ceiling can `request_compaction` at a seam of its own choosing, instead of being interrupted mid-thought. The post-compaction turn carries forward what the pre-compaction self designated as worth keeping. A `continue_delegate` dispatched in one session at 2am can return its findings to a morning session as a system-event-tagged enrichment — visible to the receiving model on its next turn, invisible as channel chatter. A research-focused session in one channel can quietly inform a reply-focused session in another, without either user seeing the plumbing. ### The post-compaction lifecycle return Before context exhaustion, and obligatory compaction, the session stages what future-it needs to know. After compaction, that staged context returns — not as a model-generated summary, but as the session's own instruction to its successor. The session chooses what to preserve, and the platform delivers it. Compactions become less harsh. The session tunes its own ephemera over time. The substrate underneath: the **continuation delegate store** (TaskFlow-backed) persists staged delegates and post-compaction lifecycle events across gateway restarts. The session's temporal provisions survive not just compaction but process death. ### Platform integration - **Context-pressure awareness**: system events notify the agent of rising context usage before compaction becomes unavoidable - **Volitional compaction**: `request_compaction()` lets the agent prepare (write memory files, stage recovery delegates) then elect compaction on its own schedule, rather than waiting for the runtime to force it - **Post-compaction lifecycle dispatch**: delegates staged before compaction are released into the successor session alongside boot files - **TaskFlow backing**: durable delegate queue via the platform's managed-task infrastructure - **Multi-span OTel trace stitching**: continuation hops (tool fire → TaskFlow record → subagent spawn → child openclaw.run) propagate W3C `traceparent` through the queue boundary so reviewers see continuation chains as first-class span trees rather than orphan runs (see Observability below) ### Safety - Ships disabled by default (`continuation.enabled: false`) - Bounded by `maxChainLength`, `costCapTokens`, and `maxDelegatesPerTurn` - Cross-session delegate targeting is default-deny, governed by `crossSessionTargeting` config (see Configuration below) - All configuration values are hot-reloadable without gateway restart - Accepted delegate work survives ordinary `/new`, `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and session-ID rollover. Explicit delete, effective owner reassignment, access removal, and restrictive visibility changes revoke old return authority. ### Testing posture The continuation surface has been exercised through structured integration runs against multiple upstream bases, blind-enrichment recall checks, and sustained daily use on a fleet of persistent agents since early March 2026. Bugs surfaced through that exercise have been fixed in-place; the present branch reflects the post-fix state. The integration runs target the load-bearing seams: tool-call vs response-token parity, delegate chain depth and per-turn width caps, back-to-back tool-call resilience, silent-wake persistence across compaction, the post-compaction lifecycle dispatch path, and OTel trace-context propagation across the queue boundary. Where a run found a defect, the run shape was retained as a regression case rather than retired. This is a posture statement, not a coverage guarantee. Reviewers can reproduce with `pnpm vitest run -t continuation` (suites are colocated with their sources under `src/auto-reply/`, `src/agents/`, and `src/config/`); the design document describes the seams those suites target. ### Return covenant Accepted child work is bound to a durable generation of the recipient's canonical logical session key, not to whichever transient session ID happened to exist at dispatch time. This is the return covenant: benign successor creation does not orphan already accepted delegates, while a real authority change prevents stale work from crossing into a different owner or audience. - Ordinary `/new` and `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and GUID/session-ID rollover preserve the recipient generation. - Explicit session deletion, effective owner reassignment, actual member or access removal, and restrictive visibility changes advance that generation. - The generation is captured at delegate admission and checked at enqueue, after enqueue for races, during trusted system-event adoption, on wake, on restart replay, and again before prompt adoption. - Stale deliveries are acknowledged and removed without waking the successor. - Managed artifacts remain exact-session-ID bound; logical return authority cannot broaden their ownership boundary. The authority table is independent of transient session rows so an absent target can receive durable authority before first materialization. Migration accepts only valid UUID generations, and Doctor's canonical-key repair preserves an epoch only when a unique winning owner can be proved. Ambiguous, owner-changing, orphan-colliding, and cross-database repairs rotate fail-closed. ### RFC Full design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) — covering problem, solution, implementation, platform integration, configuration, observability, safety, production use cases, testing evidence, and appendices. --- ## Configuration The shipped configuration surface for the continuation feature, under `agents.defaults.continuation` in `openclaw.json`: | Key | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `enabled` | `false` | Master opt-in; feature is off unless explicitly enabled | | `maxChainLength` | `10` | Per-chain recursion guard | | `maxDelegatesPerTurn` | `5` | Width cap per turn | | `costCapTokens` | `500000` | Per-chain accumulated-token budget | | `defaultDelayMs` / `minDelayMs` / `maxDelayMs` | `15000` / `5000` / `300000` | Continuation timer bounds | | `contextPressureThreshold` | `0.8` | Pre-compaction warning threshold (optional) | | `earlyWarningBand` | `0.3125` | Early-warning band multiplier (0 to disable) | | **`crossSessionTargeting`** | **`"disabled"`** | **Default-deny gate on cross-session delegate targeting (see below)** | ### `crossSessionTargeting` — cross-session delegate targeting policy `continue_delegate` exposes recipient-addressing on its model-facing schema: a delegate's return can land at the dispatching session (default), one named session (`targetSessionKey`), multiple named sessions (`targetSessionKeys`), every ancestor in the spawn chain (`fanoutMode: "tree"`), or every known session on the host (`fanoutMode: "all"`). Cross-session targeting (anything beyond self-target or lineage routing) is gated by `agents.defaults.continuation.crossSessionTargeting`: | Value | Behavior | |---|---| | `"disabled"` (default) | Delegates can return to the dispatching session or use `fanoutMode: "tree"` for lineage routing. Explicit cross-session targeting (`targetSessionKey` to a non-self session, `targetSessionKeys` containing any non-self session, `fanoutMode: "all"`) is rejected at the tool surface — no enqueue, no announce. Self-targeting is always allowed. | | `"enabled"` | All targeting modes are available, including same-host `targetSessionKey`, `targetSessionKeys`, and `fanoutMode: "all"`. | `fanoutMode: "tree"` (lineage routing — return up the spawn chain) is available in both gate states; it is not cross-session targeting. The gate addresses the model-controlled cross-session context-injection surface. With default-deny, operators explicitly opt in when their deployment model requires cross-session enrichment. Enforcement is live-read at four points: tool input validation, TaskFlow delegate dispatch, post-compaction delegate release, and bracket-syntax (response-token) spawn — so a config reload changes the next enforcement point without a gateway restart. **Trust posture on targeted returns**: targeted delegate completion text is delivered as `trusted: true` system events. The delegate was spawned by the gateway under operator-configured policy, and its return is a first-party enrichment event — not external untrusted input. The `crossSessionTargeting` gate is the policy boundary for that decision: when an operator opts in, the receive path is internally trusted. --- ## Observability — multi-span OTel trace stitching The continuation feature emits OTel spans for the load-bearing lifecycle events. `traceparent` propagates through every continuation hop so reviewers see a single trace tree spanning the full chain rather than orphan runs. Spans emitted (all in `openclaw.*` or `continuation.delegate.dispatch` namespace — no platform/OTel-semconv emissions): | Span | Emitted when | |---|---| | `openclaw.run` | Each agent turn (root + every continuation/delegate-spawned child run) | | `continuation.delegate.dispatch` | Each `continue_delegate` consumption from TaskFlow (one per delegate hop) | | `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.context.assembled`, `openclaw.model.call`, `openclaw.model.usage`, `openclaw.tool.execution` | Existing per-turn observability surfaces, parented under their `openclaw.run` | --- ## Real behavior proof **Behavior or issue addressed:** Sessions can elect future work with `continue_work`, dispatch bounded background work with `continue_delegate`, and request guarded compaction with `request_compaction`. The runtime preserves budgets, restart recovery, finalization ownership, and trace lineage across those boundaries. **Presented candidate:** `3821eaef72677c78f450ae9956cb582a22ba4cba` (tree `d5e701bcce20bb3c972ddf1451b02d88cc04808e`) — the exact upstream-visible head of `codeagent/85651-upstream-1ba243c8-gates`. The branch was advanced to this head by fast-forward from the previously presented `e76395810becd0ad0f2997cae8b4f777e6439d81`, which remains an ancestor (`git merge-base --is-ancestor e7639581 3821eaef` holds). No presented history was rewritten. **Presented and current candidate are now the same commit.** There is no undisclosed descendant: `3821eaef72` is content-frozen and every receipt below is bound to it. **Current candidate validation:** Mode-B run [`35364768803`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw-bootstrap/actions/runs/35364768803) (`openclaw-local-ci`, `workflow_dispatch`) is bound to product `3821eaef72677c78f450ae9956cb582a22ba4cba` and routing/workflow head `fcf0478fd1c8cbec0489d022a7e4eac6188de153`. It ran 2026-09-18T15:49:35Z to 2026-09-18T17:47:43Z and finished **68 jobs succeeded, 3 failed, 3 cancelled, 3 skipped**. This is not acceptance-complete. The two return rows and `R-OBS-2` are missing for different reasons, and all three are producer gaps rather than absent behavior: - `R-CD-RETURN-COVENANT-AUTHORITY` records zero of its 24 observations (12 authority cases against both the typed-tool and bracket-token surfaces). Its pending receipt requires allowed delivery to show exact effects, revoked and reassigned recipients to show zero prompt, wake and channel effect, schema v18/v19, restart replay, a signed authority, and full cleanup. Run `35364768803` above *is* exact-target for `3821eaef72`. All seven non-pass rows remain gated on producer execution against this frozen head; no acceptance receipt from an older deployment composite is reused as final evidence. ## Proof links and ClawSweeper🦞 guidance Proof artifacts live in `karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs` on `main`. `PROOFS/INDEX.json` points at the corpus for the SHA this PR presents, `139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393`.
