prs.title: feat(prometheus): expose provider usage windows
prs.body:
Closes #139188

## What Problem This Solves

Operators can monitor OpenClaw request and tool behavior through the authenticated Prometheus exporter, but cannot monitor provider subscription allowance windows or refresh health without maintaining a separate Gateway RPC collector.

## Why This Change Was Made

This extends the existing provider-usage cache with a sanitized, selection-bound metrics snapshot and gives only the official Prometheus exporter a lifecycle-scoped observer capability. The cache owns periodic refreshes and last-good retention; Prometheus scrapes remain synchronous, render-only, and network-free.

Credential-backed provider polling is explicit opt-in through `providerUsage.enabled`, which defaults to `false`. The selection contract follows the same default/legacy-agent credential selection as unscoped `usage.status`. Selection changes withdraw prior allowance series until the new selection produces an observation. Exported labels are bounded to provider, window, and refresh outcome; account emails, profile IDs, credential fingerprints, prompts, responses, and other identifiers are excluded.

## User Impact

When operators explicitly enable provider-usage polling, they can graph and alert on:

- provider allowance used ratios;
- allowance-window reset timestamps;
- last refresh attempt and success timestamps;
- refresh success and bounded failure outcomes.

Upgrades and fresh installs do not begin credential-backed provider polling unless `providerUsage.enabled` is explicitly set to `true`. No provider API call is triggered by a Prometheus scrape.

## Review Fixes

- Makes provider-usage polling explicit opt-in and default-off for upgrades and fresh installations.
- Supports lifecycle-safe hot enable/disable without changing ordinary diagnostics or Prometheus metrics.
- Releases the observer and withdraws provider metrics when diagnostics are disabled, and reacquires exactly once when re-enabled.
- Rejects callbacks from retired exporter generations and revoked service leases.
- Cancels future provider refresh scheduling after observer release.
- Reads lifecycle-managed runtime configuration instead of ambient configuration.
- Preserves bounded Z.AI window identities so allowance and reset series cannot overwrite one another.
- Integrates the restricted observer with current plugin-service ownership, reload, rollback, cleanup, retirement, pending-owner, and current-claim lifecycle fencing.
- Preserves explicit runtime-config overrides in capable-client cache tests after the latest upstream rebase.
- Updates the generated plugin config baseline for the intentional two-entry surface increase (`4623` to `4625`).

## Evidence

The exact published head `5bcdf1a3d62bf82e2badcef3919a07eab3628295` passed both the isolated Portainer candidate validator and the published-release upgrade proof before the PR branch was updated.

### Candidate validation

- Validation ref: `validate/pr-141276-5bcdf1a3d6`
- Verified target: `5bcdf1a3d62bf82e2badcef3919a07eab3628295`
- Validation base: `3150853d9dee8ad161011682c130ea5731faa365`
- Merge base: `2f228582f354803021c3d217d3a2fd79b54b0305`
- Candidate runtime handoff SHA-256: `924213e6e6d7dae92d5f038666360275f31423173fa3e87363b0a11db1235dee`
- Runtime build cache: rebuilt

Passed gates: locked dependency installation; changed-file diff hygiene, formatting, line-cap ratchet, and type-aware lint; core, extension, owning test-graph, and extension-test types; plugin contracts; focused provider-usage tests; exact-SHA runtime build; isolated managed-install lifecycle proof including auth-suspended revocation; and the final temporary-ref identity fence.

Managed-install evidence recorded an authenticated scrape, one initial provider request after explicit enablement, provider metrics observed, and zero requests caused by scraping, disabled startup, hot-disable release, plugin revocation, or authority revocation during authentication. The restricted observer capability remained unavailable to a non-official plugin.

### Published-release upgrade compatibility

- Integrity-pinned baseline: `openclaw@2026.9.4` and `@openclaw/diagnostics-prometheus@2026.9.4`
- Baseline/default-off provider requests: `0` / `0` over 65-second observations
- Database schema migration: `19` to `27`
- Operator intent and runtime invariants preserved: `true`
- Diagnostics, provider-plugin, Gateway configuration, and managed exporter installation preserved: `true`
- Initial/scheduled requests after explicit opt-in: `1` / `1`
- Observed cadence: `59852 ms`
- Scrape-triggered requests: `0`
- Requests after exporter disable: `0`
- Candidate exporter tarball SHA-256: `7fcd9712b575c84b346b6a50834f31a4f7e77a91948ec524d847b87bfbe58587`
- Final temporary-ref identity fence: passed

### Current upstream conflict check

Canonical `main` was refreshed to `2f2c09d1c12d93408692e950a82d01fd04fa5af1` after validation. An isolated real merge completed with zero conflicts.
## Maintainer Gate Still Required

The compatibility concern is addressed by making credential-backed polling explicit opt-in. The security-sensitive capability boundary still requires authorized maintainer review and approval for the exact published head.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Slow chat startup identifies project-memory recall as the system-prompt bottleneck but cannot distinguish provider preparation, audience-publication waits, candidate retrieval, rendering, or cleanup.

## User Impact

Operators get bounded owner-stage timings in existing slow-chat diagnostics. Prompt text, memory filtering, live audience authority, and provider lifetime behavior are unchanged. This is attribution, not a claim that the intermittent production delay is fixed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add 24 production lines using the existing diagnostic observer. Native and legacy owners report fixed phase names without memory content or project identifiers. Native provider handles already lease a retained storage owner; retaining another handle would not remove its candidate work. Skipping the existing scan lacks an external-edit invalidation contract. No new cache, config option, schema, or async boundary.

Related: #191437, #191487.

## Evidence

- 81 focused tests passed: bootstrap selection and budgets, native audience revocation, native/legacy provider runtime, and prompt-prefix stability. Three attribution cases fail with the original bootstrap and pass with the patch; revoked audiences still return no recall.
- Codex autoreview: final staged candidate against c8518acbb276, P0–P2, scoped-clean with no actionable findings.
- Actual isolated Gateway chat.send with the real native Knowledge provider and 6,000 synthetic records across 200 projects: first project-memory recall 6,800.978 ms, candidates 6,793.673 ms, provider preparation 6.449 ms, rendering 0.182 ms. The next recall took 81.577 ms. Captured model input contains the expected project-memory section and synthetic fact; all four proof turns completed. This is unpaired source-mode corroboration, not a before/after speedup.
- Candidate execution includes native store resolution, worker startup/queue, scanning, validation, and provider-side shaping. These timings distinguish that work from host lookup/authority/rendering; they cannot yet distinguish an intermittent queued write from scan CPU.
- Completed real-native fixture: 6,000 records / 200 projects / 9.46 MB vault, real workers and host-minted audience. Five cold-reopen A/A pairs, five timing A/B pairs, five allocation A/B pairs and two allocation A/A pairs: 34 fresh processes / 1,554 preparations, all prompt SHA-256 digests identical. No 35 GiB database, btrfs, thousands of sessions or concurrent native writer; source-mode loader cost is not a packaged-deployment prediction.
- Before/after medians: cold recall 5,122.61 → 5,056.81 ms; warm 77.46 → 76.92 ms (p95 83.87 → 82.01 ms); warm process CPU 79.98 → 79.50 ms; main-thread CPU 1.104 → 1.145 ms. Cold pair 5 regressed 27.53%, retained explicitly; unchanged A/A cold swings ranged −39.27% to +34.53%, so no cold speedup or reproducible candidate regression is claimed.
- Separate sampled main-isolate allocation: 433,874 → 450,757 bytes/warm recall (+16,883 bytes, +3.89%). Unchanged allocation controls moved −1.87% / −1.41%; report the modest positive telemetry cost rather than calling it free. Worker allocations are not measured.

prs.title: fix(telegram): route bound conversations when agent selection is ambiguous
prs.body:
Closes #159334

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Telegram conversation with an active session binding fails with `AgentSelectionRequiredError` on a multi-agent install that has no channel-wide Telegram route, so its messages are never processed.

## User Impact

User impact: runtime-bound Telegram conversations reach their bound agent regardless of how many agents are configured. Conversations without a binding, or whose binding names no agent, keep today's behavior — including still requiring an explicit channel owner. A binding revoked or replaced while a message is being routed no longer leaves the former owner selected.

## Why This Change Was Made

`prepareTelegramConversationRoute` asked ordinary agent selection for a route before looking at the binding, and ordinary selection refuses an ambiguous roster. It now selects the base route inside the SDK's `resolveRuntimeConversationBindingRouteAsync({ resolveRoute })` (and `inspectRuntimeConversationBindingRoute({ inspection, resolveRoute })` for route-owner inspection): the binding owner's canonically classified `boundAgentId` arrives before ordinary selection, and when it is set the base route is derived from session-only config with that agent as the default. This is the shared binding-owner selection Slack, Discord and iMessage use, so Telegram no longer re-implements the session-key/metadata classification. Topic overrides, configured bindings, and the runtime-binding step that follows are unchanged.

### Binding changes during resolution (review follow-up)

An earlier revision chose the agent from a synchronous binding read and then let `resolveRuntimeConversationBindingRouteAsync` read the binding again after an `await`, so a binding revoked in between could leave the former owner selected; that revision guarded it with a re-prepare/retry loop.

Since merging current `main` (`4ee4606`), agent selection runs inside the `resolveRoute` callback of the single awaited inspection, so the agent and the binding facts come from the same read. There is no second read to diverge from, and the retry loop is gone. The same applies to `prepareTelegramConversationRouteInspection` (new on `main`), whose `resolve(inspection)` now selects the agent from the inspection it is handed. `inspectTelegramConversationRouteAsync` shares the inbound path with `touchBinding: false`.

## Evidence

New cases in `conversation-route-owner.test.ts`, all on a two-agent config with no route bindings:

- inbound `resolveTelegramConversationRoute` selects the bound agent and session, reports `runtime-bound`, and touches the binding once;
- `inspectTelegramConversationRouteAsync` selects the bound agent without touching liveness;
- a sentinel `global` session with `metadata.agentId` selects that agent;
- a binding that names no agent still rejects with `AGENT_SELECTION_REQUIRED`;
- a binding revoked just before the awaited inspection rejects with `AGENT_SELECTION_REQUIRED` instead of routing to the former owner;
- a binding replaced just before the awaited inspection routes to the new owner and its new binding.

Negative controls: with `main`'s `conversation-route.ts` (`4ee4606`), 4 of these 6 fail with `AGENT_SELECTION_REQUIRED` (the bound-agent, inspection, sentinel-metadata and replacement cases); the no-agent and revocation cases pass there, as intended, since both assert that rejection.

```text
$ pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/conversation-route-owner.test.ts
19 passed (19)
$ pnpm test extensions/telegram
passed 63 Vitest shards
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions && pnpm tsgo:extensions:test
0 errors
```

prs.title: feat: let node-hosted MCP tools ask questions through the Gateway
prs.body:
Stacked on #191387.

## What Problem This Solves

A node-hosted MCP tool could execute on the harness and return a result, but it had no way to ask the user for input during the call.

## User Impact

With `mcp.apps.enabled` on the Gateway and node, a tool can present a form or URL question in the Gateway’s question UI and continue with the answer. For same-node execution, the harness keeps the tool arguments, execution, and result local. The paired connection carries the question and answer.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway already knows which session authorized the tool. It binds that session to the tool grant and accepts questions only from the paired node while the grant is live. The same handler works when Gateway policy requires routing the tool through the Gateway. If overlapping calls on a shared MCP client make a prompt ambiguous, the client rejects the prompt.

## Evidence

- A controlled Streamable HTTP MCP server asked which workspace to use. The test answered through `question.resolve` and verified that the same-node worker received `engineering` in the tool result. The paired transport and answering user were simulated. The node sent exactly one `mcp.elicitation` event to the Gateway during the call.
- Focused tests cover requester identity, cancellation, revoked grants, overlapping callers, older peers, and the separate time budgets for tool execution and human input.
- The HTTP test used the SDK client and server. A separate stdio regression test could not start its server on this host. No live provider or browser was exercised. The local core typecheck reports the same six diagnostics as the parent branch with this installation’s cached dependencies.

prs.title: fix(ci): retain pending required security reviews
prs.body:
## Problem and repair

Required Security Review jobs share a head-specific concurrency group. GitHub's default single pending slot replaces an older pending job when another same-head event arrives, leaving a required event lane cancelled before it runs. Observed for [PR #189877](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/189877) and [PR #189909](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/189909); an earlier success or later `workflow_run` publisher does not satisfy the cancelled lane.

Set the review job's supported `queue: max` policy. Keep the same head group, serial execution, `cancel-in-progress: false`, resolver coalescing, event filters, permissions and current-head/authority/publication checks. Add the existing-style exact-path queue parser exception for pinned actionlint, plus the queue assertion in the existing workflow test.

Tooling/config: **+5 lines**; tests: **+5 lines**. The added queue policy preserves the required-review invariant. No runtime paths, fallback readers or alternate writers are introduced.

## Validation

- Original unchanged workflow owner: 38 Node cases passed.
- Complete workflow/event/enforcement suites: 314 passed under Node and 314 under Bun.
- Four queue/group/cancellation mutations each fail the existing workflow assertion under both runtimes.
- Parsed workflow/config equality proves only the intended queue and exact-path parser exception change.
- Canonical actionlint revision `011a6d15e749bb3f2d771eed9c7aa0e7e3e10ee7`, built offline from cached source: candidate passes; removing the exception fails; an unrelated invalid concurrency key still fails.
- Matching scripts test-type lane, type-aware lint, formatting and diff checks passed. Independent complete-context code review found no actionable P0–P2 defects.

Trusted qualified local proof was used after the remote backend was unavailable. GitHub's current [queue contract](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency) permits up to 100 pending jobs plus the running job. Overflow can still cancel jobs. Retaining pending work can increase checkout/API/status work; no cost-saving claim. Existing workflow execution proves queue syntax acceptance; natural-burst multiwaiter retention after landing remains a named operational follow-up.

## Required approval

**Independent SecOps approval is required before merge** by `.github/CODEOWNERS:1–3,17`. This PR's independent code review and maintainer authorship do not satisfy that owner approval. No admission waiver, manual rerun, alternate event lane or fabricated head is part of this change.

Release-note context: preserve required-review jobs during same-head event bursts.

prs.title: fix(sandbox): avoid Podman discovery before every command
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Podman sandbox commands repeatedly spawn engine discovery before executing on an already prepared sandbox, adding latency and main-thread process-launch work to every command.

## User Impact

Prepared shell commands and exec specifications reuse their validated Podman target and full container ID. Initial setup still rejects unsupported remote engines; Docker daemon checks and runtime authority checks remain unchanged. Engine loss is reported by the actual command.

Native local execution explicitly selects `--remote=false`. Finish active runs before changing engine mode in `containers.conf` or replacing the Podman executable. This does not add an engine identity cache or claim daemon attestation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Preparation already owns target admission. Execution now consumes that fact directly, including the prepared resume closure, and the redundant shell-command adapter is removed. Registry-based inspection, cleanup, and initial quiescence still validate their targets.

## Evidence

- Regression fails on base `f088fab92a5c`: discovery becoming unavailable after preparation previously blocked an otherwise usable sandbox. Candidate: 79 focused tests pass across backend execution, Podman runtime, delegated scopes and workspace quiescence.
- A process-backed fixture prepares the real backend, runs actual shell content and executed specs, and verifies ambient selector changes, initial unsupported remote rejection and lost-engine errors. No real user state or production service is used.
- Measurement acceptance fixed before the comparative run: five serial interleaved A/B pairs, five warm 40-command turns per arm, A/A controls; exactly 40 fewer discovery spawns per turn, lower median main-thread CPU/allocation, and no >=20% tail regression. Cold preparation reported separately. Fixture isolates spawn overhead; it does not measure btrfs, large database scans, or whole Gateway turn latency.
- Command: `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/podman-exec-measure.ts --root <unused-absolute-path> --source-root <baseline-or-candidate> --commands 20 --turns 5`. Use `--verify-binding` on the candidate and `--cpu-profile` for a separate warm CPU capture.
- Six net test lines extend the existing regression and use the production target binder in delegated-scope tests; production code shrinks by 6 lines.

Codex autoreview completed with no actionable P0-P2 findings on the complete runtime/measurement snapshot (`35c075728af7`) against main `645c18850bac`, including the allocation-cleanup conflict resolution and the paired fixture. After main #191555 moved backend construction inside allocation cleanup, all 79 focused tests passed again (38.17s including compilation); core and script typechecks passed. Both unused-file scans passed with zero findings.

`pnpm check:changed` completed. Its benchmark type-inference failure was corrected and the scripts typecheck passed. The remaining unrelated unused export `MEMORY_PROVENANCE_CHECK_ID` reproduces on both the original parent `f088fab92a5c` and current exact parent `645c18850bac`. It was introduced by `53a06f68e729` (Doctor memory provenance). This is a main regression, not an ignored lane failure. Other changed-file checks passed.

The initial five process-paired A/B runs (25 warm samples each) reduced median main-thread CPU 176.83 -> 116.96 ms and allocated bytes 31,911,504 -> 19,860,784 per 40-command turn; processes fell exactly 80 -> 40. However wall p95 rose 9835.68 -> 12173.50 ms (+23.8%), so that run does **not** satisfy performance acceptance. A/A median wall varied 8587.14 -> 3792.63 ms. The final fixture prepares both isolated processes first and alternates individual turns; the final same-source control and ten-pair run completed. No timing outliers are discarded.

Final warm results against main `645c18850bac`, candidate `35c075728af7`: ten alternating A/B turns after both processes prepare; 20 shell commands + 20 executed specs per turn.

| Per 40-command turn | Before median / p95 | After median / p95 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Podman processes | 80 / 80 | 40 / 40 |
| Discovery processes | 40 / 40 | 0 / 0 |
| Wall ms | 3383.22 / 3503.05 | 1924.72 / 2146.12 |
| Main-thread CPU ms | 135.99 / 159.48 | 81.96 / 86.19 |
| V8 allocated bytes | 30,251,292 / 81,311,584 | 17,323,128 / 30,191,464 |

Median main-thread CPU improves 39.7%, allocation 42.7%, wall 43.1%; no warm tail regression. Per-command averages are 3.40 -> 2.05 ms main-thread CPU and 756,282 -> 433,078 allocated bytes. Every measured turn contains exactly 40 real exec processes; only probes disappear. Five paired A/A controls had median wall 3920.78 -> 3703.28 ms, main CPU 151.58 -> 163.25 ms, allocation 31,598,224 -> 36,591,016 bytes; whole-process CPU is noisier and is not the primary claim. Cold preparation still uses seven processes, including its required probe; no cold-start speedup is claimed.

Reproduce: append `--compare-source <baseline-checkout> --turns 10 --verify-binding` to the fixture command above; set both sources to baseline for A/A. CPU profiling uses a separate `--cpu-profile` pass. Shared-host measurements qualify this process-spawn path, not a live container engine or complete Gateway latency.


CI repair: run `41558930860` at `35c075728af7` found nine failures in the existing lifecycle fixture, whose parser treated `--remote=false` as a command. The test-only correction at `9817a584f399` consumes that one-argument global flag and preserves assertions about the selected target. All 36 tests in the failed file now pass (23.23s including compilation); combined focused proof is 115 tests. Scoped lint/format and fresh Codex P0-P2 review passed. Runtime and benchmark code are unchanged, so the measurement evidence above still applies. Exact-head [CI run 41560559344](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41560559344) passed, including openclaw/ci-gate; the earlier failed run was fixed, not treated as inherited or rerun without a fix. Native merge-run verified squash merge 53fb0d4fcd699d8059a945c73f2cadd2fe7524d9 from exact head 9817a584f3990edcc7d0621963ee386ebe481ed5.

A separate five-pair CPU profile (200 commands/arm) reduced sampled inclusive main-thread time under `exec-spawn.ts` from 348.730 to 179.214 ms (-48.6%); `podman-runtime` stacks fell from 189.885 to 0 ms. These overlapping sampled stacks are not additive CPU counters.

prs.title: fix(infra): reject lossy UTF-8 in managed update handoff output
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The managed update handoff lossy-decodes the updater subprocess stdout with `Buffer.toString()`, so bytes that are not valid UTF-8 are silently replaced with U+FFFD. If that lands inside the JSON diagnostics, `JSON.parse(updaterOutput)` consumes corrupted data with no signal that bytes were lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Decode updater output with the strict `decodeUtf8Input` helper (the canonical approach already used across the codebase, e.g. #180861). When invalid UTF-8 is detected, the corruption is surfaced via a log line ("managed update updater stdout contained invalid UTF-8; retained a lossy copy") while still keeping a lossy copy so the string/JSON contract and the update flow never break.

The decoder binding reaches the spawned helper through the sealed runtime module it already `require`s, so the fix runs in the real child process.

## User Impact

No user-visible change for valid UTF-8 output (including multi-byte CJK split across chunks). Invalid UTF-8 is detected and explicitly annotated instead of silently corrupted, making managed update diagnostics reliable.

## Evidence

### Committed regression (head passes, base fails)

`update-managed-service-handoff-termination.test.ts` drives one raw 0xFF byte through the shipped `runOwnedUpdateCommand` decode path as an extra case in the triage settlement table, and asserts the warning is emitted only for that case while the retained output is the U+FFFD replacement. 8/8 green on head; on the pre-fix base that case fails (`expected false to be true`) while the other rows pass (revert → 1 failed; restore → 8/8). No test-line growth: `check:test-lines-ratchets` delta 0.

### Shipped managed-handoff warning trace (Ubuntu 24.04, systemd 255, Node 24.22.1)

The Gateway runs as a real systemd user service and the update starts from a cron command job, so the updater runs inside the Gateway process tree and takes the shipped handoff. A `NODE_OPTIONS=--import` preload appends one raw 0xFF byte inside the updater's JSON stdout, arming only in the handoff updater (`OPENCLAW_UPDATE_RUN_HANDOFF=1`).

```
handoff invalid-UTF-8 lines: 1
[2026-10-28T07:52:33.425Z] managed update updater stdout contained invalid UTF-8; retained a lossy copy
[2026-10-28T07:51:15.463Z] managed update ownership transferred; validating while the gateway serves
[2026-10-28T07:51:15.463Z] starting managed update command: openclaw update --yes --tag openclaw --timeout 1200
[2026-10-28T07:52:33.425Z] managed update update command exited code=1 signal=null
injected 0xff into updater stdout pid=3659 offset=21
settings sha256: a4bb27ad…d977e1 (before = after)
workspace marker: proof-data-marker-186033
```

The published 2026.10.8 build stays silent on the same injected byte (`handoff invalid-UTF-8 lines: 0`).

### Published 2026.10.8 → this build: completed update

Candidate packaged from this head with the repository's own packager (`build` + `runtime-postbuild`, 55 plugin modules verified); it bundles the workspace `@openclaw/ai` so installation does not depend on the published one:

```

package.json            "version": "2026.10.9", "bundleDependencies": [ … ]
dist/build-info.json    {"version":"2026.10.9","commit":"090125e25e76ec49fc146e5901f4f6753bc5f099"}
package/node_modules/   645 files, including package/node_modules/@openclaw/ai
```

Version raised 2026.10.7 → 2026.10.9 with the repo's `stampFixtureVersion` helper (the official harness relabel) because the worktree version is below the published driver. Fresh `npm install -g openclaw@2026.10.8` in an isolated HOME/prefix (Debian 13, glibc 2.41, Node 24.22.1), state seeded (config, workspace marker, 2 cron jobs), Gateway `/readyz` 200, then:

```
$ openclaw update --tag openclaw-candidate-2026.10.9.tgz --yes --json
status: ok   mode: npm   duration: 517 s
before: 2026.10.8 (2026.10.8-release-dc2523e5a5c7-2026-10-27T05-21-21.733Z)
after:  2026.10.9 (2026.10.7-090125e25e76-2026-10-28T11-40-22.501Z)

database snapshot               exit=0
package-install                 exit=0
candidate-state-snapshot        exit=0
candidate-doctor                exit=0
candidate-doctor-lint           exit=0

Update report: `✅ OpenClaw updated to 2026.10.9 (from 2026.10.8)`. No rollback step ran. Post-state:

```

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes sharing failing against a Gateway that native chat can reach using an approved TLS certificate or custom service headers.

## User Impact

The share extension reuses the connected Gateway’s approved transport settings. Reconnect OpenClaw after upgrading to refresh its saved connection. Browser-based Access sign-in still requires the main app.

**Draft for local Mac runner handoff:** native qualification is pending; this PR is not ready for review or merge.

## Why This Change Was Made

Store the approved TLS fingerprint and custom headers with the existing Gateway-bound shared Keychain credentials, not App Group preferences. Use the shared TLS validator with redirects and stored URLSession credentials disabled, and reread current relay authority before supplying headers. Retire saved share settings when the host changes service credentials or certificate trust.

The extension retains its distinct device identity and cannot approve a new certificate. Access refusal is preserved. No send-admission/result, attachment extraction, or main-app handoff behavior changes are included. No new configuration or protocol version is introduced.

## Evidence

**Current source:** head `3d79cb73658405df8363be73d40f118197276a59`, tree `305beda5cdce812d4e60a2ebbf416a5ebdc78184`. The published tree exactly matches the reviewed candidate: 33 files, +214/−40 against the original source base `70c99be459a77d474f19a7eed0e575449ef088e1`.

- The latest genuine-translation follow-up against `3e236130409f6e4a329dc219a35840182f015b82` is exactly 22 files, +22/−22: 21 locale memories and the derived iOS string catalog. It changes no native source or tests.

### Completed checks

- Independent Auto Review: the initial P0–P2 source review, four-file P0–P3 repair review, and fresh P0–P3 translation/artifact review found no actionable defects. The latest review covers the exact translation delta against `3e236130409f6e4a329dc219a35840182f015b82`, producing the current tree above. These were static reviews, not native execution.
- Isolated frozen dependency installation with Node 26.12.1 and pnpm 12.15.0 completed without dependency/configuration changes or donor-install mutation.

prs.title: fix(agents): apply_patch reports earlier hunks it already applied whe…
prs.body:
# fix(agents): apply_patch reports earlier hunks it already applied when a later hunk fails

Related: #127496 (follow-up to #160409)

## What Problem This Solves

#160409 made `apply_patch` check every update hunk before writing, so a missing update target or a context mismatch now rejects the patch with no file changes. Failures that only appear while writing still leave earlier hunks applied, and the error names only the hunk that failed:

- `Add File` onto a path that already exists
- `Delete File` of a missing path
- `Move to` onto an existing file, or a move whose source removal fails after the destination was written
- I/O errors, or cancellation between hunks

The model gets a single error and has no way to tell that earlier files were created, changed, or deleted. It then resends the whole patch from an outdated view of the files.

## User Impact

When a patch fails partway through, the tool error now lists the changes that already landed, using the same `A`/`M`/`D` markers as the success summary, and tells the model to re-read those files before retrying:

```
Cannot create existing.txt: the file already exists. Use "*** Update File: existing.txt" to change it, or delete it earlier in the same patch.
The patch stopped partway; these earlier changes were applied and not rolled back:
A created.txt
M notes.txt
Re-read these files before retrying, and do not resend the hunks already applied.
```

A failure on the first write leaves the error text unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

#127496 offers two options: compensate (roll back with an undo journal) or keep the earlier changes and report them. This PR takes the reporting option:

- It adds no new state, journal, or backend preconditions. #122933 stalled while trying to model those preconditions across the host and sandbox backends.
- It follows the repo guidance to prefer cheap mechanisms, such as best-effort recording with a warning, and to accept rare, visible, recoverable edge cases.
- Rollback can still be built on top of this later if maintainers decide on it. Even then, a rollback that fails would need this same partial-effect report.

Details:

- The error object is kept and only its message is extended. `AbortError`, `ToolInputError`, and the host-root-escape markers survive, so cancellation handling and the containment hint behave as before.
- If a move writes the destination but fails to remove the source, the destination is reported as `A` (a new copy), not `M` (a finished move).
- The summary type and formatting moved to `src/agents/apply-patch-summary.ts`, because `apply-patch.ts` would otherwise go over the 700-line `max-lines` cap. Its one external type import moved with it.

Not changed: there is still no rollback, and earlier hunks stay on disk. If maintainers decide rollback is required, that is a separate follow-up.

## Evidence

New `src/agents/apply-patch.partial-commit.test.ts`, run through the public tool boundary:

| Case | Upstream main | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add + update succeed, then an add onto an existing file fails (real host fs) | only the failing hunk's error | error also lists `A created.txt`, `M notes.txt` |
| Cancellation after the first write (sandbox bridge) | `AbortError`, no applied paths | still `AbortError`, lists `M a.txt` |
| Move: destination written, source removal fails | no applied paths | lists `A new.txt` |
| Failure on the first hunk | unchanged message | unchanged message |

- `pnpm test src/agents/apply-patch.partial-commit.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 4 passed, about 45 s on a cold shard (mostly worker preparation); the tests themselves take under 40 ms. Without the source change, 3 of the 4 fail.
- `pnpm test src/agents/apply-patch*.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` (all 9 apply_patch test files): 158 passed, 2 skipped.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check` on the touched files: clean.

prs.title: chore(worktrees): attribute ignored-file provisioning time
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Managed-worktree startup can spend most of its time in `provision` without distinguishing ignored-file discovery from copying.

## User Impact

Operators can identify whether ignored-file selection, safe copying, or the existing repository setup hook accounts for the delay. This adds diagnostics only: the worktree still waits for all required files and setup before returning, with no configuration or migration required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add two fixed owner-level phases, `provisionInspect` and `provisionCopy`, to existing preparation diagnostics. The existing `setup` phase already measures repository script execution. Warm source templates do not contain ignored-file or per-destination setup results, so skipping those operations would violate readiness. The current checkout has neither an include manifest nor a setup hook; an unconditional dependency-install or deferral change is therefore not supported by the available evidence.

The existing Gateway benchmark gains a reproducible 62,000-file / 1.24 GB synthetic fixture, full post-readiness file verification, process/main-thread CPU measurement, and separate CPU/allocation profiles. Production growth is 10 lines for the two timing wrappers; no new state, cache, or runtime policy.

## Evidence

Both baseline and candidate runtime builds pass. The new diagnostic assertion fails on baseline `c557867206b6067e226d7114a01ef2084a5e9f5d`; all 29 focused provisioning, hook, and preparation-timing tests pass on the candidate. Codex autoreview is scoped-clean with no actionable P0–P2 findings. Formatting, scoped lint, and script typechecking pass.

The local source-only fixture spends 3–5 ms in provision. A separate 50,000-selected-ignored-file scenario reproduces a 122.5 s provision phase without any dependency install or setup script; this is a synthetic diagnostic scenario, not attribution of an unknown deployment manifest.

Five interleaved baseline/candidate pairs on isolated Linux/ext4 (4 CPUs, 15.8 GiB RAM), with identical-code A/A controls and full verification of all 62,000 files after every readiness response:

| Metric | Baseline | With diagnostics |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median create RPC | 34.378 s | 32.698 s |
| Median provision | 30.920 s | 29.112 s |
| Median Gateway process CPU | 38.300 s | 36.621 s |
| Median Gateway main-thread CPU | 27.930 s | 26.465 s |
| Separate sampled main-isolate allocation pass | 18.964 GB | 19.009 GB |

A/A wall times were 33.072 / 34.466 s. Pair wall deltas were +0.739, +12.889, −13.732, −1.680, +0.071 s; mean −0.343 s. Both revisions show substantial run-to-run variation; this is evidence against a material instrumentation regression, not a speedup claim. Candidate median selection is 1.320 s and copying 27.791 s. About 89% of sampled allocation has fs-safe traversal/mutation-admission ancestry. Profiles sample the Gateway main isolate, while process CPU includes its worker threads; subprocess CPU is excluded.

All 17 measured worktrees (cold, A/A, five pairs, CPU and heap profiles) passed complete payload verification. The measured candidate source tree matches the reviewed commit; baseline owner files were restored from the exact parent. The available kernel cannot mount Btrfs and native acceleration was unavailable on ext4; this does not qualify the Btrfs warm-template path. No large production database or model/first-token measurement was used.

`pnpm check:changed` completed with every gate passing except a main regression: unused `MEMORY_PROVENANCE_CHECK_ID` in `src/commands/doctor-memory-provenance.ts`. The same export failure reproduces on the exact main parent above; it was introduced by `53a06f68e7297e78c065ca8ac526944d28113efa` (#189727). Its owner is unchanged by this PR. Exact-head PR CI is green for `741ca77c1b0bc7b9ec17566d5f1f0ec9ce479a48` ([run 41559917813](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41559917813)); the native watcher excludes superseded draft-to-ready runs. No CI exception is needed.

prs.title: fix: reduce memory pressure during GitHub publication
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Preparing a GitHub publication snapshot for a large managed workspace allocates multiple complete path inventories on the Gateway thread.

## User Impact

Publication preparation uses substantially less transient memory while publishing the same settled workspace and preserving the source index. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Compare staged paths directly against the settlement owner's admitted paths. Retain only excluded raw paths, removing the duplicate hex-encoded set and arrays of every tree record/path buffer. Preserve byte-exact exclusion when invalid UTF-8 could decode to an admitted replacement-character filename.

Accepted snapshots already have an owner and reuse path. PR-panel and options reads do not capture workspaces; HEAD/index and projection revisions cannot safely cache unstaged or untracked filesystem changes. This change adds no cache and preserves settlement, authority, and confirmation checks.

## Evidence

Acceptance was declared before comparison: 62,000 synthetic tracked files (1.14 GB), real Git and production snapshot owner, at least five interleaved pairs plus A/A controls, identical snapshot IDs and source-index bytes, lower sampled allocation, and investigation of any 20% increase in median/p95 CPU or wall time. Allocation includes objects collected by minor and major GC and runs separately from timing.

| Warm metric | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Sampled allocation median, five pairs | 43,305,112 B | 7,978,944 B |
| Sampled allocation p95 | 43,940,144 B | 8,099,200 B |
| Main-thread CPU median, all 15 timing pairs | 82.282 ms | 56.286 ms |
| Main-thread CPU p95 | 100.952 ms | 71.004 ms |
| Wall median, all 15 pairs | 466.567 ms | 410.517 ms |
| Wall p95 | 2246.018 ms | 1323.553 ms |

Allocation fell 81.6%; main-thread CPU fell 31.6%. Allocation A/A medians were 42,846,728/42,968,504 B. All snapshots and source-index bytes matched.

The initial five-pair timing campaign showed a +12.0% wall median (479.359 → 536.873 ms). A ten-pair balanced AB/BA follow-up investigated that uncertainty: 424.989 → 391.779 ms, nine paired improvements, median paired difference −32.483 ms versus −4.382 ms in balanced A/A. All original samples remain included. Shared-host tails are substantial; these macOS/Node 26.12.1/APFS owner measurements do not establish Linux/btrfs or production p95 safety. First-owner timing was recorded separately and improved in both timing campaigns; first-owner sampled allocation was 47,933,912 → 9,924,688 B. The owner does not query agent databases.

Reproduce with `scripts/perf/github-publication-snapshot-measure.ts` using its documented fixture, frozen baseline, `--samples 5`, `--allocations`, and `--control` modes; use `--samples 10 --balanced` for balanced timing. Baseline: `f088fab92a5c07a779a346918df2daade4043b18`.

Focused Git/index suite: 21 passed (45.86 s wrapper), including Unicode/control-character and invalid-byte alias admission with exact index preservation. Timeout suite: 17 passed (11.25 s). Settled archive/admission integration: selected test passed (57.93 s including compilation). Snapshot siblings: 8 passed; one node-transfer setup failed because this external-volume checkout has a group-writable ancestor rejected by fs-safe. That failure precedes the node transfer and is retained as an environment limitation, not a passing check. The exact-head CI run passed; this local setup limitation remains recorded.

Existing RPC/poller fixtures measured 30 PR-panel polls and 30 options reads with zero captures and zero Git calls. These use isolated SQLite and external-I/O fixtures, not a live browser/Gateway performance claim. No changed module is imported by the Control UI.

Codex autoreview of the complete local change against the pinned baseline is scoped-clean through P2, with no actionable findings. Runtime LOC: +7 for the buffer scan and rare byte-exact check; tooling declaration: +1. A 37-line test-budget record covers the distinct raw-byte admission regression guard. The standalone benchmark adds 209 lines.

`pnpm check:changed` completed with one new test lint issue (`sort` → `toSorted`, fixed; targeted lint now passes) and a production dead-export failure in unchanged `doctor-memory-provenance.ts`: `MEMORY_PROVENANCE_CHECK_ID`, introduced by `53a06f68e7297e78c065ca8ac526944d28113efa`. The focused production scan reproduces the sole finding on clean exact parent `f088fab92a5c07a779a346918df2daade4043b18` (Knip 6.40.0, exit 1, 104.70 s, no resolution errors). This is a main regression to fix, not a passing check. All typechecks, formatting and structural guards passed. `pnpm deadcode:unused-files` passed both production and full-tree scans. Landed as `61e381808488fb081250761c7dcfc393f4da15d8` from exact reviewed head `3e7fa96285654f56fdc867651beb9ffcfbc53935`. [CI run 41559376663](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41559376663) passed (35 successful jobs, 29 skipped), and the [exact-head CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41559377020) passed. No CI rerun or admin exception was used. Native review, preparation, merge, and cleanup completed; [completion record](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191582#issuecomment-6593178435).

prs.title: fix(ui): agree with the server on loopback names
prs.body:
Fixes #190741

## What Problem This Solves

Opening the Control UI at a name under `.localhost` (for example `http://openclaw.localhost:18789`, which browsers resolve to this machine) made the Portals page report **Remote portal ingress required** for a portal on `127.0.0.1`. The UI locality check accepted only `localhost`, `::1`, `[::1]` and `127.0.0.0/8`, so the gateway origin looked remote and the loopback portal looked unreachable from this browser.

- Problem: the Portals locality check did not recognise RFC 6761 localhost names.
- Solution: a dedicated predicate for "this machine" that includes them, used only by portal locality.
- Changed: `gateway-locality.ts` adds `isLocalhostName` and `isLoopbackOrLocalhostHostname`; `portals-state.ts` uses the wider one.
- Not changed: `isLoopbackHostname`, which stays the narrow trust boundary used by credential retry.

## Why This Change Was Made

The first revision widened `isLoopbackHostname` itself. Review correctly flagged the consequence: that predicate also gates cached-device-token retry in `gateway-connect-errors.ts`, so accepting new hostname forms there widens where credentials may be retried. The portal mislabel does not need that trust expansion.

So the widening is scoped to the question Portals actually asks — "is this origin this machine?" — and the credential path keeps the narrow definition. RFC 6761 §6.3 reserves `localhost` and every name under it, and the runtime's `isExplicitLoopbackHostname` already counts them, so the new predicate matches the server without touching the retry boundary.

## User Impact

A Control UI served at `openclaw.localhost` now takes the local path, so a `127.0.0.1` portal opens instead of showing a false "ingress required". Credential retry, remote Gateways, and non-loopback origins behave exactly as before.

## Evidence

```text
# predicate tables (both boundaries)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/components/session-menu-work.test.ts -t "isLoopback"
→ 13 passed  (narrow: .localhost stays false; widened: names classify as this machine)

# the shipped page decision: same loopback portal, only the gateway origin differs
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/portals
→ 32 passed
  · gateway ws://openclaw.localhost:18789 + portal http://127.0.0.1:43123 →
    receipt new-tab-required, and the page never prints "Remote portal ingress required"
  · reverting portals-state.ts to the strict predicate → that case fails
    (it reports remote-ingress-required, the reported symptom)

# production files reverted
→ 8 failed (new predicate absent, cases unclassifiable)

./node_modules/.bin/oxlint <changed files> → 0 warnings, 0 errors
```

The page test mounts the real `openclaw-portals-page` element and drives its real probe decision; only the gateway transport is mocked. That is the same decision the reported symptom came from, one layer below a live browser session.

Not tested: a real browser session against a live Gateway at a `.localhost` origin. The predicate that gates the probe is covered directly and the probe flow is unchanged.

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Traced the reported probe decision to the predicate it calls and compared it with the server-side check. Review correctly pointed out that widening the shared predicate also widened credential-retry trust, so the widening is now scoped to portal locality. The implementer understands the code: one question is "is this loopback for trust purposes" and another is "is this origin this machine"; conflating them was the mistake.

prs.title: fix(node-host): MCP tools permanently disappear when session cleanup throws after a disconnect
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: tools from a node-host MCP server permanently disappear with no logged error when session cleanup throws during disconnect recovery.

## User Impact

User impact: when a node-host MCP server disconnects, its reconnect is now scheduled even if disposing the old session throws; operators get a warning naming the server and telling them to check the server process, instead of silently losing every tool from that server until restart.

No behavior change when cleanup succeeds or reports "uncertain" — that path already warned and retried.

## Why This Change Was Made

`disposeNodeHostMcpSession` awaited `disposeMcpClient` without catching. The real `disposeMcpClient` can throw (its `finally` calls `detachStderr()` unguarded). Three recovery call sites (`client.onclose`, failed tool refresh, expired HTTP session) schedule the retry only after that `await`, and the shared work queue swallows rejections — so one throwing cleanup skipped the retry and logged nothing. The helper now catches the rejection, logs a warning that keeps the "check the server process" operator action, and returns, so downstream retry scheduling always runs.

Review follow-ups applied on top of the initial patch:

- The cleanup-failure warning now includes the operator's next action (`check the server process`), consistent with the existing "cleanup could not be confirmed" warning, instead of reporting only the exception.
- The two new recovery tests drive the retry with the suite's fake-clock approach (`vi.useFakeTimers()` + `advanceTimersByTimeAsync`) instead of real retry timers and polling.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (live node-host run)

Driver: production `startNodeHostMcpManager`, real `@modelcontextprotocol/client`, real `OpenClawStreamableHTTPClientTransport`, real `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` over 127.0.0.1. The server is killed mid-run (sockets destroyed, listener closed) and replaced by a fresh generation on the same port; the stale session is discovered by the next call receiving HTTP 404 "Session not found", which runs the session disposer. The only injection is the first session's `detachStderr` throwing — the uncaught cleanup fault this PR guards. (The stdio child-spawn path is unavailable on this glibc 2.28 host because the shipped process-supervisor relay cannot complete its identity handshake; streamable-http exercises the same production manager, disposer, and retry code over real protocol bytes.)

<details>
<summary>Before fix (pre-PR base, stale session + cleanup fault)</summary>

```
$ PROOF_EXPECT=stranded node --import tsx --import ./register-loader.mjs driver.mts
[proof +1.854s] step 3: tools published: ["echo/echo"]
[proof +1.867s] step 4: tool call BEFORE fault -> {"echoed":"ping-before-fault","generation":1}
[proof +2.381s] step 7: stale-session call failed as expected -> Error POSTing to endpoint: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32001,"message":"Session not found"},"id":null}
[proof +7.376s] base observation: post-fault call still fails -> MCP server "echo" is unavailable
[proof +7.377s] BUG REPRODUCED on base: cleanup fault left the tools stranded (no warning, no republish)
```

No cleanup warning, tools never republished, later calls fail — tools stay lost until restart.
</details>

<details>
<summary>After fix (same driver, with this change)</summary>

```
$ node --import tsx --import ./register-loader.mjs driver.mts
[proof +1.850s] step 3: tools published: ["echo/echo"]
[proof +1.862s] step 4: tool call BEFORE fault -> {"echoed":"ping-before-fault","generation":1}
[proof +2.375s] step 7: stale-session call failed as expected -> Error POSTing to endpoint: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32001,"message":"Session not found"},"id":null}
[node-host console.warn] node host MCP server "echo" cleanup failed: injected cleanup fault: stderr detachment rejected; check the server process
[proof +2.425s] step 8: cleanup warning captured -> node host MCP server "echo" cleanup failed: injected cleanup fault: stderr detachment rejected; check the server process
[proof +2.676s] step 9: tools REPUBLISHED 251ms after cleanup fault: ["echo/echo"]
[proof +2.682s] step 10: tool call AFTER recovery -> {"echoed":"ping-after-recovery","generation":2}
[proof +2.683s] step 11: recovery served by the restarted server (generation 1 -> 2)
[proof +2.690s] step 12: manager closed cleanly. RECOVERY PROOF COMPLETE
```

The cleanup warning carries the operator action, the reconnect fires one 250 ms backoff later, the tools are republished, and the post-recovery call is served by the restarted server (generation 1 -> 2).
</details>

### Regression tests

New regression tests in `src/node-host/mcp.recovery.test.ts` exercise the real (unmocked) `disposeMcpClient` with a `detachStderr` that throws, driving the retry with the suite's fake timers.

### Before fix

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/node-host/mcp.recovery.test.ts -t "disposal throws"
 × reconnects and warns when session disposal throws after transport close
 × reconnects and warns when session disposal throws after a failed refresh
 Tests  2 failed | 28 skipped (30)
```

### After fix

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/node-host/mcp.recovery.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
 Tests  30 passed (30)
```

- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json src/node-host/mcp.ts src/node-host/mcp.recovery.test.ts` — 0 warnings, 0 errors
- `oxfmt --check` on changed files — clean
- Review gate (`openclaw-pr-review`): PASSED, best-fix verdict `best`, no P0/P1/P2 findings

Not tested locally: tsgo typecheck lanes (host glibc 2.28 < required 2.32; CI gates cover). `mcp.cancellation.integration.test.ts` fails on this machine on unmodified base as well (real-process spawn environment issue, unrelated to this change).

prs.title: fix(update): select PostgreSQL in migrated finalizer
prs.body:
Closes #191542

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: migrated update finalization starts a fresh process without the parent’s PostgreSQL selection. Its first ledger adoption opens the SQLite engine anchor as a state database, reports a missing schema role, and never publishes the final result.

## User Impact

Normal fresh-process finalization now enters the existing updater database scope before executor, ledger, and terminal-result access. It reads the configured engine and environment-backed connection through the canonical owner, preserving PostgreSQL history and the local anchor.

The capability check stays configuration-free. The Windows native Job is retained before any pool worker starts. Doctor, post-core, and plugin-cohort modes retain their existing recovery and configuration owners; cleanup remains the existing best-effort owner with database drains before pool closure. No schema, configuration, credentials-in-wire, protocol, or timeout changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Engine selection is process-local and cannot cross the spawned finalizer boundary. Reusing `withUpdateDatabaseEngine` repairs the producer rather than inferring an engine from the anchor or repairing the anchor as SQLite. The extra pool call is retained only for sibling modes; normal finalization uses the canonical scoped preparation.

## Evidence

- **Actual causal RED:** baseline `f381764cf5964d7885ed459f41a9cf8041dfd244` on pinned `bf35e054`, [PostgreSQL conformance job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41553655060/job/125648227953). The executed fresh child reports “schema role missing; expected global” for its PostgreSQL anchor, then the regression fails because no parsed child result was returned (13.2 seconds). The infrastructure group had 274 passing cases; both other conformance shards passed. Earlier skipped ordinary-node tests and static assertion-narrowing failures are not product proof.

prs.title: feat(codex): draft guarded recovery using earned quota reset credits
prs.body:
Related: #163413 (separate read-only inventory proposal; this does **not** close or fix it).

## What Problem This Solves

Codex subscription users who have earned one-time quota reset credits currently have no safe, opt-in recovery mechanism when every authorized login has genuinely exhausted its included quota.

## User Impact

This is a **Draft, not an active recovery feature**. It introduces the upstream protocol and fail-closed decision engine for the proposed opt-in. Its configuration is off by default and does not yet activate redemption in running OpenClaw. No user action or actual reset credit is required for review.

The intended behavior once the remaining integration is implemented: exhaust the normal authorized profile selection before spending a single earned credit; never spend due to billing credits, OAuth errors, network errors, natural quota renewal, or arbitrary cooldown clearing.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Validate the documented Codex App Server `account/rateLimits/read` fields and `account/rateLimitResetCredit/consume` outcomes, without private backend endpoints.
- Introduce a bounded opt-in config contract (`resetCreditRecovery.enabled: false`; `maxPer24Hours: 1` by default when enabled).
- Add an isolated policy engine that scans **every** authorized candidate before and after ownership is claimed; a usable later profile always wins before spending earned credits. The engine rejects non-quota blocks, purchased credit activity, stale identity, incomplete limit eligibility, or ambiguous outcomes, and reads the selected account again after every official consume result.
- Add a worker-backed SQLite plugin-state ledger using `observe`/`compareAndApply` (CAS), persistent per-attempt UUID idempotency keys, reclaimable fenced leases, a global 24-hour spend cap and bounded/cancellable cross-process outcome polling. A crashed logical attempt is retried only under its original key.
- Prefer earliest-expiring credit only when details are complete; for the vendor-supported count-only/capped inventory, send no `creditId` and let Codex select; malformed or expired details fail closed.
- Treat missing/partial/expired inventory and unknown responses conservatively. Handle `reset`, `alreadyRedeemed`, `nothingToReset`, and `noCredit` distinctly.
- Keep it disconnected from live redemption until the existing auth owner, shared-state initialization and replay-safe runtime path are approved and wired.

## Evidence

- Source contract inspected: [official Codex response schema](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/json/v2/ConsumeAccountRateLimitResetCreditResponse.json) and [request schema](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/json/v2/ConsumeAccountRateLimitResetCreditParams.json).
- Added Vitest source tests for account priority, complete/partial/expired inventories, purchased credits, four official outcomes, ambiguous timeout, durable-key crash replay and cancellation.
- Added ledger tests with **mocked compare-and-apply** for concurrent independent callers, commit conflict retry, fenced lease reclaim after restart, 24-hour spend caps, corrupt-state fail-closed behavior, uncertain cross-account blocks and bounded waiters.
- An externally supplied standalone archive's `node --test` suite was run locally: **13/13 passed**, but it used a legacy JSON/test harness disconnected from current OpenClaw. Its algorithms were reviewed and adapted; its passing results are not validation of the new PR code.
- **Not yet executed on this PR head:** targeted Vitest, typecheck, formatter, full build and a genuine two-process Gateway/SQLite integration test. GitHub draft CI currently skips core CI, OpenGrep and CodeQL; lightweight Workflow Sanity/Periphery results are reported by GitHub separately. The connector cannot launch a checkout test shell. No real credits were consumed.

## Blocking work and product decision

**Do not merge in this state.** The pure policy and plugin-state ledger exist as unregistered modules, not a working live route. The remaining work is to bind the ledger to the actual shared SQLite-backed plugin-state owner, resolve authorized account identity/credential generation through the existing auth-profile owner (including explicit pins/agent isolation), adapt the selected Codex App Server connection, preserve tool-side-effect/replay decisions in the native turn owner, and run genuine two-process restart/credential-rotation/e2e tests. Add safe production observability, run focused tests/typecheck/format/build and pass CI and the security-sensitive-change review guard before leaving Draft.

Maintainer guidance requested: Is the appropriate shared-auth/extension boundary a narrow host-owned provider recovery hook, or should a separate existing runtime seam be used? Please confirm which durable owner and API surface should host the credit-spend state before this is wired. This is not the read-only inventory placement question in #163413.

## AI disclosure

Draft code and description were prepared with assistance from OpenAI GPT-6 at the contributor's request. No independent local build or live integration execution is claimed; the author is responsible for reviewing the implementation before any merge.

prs.title: fix(voice-call): keep the opening greeting from being wiped by barge-in
prs.body:
Closes #159139

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a realtime call's opening greeting is cut off a fraction of a second in when the callee barges in, because a barge-in clears the whole queued greeting burst and cancels the greeting turn.

## User Impact

User impact: the callee hears the complete opening greeting (including any consent or intro question) before barge-in takes effect; barge-in behaves normally again once the greeting has played.

## Why This Change Was Made

The greeting is generated once and queued as a single large burst, so any barge-in — the local RMS gate or a provider VAD interrupt — during that burst was destructive. A greeting-protection window, armed when the provider becomes ready with an initial greeting, now holds both barge-in entry points off and mutes the caller's audio to the provider so a barge-in is not interpreted as an answer; the window disarms once the greeting has actually played out (turn complete, pacer drained, sustained quiet) or after a hard timeout, whichever comes first.

## Evidence

Live calls before the change: `6240a23d` lost a full 53 760-byte opening 0.3 s after the callee said "Hello"; `8d938602` lost the rest after an early disarm with 34 240 bytes queued. After the change, `3f7686b0` and `d003a231` kept the greeting intact through two provider barge-ins (log: `outbound audio kept by provider barge-in during greeting protection`), with no `cleared by` line, and disarmed `reason=played-out` after the full consent question. `pnpm tsgo:extensions` passes on the branch.


## Review response

Reworked on head `e19494fa` in response to the review:

- **The protection window could end before the carrier had actually played the greeting (carrier-lag).** Protection is no longer released on queue-emptiness alone. It now stays armed until the greeting turn has completed, the paced queue has drained, **and** the carrier has confirmed the greeting played out (its playback mark acknowledged / sustained quiet), or the hard timeout elapses — whichever comes first. An empty queue while the carrier is still playing no longer disarms.
- **Caller-speech handling inside the protected window.** Caller audio is muted to the provider for the whole protected window, and the release path is now covered on both branches: an actual played-out greeting resumes caller audio, and a greeting that never produces audio releases protection without muting the caller indefinitely.

Tests added (green):
- `mutes caller audio to the provider while the opening greeting is protected`
- `keeps protection until the carrier confirms the greeting played, then resumes caller audio`
- `releases caller audio when the greeting never produces audio`

Command: `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/voice-call/src/webhook/realtime-handler.greeting-protection.test.ts` — observed `3 passed`.

`pnpm tsgo:extensions` passes on the branch.

CI `check-lint-core-2` failed on the new greeting-protection test: oxlint `typescript(no-base-to-string)` flagged `data.toString()` on the untyped `ws` message payload.

Fixed in `c39c530f` — the `ws.on("message")` callback is typed as `RawData` and normalized to a `Buffer` (same pattern as `realtime-handler.test.ts`).

prs.title: fix(voice-call): keep opening greetings audible during caller interruptions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: early caller speech or noise clears the opening greeting before callers hear it.

Supersedes #159144, thanks @mnowrot. Related: #159139.

## User Impact

The opening greeting plays through, and callers can interrupt subsequent replies normally. Overlapping caller audio and transcripts are discarded during the opening. Input before the first greeting audio remains live; no pre-audio mute, new option, or migration is introduced.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing audio controller protects the opening until its response ends and the existing carrier playback clock drains. It excludes the answering-machine hold acknowledgement, and releases on explicit clear or continuity reset. Provider-side cancellation already caused by input sent before playback starts remains outside this host playback fix. Carrier timing uses the existing send-time estimate rather than adding an acknowledgement waiter.

This builds on #191537's echo admission and leaves #191498's Deepgram UtteranceEnd behavior intact. Production delta is +29 lines net; the redundant audible-output forwarding callback was removed. The remaining state distinguishes the opening from later turns and keeps response completion from exposing its queued tail. The separate 60-line regression allocation covers both interruption owners, a generation gap, the queued tail, complete carrier audio, and resumed later-turn interruption without another test harness.

## Evidence

- Red on current main `8654e159b99e545d5fd982791bafdcd988432611`: real handler, fake carrier WebSocket, queued opening audio and loud caller media. Both local/provider cases received a `clear` frame instead of preserving the greeting; 35 existing handler tests passed. The named-file wrapper took 45.73 s including a cold worker compilation.
- Green after: handler/lifecycle/audio-controller/pacer plus Deepgram's named file passed 99 tests. The final handler/audio-controller/call-control run passed 59 tests in 11.92 s wrapper wall time (10.11 s Vitest); the final two-case regression also covers a pause between greeting chunks and later-turn cancellation. [Blacksmith Testbox through Crabbox](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41558993359), lease `tbx_01m6fftwtrbdc7vsqzqevtj1ka`.
- Touched-file formatting corrected with oxfmt. Type-aware lint passes for all four touched TypeScript files (zero problems, 6.03 s; artifact preparation also ran remotely). `git diff --check` passes. PR CI supplies broad validation.
- Local autoreview through the shared helper, Codex, P0–P3: `scoped-clean`, no actionable findings. Local ClawSweeper is unavailable on this host; its initial hosted review is already queued, so no duplicate request was posted.
- [Exact-head PR CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41559904533) passed on `04953ae0030b8228deaa93165c0abb786b87f951`: 31 successful jobs, no failures, 10m13s elapsed. Native preparation retained that head without a rebase or extra push.
- Contributor code was read with `gh pr view`/`gh pr diff` only and was never checked out or executed. Human credit is deduplicated to @mnowrot; the original agent coauthor is excluded. No live carrier/model call is claimed. Tests, their dependencies and worker compilation ran remotely. Native landing uses scripts/pr's managed, lockfile-keyed dependency cache locally under the authorized exception; the production Team Gateway was untouched.

prs.title: fix(exec): dollar amounts in agent messages are corrupted when exec text uses $<digit> in double quotes
prs.body:
Closes #179890

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: dollar amounts in agent-sent messages are silently corrupted ("$900" becomes "00") when an `exec` command passes the text in double quotes.

## User Impact

User impact: exec commands that would deliver a corrupted dollar amount are refused before they run. The refusal shows the text as written next to what the shell would deliver, and how to fix it (single quotes, `\$`, or a quoted heredoc), so the agent retries correctly instead of sending the wrong amount to a customer. It can be disabled with `OPENCLAW_EXEC_DOLLAR_GUARD=off`.

**Open question for maintainers:** this is default-on and uses an environment switch. If you'd prefer it opt-in, or shipped as a plugin on the existing `before_tool_call` hook instead of in core, I'm happy to rework it that way. Tell me which shape you want.

## Why This Change Was Made

`runBeforeToolCallHook` checks `exec` command text for a `$<digit>` that the shell would expand, before any plugin or approval policy runs. Codex-native shell commands reach the same policy through the PreToolUse native hook relay. Relay planning now counts the guard as a before-tool-call policy and keeps `exec` in the PreToolUse matcher, so native commands are covered even with no other policy installed.

The scanner is deliberately conservative. It only flags an expansion it can show would be empty:
- It honours single quotes, `\$`, `$'...'`, quoted heredoc delimiters, `${...}`, `$((...))` and comments.
- It recurses into `$(...)`, including substitutions inside unquoted heredoc bodies, with their own quoting.
- It ignores `$0` (the shell or script name) unless it reads as money (`$0.50`).
- It stays out of commands that define functions or set positional parameters (`set --`, `shift`, `getopts`), where `$1.00` may be intended.
- It fails open on anything it cannot parse.

Code-mode `exec` (JavaScript) is excluded.

## Evidence

- `src/agents/shell-dollar-expansion-guard.test.ts` (35 tests): the hazard shapes, every safe quoting form, `$0`, populated positional parameters, heredoc command substitution, `bash -lc` unwrapping, fail-open, and the `runBeforeToolCallHook` veto, allow and disable cases. The `$0`, positional-parameter and heredoc-substitution cases fail on the previous revision and pass now.
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.dollar-guard.test.ts` (6 tests): Codex `Bash` and `exec_command` are denied and single-quoted amounts pass. Relay planning enables PreToolUse for `exec` with no other policy and keeps it in a relay scoped to other tools; these planning cases fail without the relay change.
- The existing `agent-tools.before-tool-call*` and `native-hook-relay*` unit suites pass. `native-hook-relay.participants` and `native-hook-relay.remote-http` fail identically on `main` without this change in my environment.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, oxlint and oxfmt are clean.
- Replayed against 391 unique `$`-bearing exec commands from a production deployment: 18 were flagged, all genuine expansion bugs, with no false positives.
- Still to add: a gateway trace of a real agent refusing and retrying. I'll attach it before asking for re-review.

prs.title: fix(codex): name incompatible settings in thread rotation refusals
prs.body:
Supersedes #148530, thanks @DasX.
Related: #135310

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Codex thread rotation refusals that hide which incompatible setting changed.

## User Impact

The existing refusal now names the changed setting, such as runtime identity or dynamic tool loading. Native thread preservation and rotation decisions are unchanged; no configuration or migration is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the setting label already available to the comparison owner in its existing error. This replaces the larger proposal with one changed production line and no added state or rotation logic. Production LOC: +1/-1 (net 0); regression LOC: +16/-6 (net +10). The separate 10-line test allocation covers the added native-ownership refusal case in the existing lifecycle table.

## Evidence

- On current-main baseline `bf35e054b0062c64e5577b165a3ae629adc3d2d0`, the focused lifecycle file failed only the new setting-name assertion (6 passed, 1 failed; 44.00s runner duration).
- After the fix, all 7 cases passed (39.34s runner duration, about 1.8s test time), including unchanged-binding and no-replacement assertions. Tests use the production lifecycle and a synthetic native server; authenticated Codex inference was not exercised.
- Named file: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/thread-lifecycle.adoption.test.ts`, run through `pnpm test ... --maxWorkers=1` on Crabbox Blacksmith Testbox. Remote worker compilation was required; no suite ran on the production Team host.
- Touched-file lint/format and `git diff --check` passed. PR CI supplies broad proof.
- Independent autoreview: scoped-clean through P2, no actionable findings. Simplification retained only the existing diagnostic label and one regression case.
- Contributor source was read with `gh pr view` / `gh pr diff`; it was never checked out or executed.

prs.body:
Closes #191209
Related: #124021 (older, separate dark-mode detail-text fix)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where iOS chat users expanding a run's work list see an oversized accent-colored "Tool details" label between smaller tool rows when the run contains quiet tool calls.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the shared chat caption font and semantic secondary color for the disclosure label, with a secondary chevron tint. The disclosure string, expansion behavior, row filtering, and tool results are unchanged. This shared view also gains matching caption styling on macOS; no platform-specific behavior is added.

## User Impact

The quiet-tool disclosure fits the surrounding tool rows instead of looking like a prominent accent heading. Semantic colors and Dynamic Type remain supported.

## Evidence

Cropped before/after screenshots below show the same synthetic chat fixture in the iOS simulator with the work list and quiet-tool disclosure expanded. Only this styling change differs; the expanded tool row remains visible. The recorded label frame height changes from 28.7 pt to 22 pt.

The device tester confirmed the large red label was gone. That observation is not an isolated A/B; the simulator pair above isolates this PR. Each tool-row fix changes a different element.

AI-assisted change. Public review-session summary: both reviewers inspected the seven-line diff and surrounding disclosure/row code; no new state, concurrency, or call assumptions were introduced. The cross-family review checked tint inheritance, semantic colors, macOS impact, and Dynamic Type. Screenshots are synthetic fixtures cropped to the tool list; no private conversation log is published.

prs.title: feat(pdf): add explicit OpenAI native document opt-in
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI Platform users cannot explicitly choose native PDF document input through the PDF tool while preserving existing upload and model-selection behavior.

## User Impact

`agents.defaults.pdfNativeOpenai: true` opts an already-selected OpenAI vision model into complete-document input. **Unset or false preserves extraction and the existing provider order**, including saved configurations upgraded from the latest stable release. Selecting an OpenAI model alone does not authorize complete-document upload.

Page selection, passwords, unknown completeness, page/text/image truncation, size-limit violations, custom endpoints, Codex/ChatGPT transports and text-only models retain bounded extraction. Completeness checks still require the configured extractor. Existing Anthropic and Google paths are unchanged.

## Implementation

This replaces the earlier automatic-upload/provider-preference proposal with one default-off core boolean at the existing PDF configuration owner. The bundled OpenAI provider implements a narrow optional media-understanding hook using the official [PDF input contract](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/file-inputs): inline `input_file`, official Platform HTTPS `/v1/responses`, `store: false`, each PDF under 50 MB and combined PDF input at most 50 MB. There is no persistent Files upload, automatic provider preference or new dependency. The official configuration generator records the single additional core leaf; channel/plugin surfaces are unchanged.

Prepared credentials, headers and symbol-attached request/auth overrides use the existing scoped egress helpers. The native branch also reuses the host-owned `withGuardedFetchRequestAuthority` scope with `assertModelCurrent`, the **original model's** credential authority and the retained provider-resource assertion. The existing HTTP guard rechecks these synchronously immediately before dispatch after asynchronous preparation and on redirects. This closes the assert-only operator/credential retirement gap across lazy provider and DNS awaits without adding an authorization abstraction or changing shared HTTP behavior.

Capability adoption and the proposed setting placement remain normal maintainer product decisions. This branch provides a concrete default-preserving candidate for that decision.
