prs.title: fix(deepgram): callers hear nothing when endpointing never ends a turn
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves A Deepgram realtime turn only completes on `speech_final` or `from_finalize`. When endpointing stays silent mid-call, neither ever arrives: the stream stays open, results stop coming, and the caller's question is never handed to the agent. The call is not degraded, it is lost. The existing `finalizeFallbackTimer` does not cover this. It is armed on **close**, to preserve already-finalized text when `Finalize` yields no Results event. It is not a mid-call mechanism. ## Why This Change Was Made An earlier attempt (#123487, closed by me) solved this by committing the turn from a host-side timer. That was correctly rejected: turn completion must stay provider-authoritative, and `main` now enforces it with two tests. This change keeps that rule. The backstop decides nothing: it sends `Finalize` and lets Deepgram decide. Deepgram answers with `from_finalize`, which the existing terminal path already commits. Both halves already existed in the factory and were simply never wired together. When the provider does not answer, the host still does not decide. The turn stays pending and the unanswered request is reported as a recoverable failure, so the only thing that ever ends a turn is the provider. ## User Impact **Opt-in.** `idleFlushMs` defaults to `0`, so no existing installation changes behaviour on upgrade. Operators who actually see stalled turns set it; everyone else is untouched. Where enabled, a stalled turn recovers instead of hanging until hangup. Healthy calls are unaffected, because the timer runs longer than the provider's own endpointing window and `speech_final` wins the race. ## Review response | Finding | Resolution | Covering test | | ------- | ---------- | ------------- | | **[P1] Keep unanswered Finalize requests from completing open turns** | Conceded; the previous revision was wrong. An `is_final` segment is confirmed text, not a completed utterance, and the old recovery timer committed the turn on exactly that non-terminal evidence, inventing a boundary the provider never gave. The watchdog no longer completes anything. While the call is open the turn stays pending, the unanswered request is surfaced through `onError` as a recoverable failure, and the cleared coverage marker lets a later Results event ask again. The close path still preserves confirmed text at hangup, and `speech_final` / `from_finalize` remain the only signals that end a turn. | *keeps a turn pending when the provider never answers the idle finalize* | | **[P2] Reset the idle timer only when transcript text progresses** | Conceded; the finding is real. Both nonterminal Results branches re-armed the timer for every nonempty event, so a provider that repeats the same interim transcript without any terminal signal postponed `Finalize` on every repeat and the reported stall survived the patch. The session now tracks the effective transcript the backstop already covers (`idleFinalizeTranscript`, replacing the old boolean `idleFinalizeSent`), and `armIdleFinalize` takes the new effective text: an identical repeat returns without touching the pending timer, and only text that moved past the covered value re-arms it. The comparison happens on the effective transcript (`joinTranscript(finalized, partial)`), so an `is_final` echo of the same words is a repeat too, not progress. A request that was never sent, and an unanswered request after its watchdog window, both clear the marker so a later Results event can ask again.

Baseline, captured by removing only the new progress comparison and leaving everything else in place:
```
FAIL extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts > still finalizes when the provider repeats one interim transcript forever
AssertionError: expected 0 to be greater than or equal to 1
❯ extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts:491:55
491| await vi.waitFor(() => expect(finalizeRequests).toBeGreaterThanO…
```
The guard was then restored and the file re-verified green. | *still finalizes when the provider repeats one interim transcript forever* | | **[P2] Stop recovery when the Finalize request was not sent** | Conceded. `sendJson` returns `false` before it touches the socket for a stale, closed or superseded connection and again for backpressure, and a throw leaves the frame unsent too; the old code ignored both and armed the watchdog anyway. The return value is now captured, the throw is caught, and either outcome clears the coverage marker and returns without arming anything — a request that was never sent cannot draw a provider terminal result, so nothing is waiting on one. | *does not watch for an answer when the idle finalize request was refused*, *does not watch for an answer when the idle finalize request throws* | | **Decision needed: should `idleFlushMs` exist despite its Results-gap risk?** | Accepted as recommended; the setting stays. The default is `0` (`DEEPGRAM_REALTIME_DEFAULT_IDLE_FLUSH_MS = 0`) and `config.idleFlushMs <= 0` returns before any timer is armed, so **explicitly opting in is the only way the code path engages** and no install inherits the tradeoff on upgrade. The config reader accepts exactly one spelling, `raw.idleFlushMs` — no alias family, unlike the neighbouring `endpointingMs` / `endpointing` / `silenceDurationMs` group. `docs/providers/deepgram.md` lists it in the settings table and now spells out the tradeoff: the timer keys on Results activity rather than caller silence, so if Deepgram pauses Results mid-utterance for longer than the window, the request goes out while the caller is still speaking and can split one question into two turns; pick a value comfortably longer than the longest Results gap you observe. Shipped in the disabled state, the remaining question — whether the opt-in should exist at all — is a plugin owner's call, and this PR waits on it rather than pre-empting it. | *leaves the idle finalize request disabled unless idleFlushMs is configured*, *does not arm the idle finalize request when idleFlushMs is zero* | Merged onto current `main` (no conflicts), so the branch applies as-is. The earlier deslop pass (#158437) replaced `flushFinalizedTurn()` with `flushTurn(includePartial)`; this revision removes the idle path's call to it entirely, so nothing dangles, and the reconnect tests use `main`'s parameterised form. ## Evidence ### Real-call capture (unchanged, previously accepted) Two real Twilio + Deepgram calls, same machine, same account. The capture ran with `endpointingMs: 2000` and `idleFlushMs: 1000` explicitly configured, i.e. an install that has opted in, which is now the only way the backstop engages. Redacted. **Before** - pinned `main` at `8518d391`, no patch: ``` 12:23:56 Speaking initial message <- caller heard this 12:24:05 Partial transcript chars=10 ... partials climbing, no speech_final 12:24:48 Partial transcript chars=530 <- last result -- 12 minutes, stream open, nothing committed -- 12:37:10 Media stream disconnected <- caller gave up 12:37:10 Transcript received chars=582 12:37:10 Ignoring transcript from inactive stream 12:37:10 Call finalized endReason=completed ``` 582 characters transcribed and never delivered. The close-scoped fallback did fire, but only at teardown, when the stream was already inactive. **After** - four consecutive turns, every one completed mid-call: ``` 13:41:25.479 Partial transcript chars=20 <- growth stops 13:41:28.603 Transcript received chars=20 <- +3.124s 13:41:31.250 AI response queued chars=59 13:41:43.375 Partial transcript chars=32 13:41:46.478 Transcript received chars=32 <- +3.103s 13:42:03.558 AI response queued chars=319 13:42:36.976 Partial transcript chars=20 13:42:40.071 Transcript received chars=20 <- +3.095s 13:42:43.884 AI response queued chars=50 13:43:59.498 Partial transcript chars=12 13:44:02.630 Transcript received chars=12 <- +3.132s 13:44:04.700 AI response queued chars=92 13:44:18.829 Media stream disconnected <- caller hung up, having been answered 13:44:19.190 Call finalized endReason=completed ``` | Turn | Last partial -> transcript committed | | ---- | ------------------------------------ | | 1 | 3.124 s | | 2 | 3.103 s | | 3 | 3.095 s | | 4 | 3.132 s | The configured backstop is `endpointingMs + idleFlushMs` = **3000 ms**, and all four turns committed between 3.095 s and 3.132 s after their last result. Native endpointing alone would have committed at roughly 2.0 s. That spread is the backstop firing, plus the `Finalize` to `from_finalize` round trip. **How to read this, precisely:** the `Finalize` frame is a WebSocket send and is not itself logged, so the evidence for it is the timing signature above rather than a log line naming it. What the log shows directly is that turns now commit mid-call, while the stream is still open, which never happened before the change. **One honest anomaly:** a 2-character fragment at 13:42:47 produced partials but no transcript. The most likely explanation is that Deepgram returned an empty final for a noise fragment, in which case the turn correctly emits nothing. I have not proven that. ### What this revision changed, and what the capture does and does not cover This revision touches the two failure branches and the timer's re-arm condition. The request-and-commit path the capture exercises — arm, send `Finalize`, receive `from_finalize`, commit through the existing terminal handler — is unchanged in behaviour, so the timings above still describe what happens today. The capture is **not** exact-head proof of the changed lines, and I am not presenting it as such. In those four turns Deepgram answered every request, so the watchdog never fired: it would have needed 5.0 s (3.0 s backstop + 2.0 s wait) and every turn had committed by 3.132 s. The two failure branches this revision rewrites therefore never executed during that call, and the repeated-identical-Results case the progress guard addresses did not occur in it either. All three are covered at unit level below. I can capture a redacted exact-head trace on request, though inducing an unanswered `Finalize` on a live Deepgram socket is not something I can arrange by configuration alone. ### Changed-code regressions (unit level, fake timers, no live call) Each new guard was neutralised in isolation on this head, the test run, the failure captured, and the guard restored from a backup; the file was then re-verified green and grepped to confirm no neutralisation survived. **[P1] Guard neutralised** — recovery timer restored to committing the turn on non-terminal evidence (`flushTurn(false)`): ``` FAIL extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts > buildDeepgramRealtimeTranscriptionProvider > keeps a turn pending when the provider never answers the idle finalize AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times Received: 1st vi.fn() call: Array [ "stalled question", ] Number of calls: 1 > extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts:532:32 531| await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(5_000); 532| expect(onTranscript).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); | ^ ``` That is the defect in one line: the call is still open, no `speech_final` and no `from_finalize` ever arrived, and the host hands up `"stalled question"` anyway. **[P2 — new, transcript progress] Guard neutralised** — the progress comparison (`if (effectiveTranscript === idleFinalizeTranscript) return;`) removed, so every nonempty Results event re-arms the timer again. The fake Deepgram server repeats one identical interim transcript every 25 ms with no terminal signal, inside a 75 ms window (`endpointingMs: 25` + `idleFlushMs: 50`), and never stops: ``` FAIL extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts > buildDeepgramRealtimeTranscriptionProvider > still finalizes when the provider repeats one interim transcript forever AssertionError: expected 0 to be greater than or equal to 1 ❯ extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts:491:55 489| // The repeats never stop, so a timer rearmed by every nonempty … 490| // would never fire and this would time out. 491| await vi.waitFor(() => expect(finalizeRequests).toBeGreaterThanO… | ^ ``` Zero `Finalize` requests: the timer was postponed on text that never grew, so the backstop this PR exists to add never engaged and the dead-air stall survived. With the comparison in place the request goes out once, 75 ms after the transcript stopped moving, while the repeats continue. The whole sequence is driven from the fake server rather than from an awaited midpoint, because under `vi.useFakeTimers()` `vi.waitFor` advances timers while it polls. **[P2] Guard neutralised** — `if (!requestSent) { ; return; }` removed, so the watchdog arms regardless of whether the frame left: ``` FAIL ... > does not watch for an answer when the idle finalize request was refused AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times Received: 1st vi.fn() call: Array [ [Error: Deepgram realtime idle finalize request went unanswered; turn left pending], ] Number of calls: 1 > extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts:586:27 585| expect(onTranscript).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); 586| expect(onError).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); | ^ ``` ``` FAIL ... > does not watch for an answer when the idle finalize request throws AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to be called once with arguments: [ ObjectContaining{...} ] Received: 1st vi.fn() call: [ - ObjectContaining { + Error { "message": "socket send failed", }, ] 2nd vi.fn() call: [ - ObjectContaining { - "message": "socket send failed", + Error { + "message": "Deepgram realtime idle finalize request went unanswered; turn left pending", }, ] Number of calls: 2 > extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts:632:23 631| expect(onTranscript).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); 632| expect(onError).toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith( | ^ ``` Both show the same shape: a request that never left the process is reported as having gone unanswered. The failure branches are reached through a host wrapper that substitutes `sendJson` on the transport handed to the provider's message handler, reproducing the two documented failure forms (`false` return, and a throw) without patching `websocket-session.ts`. ### Automated coverage `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts`: - asks the provider to finalize a turn whose transcript stopped growing - **still finalizes when the provider repeats one interim transcript forever** - lets provider endpointing win before the idle finalize request - **keeps a turn pending when the provider never answers the idle finalize** (replaces the previous *releases a turn...* case, which asserted the behaviour review rejected) - **does not watch for an answer when the idle finalize request was refused** - **does not watch for an answer when the idle finalize request throws** - keeps a turn pending when an idle finalize cannot complete it - leaves the idle finalize request disabled unless idleFlushMs is configured - does not arm the idle finalize request when idleFlushMs is zero **24/24 pass** on this head, including the pre-existing provider-authority tests (*does not commit a turn on an utterance-end gap before speech-final*, *does not infer silence from a gap between provisional results*), unmodified. ### Local gates ``` npx oxlint extensions/deepgram Found 0 warnings and 0 errors. ``` Both baseline ratchets now run and pass on this head (the earlier `api.createSnapshot is not a function` abort was stale local `node_modules`, not this branch): ``` npx pnpm check:max-lines-ratchet --base upstream/main max-lines ratchet OK: 702 grandfathered suppressions. OPENCLAW_* count 476/476 npx pnpm check:assertion-safety --base upstream/main assertion SAFETY ratchet OK: 3206 files, 8257 grandfathered assertions. ``` The diff adds no type assertions at all, so the assertion baseline is untouched. ### Merged with current main (head `2d1089dd625`) `upstream/main` moved to `7cf9ad48b8b` and the branch went `CONFLICTING`. One file conflicted: `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider-factory.ts`, against `refactor(plugins): deslop long-tail extensions second pass (#161390)`, which collapsed the `Results` handler's `if (event.is_final) { ... } else { ... }` into a single ternary path. Resolved by adopting upstream's new shape and re-expressing this PR's backstop against it, not by restoring the old branches. The whole change in that handler is now three lines: ```ts const nextFinalized = event.is_final ? joinTranscript(finalizedTranscript, text) : finalizedTranscript; if (!updateTurn(nextFinalized, event.is_final ? "" : text, transport)) { return; } const effective = event.is_final ? nextFinalized : joinTranscript(nextFinalized, text); armIdleFinalize(transport, effective); config.onPartial?.(effective); ``` `effective` is identical to the value upstream already passes to `onPartial`, so the transcript the backstop keys on is unchanged and the transcript-progress comparison in `armIdleFinalize` is untouched. The diff against `upstream/main` is still only the three intended files. Gates re-run on the merged head: ``` npx vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-media.config.ts \ extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 24 passed (24) npx oxlint extensions/deepgram Found 0 warnings and 0 errors. npx pnpm check:max-lines-ratchet --base upstream/main max-lines ratchet OK: 702 grandfathered suppressions. OPENCLAW_* count 476/476 npx pnpm check:assertion-safety --base upstream/main assertion SAFETY ratchet OK: 3198 files, 8196 grandfathered assertions. ``` The transcript-progress regression (*still finalizes when the provider repeats one interim transcript forever*) is among the 24 passing, so the repeat-does-not-postpone behaviour survives the refactor. The real-call capture above was taken on the earlier head and is unchanged by this merge; the merge touched only the `Results` dispatch shape, not the timer, the request, or the watchdog.

prs.title: fix(github): keep detail cache windows on elapsed time
prs.body:
<details>
<summary>maintainer-edits</summary>

Maintainer edits are enabled on this branch: feel free to rebase, tweak comment wording, adjust how the rewritten cases are grouped, or land it directly without waiting for another round from me.

</details>

<details>
<summary>maintainer-options</summary>

**Land-ready rationale**

- **Owner:** `detailCache` is a module-private `Map` in `extensions/github/src/detail.ts:66`; all three `entry.expiresAt` writes (:535, :542, :550) and both reads (:300, :322) live in the same `loadGitHubDetailWithIdentity` closure. The five `Date.now()` sites in the file are exactly these TTL sites — after this change the file contains zero `Date.now()` calls, so no mixed time base is possible inside the owner.
- **No contract change:** `grep -rn detailCache` across the repo hits only this file (12 sites); the entry type is never exported, serialized, written to disk or compared anywhere else, so the reading is process-local by construction — what `src/shared/monotonic-time.ts` documents for elapsed readings.
- **Completes the cutover already made next door:** #190894 (merged 2026-11-02) converted the *same shape* in this same extension's sibling store — `extensions/acpx/src/pi-session-store.ts` cache windows went to `performance.now()` — plus `src/gateway/server-methods/usage-cache.ts` and `extensions/github/src/preview.ts` (every timing in it is already `performance.now()`). `detail.ts` is the leftover point.
- **Proof is deterministic and cheap:** two regression cases fail at their intended assertions on current main and the whole file passes at head (5.71s), plus an 8-run real-entry matrix over real HTTPS with control groups.

**Alternatives considered**

| Option | Effect | Cost if chosen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Accept (this PR)** | 5-minute/30-second detail windows are measured on elapsed time; clock corrections neither stampede GitHub reads nor serve stale details | none beyond the 5 one-token changes + comment |
| Keep `Date.now()` and document it | no code change | a `+5 min` jump drops every cached issue/PR detail at once (immediate re-read burst against GitHub rate limits right after a resume); a `−5 min` jump serves PR-head/check state past its 30-second partial window |
| Convert the 429 cooldown in `github-api.ts` too | — | **rejected:** that deadline must stay wall clock — it compares against GitHub's own epoch (`x-ratelimit-reset`, `retry-after`); mixing domains there would be wrong. Out of this PR's scope by design. |

**Scope statement:** 2 files, +46/−5; production change is 5 token swaps plus a 3-line comment. No new option, validator, config key, schema, persistence or shared API. No other extension or core clock site is touched.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

The Control-UI/tool GitHub detail reader (`controlUi.githubDetail`, `tools.github read`) caches issue/PR/commit documents in a process-local map whose windows are computed on the host wall clock:

- `+5 min` wall-clock correction (laptop resume, NTP step, VM restore): every cached detail instantly reads as expired — the next Control-UI render or agent tool read re-issues the repository + item reads immediately, a stampede against GitHub exactly when the host is also re-syncing.
- `−5 min` correction: an entry that passed its 30-second partial window (pull requests, whose heads and checks move independently of the body) keeps being served — stale PR-head/check state stays visible past its designed refresh window for as long as the wall clock lags.

Precedent: [#190894](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/190894) (merged 2026-11-02) moved probe timings and cache windows onto `performance.now()` / `monotonicNow()` across ~20 sites **including the same-shape cache in `extensions/acpx/src/pi-session-store.ts` and every timing in the sibling `extensions/github/src/preview.ts`**; [#190997](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/190997) (same day) applied it to the Discord entity cache. This PR switches the remaining cache window in `detail.ts`.

## Why This Change Was Made

All five TTL sites now read `performance.now()` instead of `Date.now()`: the two freshness reads (:300 hit check, :322 overview reuse) and the three entry writes (:535 success 5 min, :542/:550 partial 30 s). The five sites form one closed loop inside a single function — there is no sixth reader that could compare the stored value against wall time (grep-verified), so the swap cannot split the time base.

Nothing else changes: `SUCCESS_CACHE_MS`/`PARTIAL_CACHE_MS` keep their values, LRU pruning, `refresh` sweeps, the 409 head recheck, identity revalidation and the GitHub-driven 429 cooldown are untouched, and no option/validator/config/persistence is added. The existing `expires cached visibility failures` case now spies both clocks (`Date.now` and `performance.now`), the same adaptation #190894 made in `preview.test.ts`.

Production LOC is `+8/−5` (five swaps plus a 3-line comment).

Classification: `behavior-completing` — it completes the elapsed-time cutover the sibling files already made.

## User Impact

Operators running a long-lived Gateway with the Control UI or GitHub tool reads no longer see detail-cache churn or stale PR state when the host clock is corrected: after a resume the reader keeps serving an entry until its real 5 minutes / 30 seconds pass instead of bursting fresh GitHub requests, and entries never outlive their real window. Under an uncorrected clock the read pattern is identical to before (control runs match request-for-request).

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `2585a253a28c042c58feac36d856d1a5c155640a`
- Current-main RED baseline: `d56403f0c3c25e5d579ba26d49db12b26ece6814` (production untouched; only the new/updated tests applied)

prs.title: fix(gateway): preserve concurrent empty session group creation
prs.body:
Related: #106362 (API foundation only; bundled UI adoption is not included).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: creating an empty session group from a cached catalog can remove an empty group another client just created.

## User Impact

User impact: API clients that adopt `sessions.groups.create` can create empty groups without replacing another client's groups or changing saved defaults and sidebar order.

This is an additive Gateway API, not a change to existing `sessions.groups.put` replacement semantics. Clients must detect `sessions.groups.create` in the advertised methods and call it to benefit; existing clients are not automatically migrated. The operation requires `operator.write` or admin, not `operator.sessions.write`. No database migration or production Gateway changes are included.

**Maintainer decision before merge:** accept this as an API-only foundation, or include bundled group-creation adoption. The existing Control UI race is not fixed by this PR alone.

## Why This Change Was Made

Expose `sessions.groups.create({ name })` through the existing atomic catalog registration owner. Names are bounded, nonblank, trimmed, and idempotent; the response is `{ ok: true, groups, sectionOrder? }`. The existing worker admission rechecks current request authority before committing, and successful requests publish the normal catalog-only `sessions.changed` notification. Refresh-then-put cannot eliminate the original race.

Regenerating protocol validators on Windows exposed backslashes in declaration import specifiers; normalize them in the generator rather than hand-editing generated output. The large generated predicate diff is automatic helper-index renumbering.

Simplification retained one storage owner and introduced no new state, cache, migration, compatibility fallback, or caller-side replacement path.

Excluding generated output, the production/tooling growth is the new public RPC boundary. Its test coverage exercises distinct validation, concurrency, notification, and live-authority regressions. The CI mock repair preserves real module exports and removes one obsolete closed-mock exemption.

## Evidence

### Conflict and CI-budget repair — 2026-11-02

Candidate **43d36364aeb85fb79c465aa702fb949f36dc44c1**, rebased onto **b8ed94ff73d6d10a2e0bbae56cbe6c68f72064c1**. Resolved conflicts by retaining main's appended method descriptors, moving the schema export into the current `public-schema-sessions.ts` owner, and regenerating the canonical protocol predicates. The runtime handler and regression semantics are unchanged. Independent inspection of the authored range-diff found no actionable conflict-resolution issue.

**Passed on the exact final source:** canonical validator generation/parity, protocol registry and since guards, test-line and mock-export guards; **43 tests across five files** (85.59s wrapper wall time); Gateway-method-test and scripts typechecks; targeted lint/format; Gateway protocol package/declarations build and public-mutability contract; normal commit hook and whitespace checks. Compiler preparation dominates the 74.01s Gateway shard; the declaration and protocol-validation shards took 1.37s and 3.08s respectively. Hosted CI timing remains pending for this revision.

Proof used a fresh secretless AWS Crabbox `m7a.xlarge` with **4 CPUs / 15,614 MiB RAM**, Node 24.22.1 and pnpm 12.15.0. Generation run: `run_dbfff24c5d39b978577778a7a84f56c5`; remaining checks continued through the lease's SSH transport after correcting the proof setup to track the two new test files. The first budget invocation counted only 30 lines because those files were untracked; the corrected final check passed at 6,408,379 counted lines with a 6,411,381 ceiling. No source assertions or guard thresholds were weakened. Final full-index patch SHA-256 against the pinned base matched remotely and locally: `4f1e0c19b7f0cb47b9af2e6be00f1458cb782c4edd9b2ca91e388415aa6ed367`.

The unique `config/test-lines-allocations/session-groups-create-186896.txt` grants **exactly +197 net regression-test lines**, justified by distinct concurrent-creation/preservation, current-authority revocation, input validation, method advertisement and portable-declaration contracts. The shared baseline scalar is unchanged; inherited debt is not forgiven. This fixes the earlier PR-attributable budget failure under the current allocation policy.

The earlier live Gateway, restart and released-state upgrade evidence below remains bound to its tested revision; it is not represented as a fresh live execution on this rebase. The [fresh exact-head ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/clawsweeper/actions/runs/41512954401) completed with **no code findings**, **diamond-lobster proof** and **platinum-hermit patch quality**. Overall gold is capped solely by the unresolved API-only scope and current-head maintainer security decisions. [Hosted CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41512859566) is still running; no failed code jobs were observed at this update. The failing `openclaw/ci-gate` status currently states that a maintainer must approve this revision. This preparation supplies neither owner decision nor security approval and does not claim merge readiness.

### Earlier CI repair — head 0a2bb47d720a300193ec511d34b97fa1111ac818

Fixed the actual mock-exports CI failure in [the previous run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40731765379/job/122970522364). **Bounded reproduction of the UI failure:** one fresh secretless AWS run, run_8b527044ac31279367b31f1a7e10392b, tested the exact failed synthetic merge d75df1cfa7dfabb8ce82f08f93c209ad2d20cb1f. It replayed the same 22-file selection through the repository E2E wrapper and cold sequencer with four workers, matching the CI source, Node 24.22.1, pnpm 12.15.0, and selection flags. All **100 tests across 22 files passed**, including the exact annotations test (10.94s), without changing source or assertions. The allocated AWS m7a.xlarge exposed four CPUs / 15,614 MiB RAM; the selected test invocation took 158.84s. This was an isolated reproduction, not a rerun of the hosted check, and does **not** establish a root cause or repair. The original hosted failure remains unresolved. No retries, timeout increases, or speculative UI changes were committed. The test lease was released.

The API-only scope decision and current-head maintainer security approval also remain open. This is an open, reviewable PR, **not a claim of green required checks or merge readiness**.

### Earlier runtime validation — 2026-10-28 (unchanged runtime implementation)

Tested unchanged head **c9f1389fd5e606bb9bac310e6324c11df9454bef** (tree 2ab9157b6e2ab19ee9e20f0a06bc092c1444c6b2). Environment: Linux x86_64, Node **24.22.1**, pnpm **12.15.0**, fresh secretless AWS Crabbox m7a.xlarge (**4 CPUs / 15,614 MiB RAM**). Isolated synthetic state, real loopback Gateway, signed paired-device WebSocket clients; no operator state or provider credentials.

**Reproduction and observed fix:**
1. Two clients read the same catalog containing Existing. Client A writes Existing + First using the unchanged replacement RPC; client B writes its stale Existing + Second. First disappears. This demonstrates why refresh-then-put is not safe creation; replacement semantics intentionally remain unchanged.
2. Three separate write-scoped clients concurrently call the new create RPC with First, Second, and a whitespace-padded First. All three succeed; the final catalog contains exactly Existing, First, Second at positions 0, 1, 2.
3. Existing working-directory/worktree defaults and section order remain exact. Responses are path-free; a separate read-scoped subscriber receives a catalog-only groups notification.
4. Read-only and narrow session-write clients receive FORBIDDEN. Six malformed payloads receive INVALID_REQUEST without changing the catalog. An admin duplicate is a no-op.
5. Stop the Gateway and start a new process on the same synthetic state. Reconnect with the same paired-device credential: the complete catalog, defaults, and section order survive.

**Validation passed:** 47 selected tests across seven files (22 unrelated catalog cases not selected); core, Gateway-method-test, root-tooling-test and scripts typechecks; generated-validator parity, protocol registry and since guards; runtime build; Gateway protocol package/declarations build and public-mutability checks; formatting for all 17 changed files; bounded core/tooling lint; changed-doc MDX; whitespace and clean-source checks.

**Independent review:** exact-head helper-isolated P0–P2 review across three diff partitions, with intact implementation/authority-owner context: no actionable findings, scoped-clean, exit 0. Regeneration parity was verified separately by the executed generator check.

prs.title: fix(ios): nest child sessions and fold subagent runs in the sidebar
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The iPhone sidebar listed far more chats than the Control UI sidebar. Every child session was flattened into a peer row, and subagent runs — which have no transcript of their own — got a row each. One conversation with two runs and a follow-up chat took five rows in the drawer.

Runs spawned from Home were the worst case: Home is not a session row in the drawer, so those runs had no parent to nest under and appeared as extra top-level chats.

Archived chats were already hidden (the Gateway list is queried with `archived: false`, and the shared model filters archives), so they are not part of this fix.

## User Impact

- The drawer lists the same top-level chats as the Control UI. Child chats sit under their parent behind a chevron with a child count, collapsed until opened, and open automatically when one of them is the current chat.
- Subagent runs no longer appear as chats. The row that replaces them still says what they were doing: a spinner while one runs, a clock and "Waiting for a concurrency slot" while one is queued, a warning triangle and the error line when one failed, and an unread dot. Any conversation a run started appears in its place. This holds whether the parent lists the run as a child or only the run names its parent.
- Runs started from Home show on the Home row whether they are running, failed (with the error line), or unread.
- Pinning and groups still own placement: a chat you pinned or moved into a group stays in that section rather than following its parent into another one.
- The 20-row recent cap now counts top-level chats, so one busy parent cannot push the rest of the list away.

No configuration, migration, or data change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two owners disagreed with the drawer. `RootSidebar.sessionNodes(for:)` flattened each section's session tree into peer rows, and the iOS path never folded subagent runs. The shared `sections()` owner also builds one tree per placement bucket (pinned, each group, recent), so a run whose parent sits in another bucket — a pinned parent, a grouped parent — had no parent row in its own section and became a root.

The shared model now folds runs after placement instead of assuming parent and child share a section:

```diff
 ChatSessionSidebarModel.foldingSubagentRuns(sections)
-  runs become rows when their parent is in another section
+  run nested in a conversation's tree -> folds there (its badges are already counted)
+  run at the top of its section       -> owningConversationKey, badges added once
+  run's own conversations -> rows in its place
 ChatSessionSidebarModel.foldedRuns(in:under:)   # Home
+  same owningConversationKey walk, so backref-only runs reach Home too
 RootSidebar
-  flattened(section.nodes).prefix(20)      # every descendant as a peer row
+  sessionTreeRows(roots.prefix(20), childExpansion)
+  childToggle                              # chevron + child count
+  sessionSubtitle: failed child > own status > queued child > work line
+  Home row: failed-run triangle and error line
```

`owningConversationKey` prefers the roster's own child link (`childSessions`), falls back to the run's `spawnedBy`/`parentSessionKey`, and walks through intermediate runs that have no row, stopping at the first ordinary conversation. Section folding and Home both use it, so a run lands on one surviving row. A run whose ancestor has no row at all (an archived parent, a filtered search) hands its conversations over as rows instead of vanishing with it.

The rules come from the Control UI session tree (`ui/src/components/app-sidebar-session-tree.ts`), not new ones: runs are never rows, their persistent children take their place, and the owner keeps their badges and attention. `Node.previewSessions` and the run classifier moved to the shared model so the macOS sidebar and iOS use one copy; macOS behaviour is unchanged.

### Review follow-up (revision 3)

ClawSweeper's revision-2 review found four places where folding dropped a run's status along with its row. All four are fixed in `34d59f2`:

- **Badges counted by section membership.** A run linked to its parent only by `spawnedBy` stays a separate root in the section tree, so the parent never counted it, yet folding skipped its badges whenever the parent sat in the same section. Folding now treats a run as counted only when it is nested in the owner's tree; top-level runs add their badges once.
- **Home ignored backrefs.** Home collected runs through forward `childSessions` links only, which the Gateway freshness-filters. Home now uses the same ownership walk as folding, still stopping at an ordinary child conversation.
- **Home hid failed runs.** The Home row now shows the warning triangle and "Child session … failed: …" line for an unread failed run.
- **Queued runs looked idle.** A queued run's parent now shows a clock and "Waiting for a concurrency slot" in place of the work line.

The two overlapping fold tests ClawSweeper flagged are merged into one, keeping the all-run empty-section assertion.

## Evidence

Synthetic demo data only: the app's screenshot/demo transport with a temporary fork-only fixture flag (not part of this PR). GitHub-hosted macOS runners.

**Review follow-up** ([fork screenshot run](https://github.com/jorge-monalee/openclaw/actions/runs/40895184173)). The fixture adds three runs that name their owner only through `spawnedBy`: "Morning digest" (failed, unread, started from Home), "Hotel booking" (queued, under the idle "Trip planning"), and "Itinerary summary" (finished, unread, under "Trip planning").

| Prior PR head (`ad293c2`) | This head (`34d59f2`) |
| --- | --- |
| ![Prior head: Home shows only a spinner with no sign of the failed Morning digest run; Trip planning looks idle with no subtitle, no queued icon and no unread dot](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d758f887-dd94-4e07-9aab-d6ba595411ab) | ![This head: Home shows a warning triangle and "Child session Morning digest failed: Digest timed out"; Trip planning shows a clock, "Waiting for a concurrency slot" and an unread dot](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d5d48d0-2d1a-4934-80d0-e5ec27c12a6a) |

Before, Home keeps only its running run's spinner and "Trip planning" looks idle. After, Home names the failed run and its error, and "Trip planning" shows its queued run and its unread finished run. "Release plan" is unchanged. Captured on the `xcode-27` image (iPhone simulator, iOS 27) because `macos-26` arm64 runners were unavailable; both columns come from the same run.

**Original change** (revision 1, iPhone 17 Pro simulator on `macos-26` / Xcode 26.6, earlier fixture: "Release plan" with a running run, a failed unread run and one child chat; "Trip planning"; an archived "Q3 plan" with an orphaned run; a run started from Home):

| Before (`main` at `dadf912`) | After, default | After, expanded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![Before: Inbox triage, Release plan, Collect release notes, Competitor research and Changelog draft are separate rows](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5d72dd15-cc54-4ed6-9e55-eea949bdf352) | ![After: Release plan carries the spinner, failed warning, unread dot and a collapsed child count; Home shows its run](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f19c80eb-6330-48cd-9c70-2d8c46f3580d) | ![After expanding: Changelog draft nested under Release plan](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9a7b50e1-c367-4831-8b93-b423ce28bd01) |

Tests:

- **Red on the prior head, green on this head** (shared package): the new tests run against `ad293c2`'s sources fail exactly where the review said: with only a `spawnedBy` link, the parent's badges are `failedCount 0, hasUnread false` instead of `1, true`; and Home's runs are `[home-run, nested-run]` without `backref-run`. The forward-linked case passes on both heads, so the fix does not double count. With the fix, `swift test --filter 'ChatSessionSidebar|ChatCommandPalette'` passes 310 tests in 24 suites ([run](https://github.com/jorge-monalee/openclaw/actions/runs/40885246537); that run's head differs from `34d59f2` only by `///` → `//` on one nested-function comment).
- **iOS**: `RootTabsPresentationTests`, `RootSidebarTypographyTests`, `OpenClawTypographyTests` pass on this head (85 tests, including the new `drawer row says its folded run is waiting for a slot`), plus the sidebar UI test that produces the screenshots ([run](https://github.com/jorge-monalee/openclaw/actions/runs/40895184173)).
- **Original change** ([run](https://github.com/jorge-monalee/openclaw/actions/runs/40807125391)): `drawer folds subagent runs into their parent session` fails on `main` and passes on the PR.
- SwiftFormat and SwiftLint (iOS and macOS scopes) clean and `pnpm native:i18n:verify` passes on this head ([run](https://github.com/jorge-monalee/openclaw/actions/runs/40885839927)); `git diff --check` passes.

Not covered: a physical iPhone.

Prepared by Jorge's AI assistant on his behalf.

prs.title: fix: configure, classic onboarding and agents add save new channel tokens as plaintext in openclaw.json
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/175333

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a channel token entered in `openclaw configure`, classic onboarding (and the Gateway's default `wizard.start` flow, which runs the same setup), `openclaw agents add` or the chat's channel setup in Control UI is saved as plaintext in `openclaw.json`. The same token entered through `openclaw channels add` goes to the protected secret store since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/169732. Doctor then warns about plaintext secret-bearing fields, and the prompt's plaintext option says "Stores the credential directly in OpenClaw config".

## User Impact

User impact: a new or changed channel credential entered through any of these setup paths is saved as a protected entry in the shared secret store, and `openclaw.json` keeps a `store` SecretRef, as with `openclaw channels add`. The plaintext entry option now reads "Saves the credential in the protected secret store". Existing config is not rewritten: only credentials that differ from the config the setup started from are moved, so plaintext tokens, SecretRefs and env references saved by earlier releases stay as they are.

`--secret-input-mode plaintext` (the onboarding default) still means typing the value in. Channel credentials entered that way now go to the store as well, as they already do in `channels add`.

## Why This Change Was Made

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/169732 put the protected-store step inside `persistChannelPluginConfig`, the save path of `channels add` and the Gateway's channels wizard. The other setup paths run the same `setupChannels` prompts but commit config through their own writers, so they never reached it.

What changes:
- The store loop moves unchanged out of `persistChannelPluginConfig` into `storeChannelSetupCredentials` in the same module. `persistChannelPluginConfig` calls it as before, so `channels add` keeps its retained-entry notice and its authority checks.
- `configure`, onboarding, `agents add` and `runHostedChannelSetup` call it at their config commit point, comparing against the config the channel step started from. The hosted chat setup passes its existing `beforePersistentApply` and live-owner assertion, so a stale chat session still cannot write.
- The Gateway's `wizard.start` setup flow passes the wizard session's cancellation lock and liveness check into that store write, as its channels flow already does: if the client cancels after the token prompt and before the store write, the write throws and nothing is saved; once the write has begun, cancellation is refused until the next prompt. Because setup keeps prompting after the channel step, it takes that preparation lock rather than the permanent one. A setup session cannot be replaced mid-flow: setup admission rejects a second setup session as busy.
- `wizard.ts` composes that liveness check with the `assertCurrent` callback `startGatewayWizard` gives the session. Since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/183777, that callback checks the starting operator's retained grant, so a revoked device, a lost operator scope or a rotated shared credential now fails the check. Both `wizard.start` flows use it, so this also closes the same window in the existing channels flow.
- The check runs at the store writer's admission and inside the config writer's `assertBeforePublish`, the synchronous hook `config.patch` uses. Before, both flows checked once before awaiting the config commit, and an isolated Gateway showed the commit publishing after a device removal while it waited on locks. A store write already admitted settles; its entry then stays unreferenced (see the first accepted limit).
- The Control UI chat follows the same rule. `ChatWizardHost.forTurn` binds each queued chat turn to its Gateway request's `hasCurrentClientAuthority`, and the host's persistent-effect check, already used at the hosted store write, now also fails once that authority is gone. `runHostedSetup` runs the channel setup's check in the same `assertBeforePublish` hook. CLI chat has no request scope and passes no authority, as before.
- The plaintext option's hint and `docs/start/wizard-cli-reference.md` describe where the credential goes.

The store step runs where each path commits config, not inside `setupChannels`: a later prompt, a cancel or a failed check before the commit then leaves no store entries behind.

Accepted limits:
- If the config write fails after the store write (including a requester whose authority ends between the two), `configure`, onboarding, `agents add`, the Gateway setup flow and the hosted chat leave unreferenced store entries without the "retained" notice that `channels add` prints. The entries are unused and the config keeps its previous value; a retry stores the credential under a new name.
- Like `channels add`, the store step covers credential paths registered as channel secret-input targets. A plugin credential outside that registry is still saved as entered, under the same option hint.
- While the store write holds the preparation lock, `wizard.cancel` is refused and returns `status: "running"`; the cancel is not queued, so the client cancels again at the next prompt.

<details><summary>Writers and overlapping PRs</summary>

Writers that skipped the store step: `writeWizardConfigFile` in `configure` and the hosted chat setup, `commitSetupConfigFile` in onboarding and Gateway `wizard.start` setup, `createAgent` and `commitConfigWithPendingPluginInstalls` in `agents add`.

Open PRs touching the same files (none changes the channel save step):
- `src/wizard/setup.ts`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/127083, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/163527, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166573
- `src/commands/configure.wizard.ts`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166573, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/131153
- `src/commands/agents.commands.add.ts`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/174857, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/175069, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168268
- Draft https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/121563 adds a shared credential-mode hint in `src/channels/plugins/setup-wizard-credential-mode.ts` that still says "Stores the credentials directly in OpenClaw config"; whichever lands second should use this PR's wording.

</details>

## Evidence

The CLI built from this branch and from the base `19c5e58c2e8`, each run in a fresh `HOME` and state directory under `env -i`, with synthetic tokens. The prompts were driven in a pseudo-terminal by the same step file on both sides. Runs that start the Gateway or the bundled Codex app-server were in a network namespace with only loopback.

Re-run on 2026-10-30 at the head `e268f2377da`, after merging `main` `885e57e9f9d`, with the same scripts on Node 24.22.1:
- `configure`: `botToken` is a `store` SecretRef, `openclaw.json` holds no copy of the token, the entry option says "Saves the credential in the protected secret store", and `secrets audit --check` exits 0, clean.
- Gateway `wizard.start`: the forbidden, cancel and complete scenarios match the first table below. With the answering device removed 2 to 100 ms after its last answer, 0 of 23 runs published the token to config. At 2 and 15 ms (10 runs) the removal cut off the answer before it reached the session, so nothing was written. From 25 ms on (13 runs) the session ended with one unreferenced store entry each (the first accepted limit above).
- Hosted chat: the forbidden and complete steps match the hosted chat table below. With the answering device removed at its last answer, 0 of 5 runs published config or stored an entry.

The hosted chat table no longer lists a second `operator.admin` device answering the admin's step. Since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176587, shared-token operator connections share the Gateway owner profile, so a second shared-token admin device is the same chat owner on `main` too. This PR does not change session ownership.

The tables below keep the commits they were first measured at.

`openclaw configure --section channels`, Telegram, "Enter Telegram bot token":

| Check | Before (`19c5e58c2e8`) | After (`dd48b4790aa`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entry option hint | "Stores the credential directly in OpenClaw config" | "Saves the credential in the protected secret store" |
| `channels.telegram.botToken` in `openclaw.json` | **the token** | `{"source": "store", "provider": "default", "id": "CHANNEL_SETUP_…"}` |
| `doctor --lint` `core/doctor/security` plaintext warning (`Paths: channels.telegram.botToken`) | **present** | absent; the other five findings are unchanged |
| `secrets audit --check` | **exit 1, plaintext=1** | exit 0, clean, unresolved=0 |

`openclaw onboard --classic --flow quickstart --mode local --auth-choice skip --skip-…`, Telegram at "Select channel (QuickStart)", After at `6719dd19adc`:
- Before: exit 0; the token is in `openclaw.json` and `openclaw.json.bak`.
- After: exit 0; `botToken` is a `store` SecretRef and only the state database holds the token. `secrets audit --check` lists only `gateway.auth.token`, which onboarding generates and which this PR does not touch.

`openclaw agents add helper` on the onboarded state (After only, `6719dd19adc`), Discord at "Set up a chat channel now?": exit 0, "Agent "helper" ready.", `channels.discord.token` is a `store` SecretRef, resolves, and only the state database holds the token.

Gateway `wizard.start` setup, built at `786f6bc8daf` (the production code of the then-head `080097ce070`, which added one test-only commit): an isolated Gateway with token auth and a driver on the real `callGateway` client, answering each `wizard.next` step and reading the config file and `secrets.store.list` after each scenario.

| Scenario | Result | `channels.telegram.botToken` | Store entries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| client with `[operator.write]` calls `wizard.start` | rejected: "missing scope: operator.admin" | absent | none |
| admin client enters the token, cancels at the next prompt | `cancelled` | absent | none |
| admin client completes QuickStart setup | `done` | `store` SecretRef | exactly the referenced entry |

The cancel above stops at a prompt, which the flow already honored. The new guard covers a cancel that lands after the last prompt and before the store write; the `wizard.test.ts` case below shows that window.

Device revoked after the last prompt, same Gateway setup: a client with its own paired device answers every step. At "Set up administration from your own chat account?", the last prompt before the store write, it sends its answer, and an admin client removes that device with `device.pair.remove` at once. Each run used a fresh state.

| Gateway build | Runs | Token stored after the removal | `wizard.status` after the answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `6719dd19adc` (session hooks only) | 5 | **5** (config published 154–173 ms after the removal) | `running` |
| `fcc798f1332` (client check before the awaited commit) | 5 | **1** (config published 167 ms after the removal, after a lock wait) | `running` in the stored run, once `error` "Gateway caller authority is no longer active.", otherwise already ended |
| `3e378f75424`, a local build of `70078921176`'s production code before a test-only amend; it differs from `080097ce070` only in `src/system-agent` and `setup.test.ts` (check at publication) | 10 | 0 | already ended and collected |

Hosted chat in Control UI (`openclaw.chat`), the same isolated Gateway setup, built at `786f6bc8daf`, the production code of the then-head `080097ce070`. A chat session needs a verified model before it starts, so a loopback stand-in for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint answering "OK" was the default model; it was called once, for that check. The admin, a client with its own paired device, sent "connect telegram" and answered each hosted wizard step with `wizardAnswer`, as Control UI does.

| Step | Result | Config field | Store entries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[operator.write]` client sends "connect telegram" | rejected: "missing scope: operator.admin" | absent | none |
| at the admin's token step, an `[operator.write]` client answers it | rejected: "missing scope: operator.admin" | absent | none |
| the admin answers through the last step | "Done — telegram is configured." | `store` SecretRef | exactly the referenced entry |

Hosted chat, answering device removed at its last chat answer ("Set up administration from your own chat account?"), a fresh state per run. Counted runs are those where the removal closed the answering request (4001); two `786f6bc8daf` runs where the request completed instead are listed in the proof file and excluded. In one, the answer's connection was silently re-paired on loopback after the removal. In the other, its handshake finished as the removal ran. `device.pair.remove` closes only registered connections, so a connection whose handshake completes during the removal keeps its capture, and loopback silent pairing can approve the device again; that is an existing Gateway race outside this PR.

| Gateway build | Removal | Counted runs | Config published after the removal | Store entry left |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before the hosted fix (`wizard.start` fixes only) | at once | 5 | **3** | 3 |
| `786f6bc8daf` | at once | 13 | 0 | 0 |
| `786f6bc8daf` | after 30 ms | 10 | 0 | 10, admitted before the removal; unreferenced (first accepted limit) |

## What Problem This Solves

<!--
Describe the concrete user, product, or operational problem.
Use one short, plain-language sentence. For fixes, prefer:
"Fixes: <what goes wrong> when <trigger or condition>."
For other changes, describe the need without inventing a bug.

Independently versioned chat clients cannot discover the existing queue-mode and exact input-receipt contract without guessing from a protocol version or an unrelated capability.

**This is an additive compatibility-contract feature, not a fix for a demonstrated data-loss or model-steering bug.** The regression below proves missing discovery before the change and correct advertisement afterward; it does not prove that the marker itself repairs queue execution.

## User Impact

<!--
"User impact: <what users, operators, or developers can now do or expect>."
Lead with the concrete outcome in plain language, usually one sentence.
For internal-only changes, say there is no user-visible change; do not invent a benefit.
Keep important risks, breaking changes, migrations, and required user actions visible here.
-->

Clients can check `hello-ok.features.capabilities` for `chat-input-custody-v1` before offering the existing `chat.send.queueMode` and `chat.history.inputRunIds` / `inputReceipts` contract. If absent, support is unknown and the client retains its existing send behavior.

The marker is **not permission, active-backend injection availability, acknowledgment-as-consumption, or permanent exactly-once delivery**. Requested scopes are not increased. No new RPC, protocol version, queue policy, backend, migration, bundled UI or consumer implementation is added.

## Why This Change Was Made

<!--

Keep the body short. Leave file lists, internal acronyms, and root-cause walkthroughs
in the diff or optional <details>; include technical detail only when it explains
behavior or a material tradeoff. Do not hide risks or required actions in <details>.
-->

The existing server capability registry and hello owner are the discovery boundary. One constant and one hello-array entry expose the transport contract; the owner regression also checks unchanged read-only scopes. The handshake documentation explains pending versus consumed receipts, bounded idempotency, and retention of uncertain input.

At upstream main [`6c672d42f2dec42b7917f34dfe5ae8157b9b0abb`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/6c672d42f2dec42b7917f34dfe5ae8157b9b0abb) (2026-10-29), both the capability registry and hello response still omit this marker. The existing `chat-send-routing-contract` is not this input-custody discovery contract. No current-main code was substituted for the tested historical base.

## Evidence

The **same** `advertises input custody without changing negotiated scopes` regression and command were used on both sides. Test-file SHA256 was `0FC3C374ABE9B8DE48513DE1492330E1E36A7A5FBAF0E822161542C281C5ACFC` in both runs and matches the committed head.

prs.title: fix(plugins): keep Matrix and Copilot libc detection from blocking the Linux Gateway on slow DNS
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/188930

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: on Linux, the whole Gateway stops for seconds when the Matrix plugin prepares its crypto runtime for the first E2EE attachment, or when the Copilot harness captures or validates its runtime artifact, on a host whose DNS is slow or unreachable.

## User Impact

User impact: Matrix E2EE media and Copilot runtime artifact capture and validation no longer stall every other channel, the Control UI and RPC calls on Linux hosts with a slow resolver.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both plugins told glibc from musl with `process.report.getReport()`. Node builds that report synchronously and, unless `process.report.excludeNetwork` is set, reverse-resolves the peer of every open socket, so each socket can cost a full resolver timeout on the Gateway's main thread. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/188521 replaced the same detection in the CUA plugin with a read of the loaded libc from `/proc/self/maps`.

- Matrix (`isMuslRuntime`) and Copilot (`runtimePlatform`) now read `/proc/self/maps`, as in the CUA fix, keeping each plugin's existing result shape.
- Matrix also loads `@matrix-org/matrix-sdk-crypto-nodejs`, whose native loader builds the same report once to pick its binding. `ensureMatrixCryptoRuntime` now sets `process.report.excludeNetwork` only for that synchronous `require` and restores the previous value afterwards (skipped when the runtime has no `process.report`). It is the package's first load in the process: the crypto bindings module is imported only after `ensureMatrixCryptoRuntime`, and `matrix-js-sdk` does not load the package.
- Matrix keeps its existing fallback: if `/proc/self/maps` cannot be read, it assumes musl, as it did when the report failed.
- Copilot has no fallback: if `/proc/self/maps` cannot be read (a heavily restricted procfs), the runtime artifact capture fails with the read error (validation reports the runtime as changed) instead of guessing a platform package. A Linux host without a readable `/proc` is rare and the failure is visible, so this is an accepted edge case.
- The obsolete assertion allowance for `deps.ts` is removed (2 to 1), as the assertion-safety ratchet asks.

## Evidence

Tested at `fb4e388d729d` (base `upstream/main` `cf83a69f74ee`).

The real QA Matrix lane on Ubuntu 22.04 with Node 24.22.1: a disposable local homeserver, a real Gateway child process, synthetic accounts and the mock model provider. Inside a private mount namespace only, `/etc/resolv.conf` points at an unreachable server (`nameserver 10.255.255.1`, `options timeout:1 attempts:1`). A preload wraps `process.report.getReport()` and logs each call's duration and caller. Same command on both sides:

```text
OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node pnpm openclaw qa matrix --provider-mode mock-openai --scenario matrix-e2ee-media-image
```

Before (base `cf83a69f74ee`):

```text
gateway.stderr.log:
09:50:45.485 [spy] getReport took 27.4ms     at isMuslFromReport (@openclaw/fs-safe/dist/native.js:78:39)
09:51:22.571 [spy] getReport took 24.8ms     at isMuslFromReport (@openclaw/fs-safe/dist/native.js:78:39)
09:53:51.916 [spy] getReport took 4166.2ms   at isMuslRuntime (dist/extensions/matrix/.setup/deps-D-W_QQjz.mjs:38:39)
09:53:56.087 [spy] getReport took 4167.1ms   at isMusl (@matrix-org/matrix-sdk-crypto-nodejs/index.js:26:52)
09:53:56.105 [event-loop] main-thread stall: elapsedMs=6104 task=unattributed stallStartMs=1793408030001 stallEndMs=1793408036105
qa-suite-report.md:
- Passed: 0
- Failed: 1
- Details: QA scenario flow timed out after 180000ms
```

After (this PR):

```text
gateway.stderr.log:
09:59:39.388 [spy] getReport took 31.5ms     at isMuslFromReport (@openclaw/fs-safe/dist/native.js:78:39)
10:00:16.317 [spy] getReport took 24.4ms     at isMuslFromReport (@openclaw/fs-safe/dist/native.js:78:39)
10:00:58.796 [spy] getReport took 118.7ms    at isMusl (@matrix-org/matrix-sdk-crypto-nodejs/index.js:26:52)
10:01:34.246 [spy] getReport took 25.0ms     at isMuslFromReport (@openclaw/fs-safe/dist/native.js:78:39)
no "[event-loop] main-thread stall" line
qa-suite-report.md:
- Passed: 1
- Failed: 0
```

Observed result: on the base, preparing the Matrix crypto runtime for the first encrypted image builds the report twice in the Gateway, once in OpenClaw (4,166.2 ms) and once in the dependency's loader (4,167.1 ms), and the stall monitor logs a 6.1 s stall (it records a lower bound). The scenario times out because the QA driver, which loads the same plugin code and holds more sockets, blocks in the same two calls for 51,255.6 ms and 51,259.3 ms. On this branch OpenClaw's own call is gone, and the dependency's call runs without the network section (118.7 ms in the Gateway, 4.7 ms in the driver). The Gateway logs no stall and the scenario passes. The stall was observed with the Gateway on Node (`OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node`); an earlier base run on the default Bun test runtime passed without it.

Timed directly, `ensureMatrixCryptoRuntime` from the built plugin, in a Node process holding 3 loopback sockets with the unreachable resolver: base 26,145.1 ms (two report calls, 13,068.7 ms and 13,067.5 ms), this branch 3.3 ms (one call, 1.3 ms).

Copilot setup verification, same host and Node, both sides built from source:

- **Entry point:** the real Gateway RPC `openclaw.setup.verify`, with `github-copilot/auto` on the `copilot` agent runtime.
- **Network:** a private user, mount and network namespace whose resolver never answers.
- **Sign-in stand-in:** a real run needs a Copilot sign-in, because the account lookup runs before the harness starts. A loopback stand-in for a GitHub Enterprise tenant answers only that lookup (`/copilot_internal/user`), with `COPILOT_GITHUB_DOMAIN` set to a synthetic `*.ghe.com` tenant (shown here as `example.ghe.com`), a self-signed certificate trusted through `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, and a synthetic token.
- **Logging:** the same preload also logs `/proc/self/maps` reads and the Copilot runtime spawn.

Nothing serves Copilot's API, so the model turn then times out on both sides. That part is not under test.

Call chains condensed.

Before (base `cf83a69f74ee`):

```text
09:23:46.074 [spy] getReport took 5073.8ms   at runtimePlatform < captureCopilotRuntimeArtifact < acquire
09:23:46.078 [event-loop] main-thread stall: elapsedMs=5089
09:23:46.333 [spy] child_process.spawn @github/copilot-sdk-linux-x64/prebuilds/linux-x64/copilot-runtime
09:23:50.450 [spy] getReport took 4076.1ms   at runtimePlatform < captureCopilotRuntimeArtifact < validateCopilotRuntimeArtifact
09:23:50.470 [event-loop] main-thread stall: elapsedMs=4095
... 5 more captures on same-model retries, 4,063.4 to 4,070.2 ms each, each followed by a stall line
transient retry window elapsed for github-copilot/auto after 5/8 retries
```

After (this PR):

```text
09:21:46.720 [spy] readFileSync /proc/self/maps took 1.1ms   at runtimePlatform < captureCopilotRuntimeArtifact < acquire
09:21:46.807 [spy] child_process.spawn @github/copilot-sdk-linux-x64/prebuilds/linux-x64/copilot-runtime
09:21:46.841 [spy] readFileSync /proc/self/maps took 1.4ms   at runtimePlatform < captureCopilotRuntimeArtifact < validateCopilotRuntimeArtifact
... 6 more captures on same-model retries, 0.8 to 1.2 ms each
no getReport call from Copilot code, no "[event-loop] main-thread stall" line
transient retry window elapsed for github-copilot/auto after 6/8 retries
```

Observed result:

- **Base:** capture and validation build the report once each (5,073.8 ms and 4,076.1 ms). The time from capture to a validated runtime is 9.5 s, 9.2 s of it blocked. Every retry blocks it again for about 4.1 s: 29.5 s and 7 stall lines over the run. The stalls also used up part of the retry window (5 retries, against 6 to 7 on this branch).
- **This branch:** capture to validated runtime takes 0.12 s. Each libc check is a map read of about 1 ms.
- **Both sides:** setup verification selects and spawns the same packaged `copilot-runtime`, and validation passes (no "runtime changed" error). The Copilot SDK builds no report on this path: OpenClaw passes the packaged executable, so the SDK skips its own bundled-runtime lookup (`ensureRuntimeBundle`), which builds one. The only other report is `@openclaw/fs-safe` at startup (24.0 ms and 24.8 ms).

Regression tests: the Copilot test "preserves native links across equivalent captures and invalidates changed bytes" asserts that no report is built; both Matrix "bootstraps a missing/truncated runtime once" tests assert that the crypto package is loaded with `excludeNetwork` set, that it is restored afterwards, and that OpenClaw builds no report. They fail on the base and pass on this branch; the other 6 tests in the two files pass on both.

Checks: the touched tests (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`, wall time per file in the table below), `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`, oxlint and format on the changed files, `pnpm check:assertion-safety`, and the test-lines ratchet (net delta 0; the tree at the base is already 1,033 lines over its ceiling: 6,313,571 lines, ceiling 6,312,538). The broad suites run in this PR's CI.

| Test file                                         | Local `--maxWorkers=1` wall                      | CI seconds       |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- |
| `extensions/copilot/src/runtime-artifact.test.ts` | 5.7 s (mostly transform; tests themselves 39 ms) | 25 ms (4 tests)  |
| `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/deps.test.ts`       | 6.5 s                                            | 235 ms (5 tests) |

The CI column comes from [checks-node-changed-extensions-bundle-1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41156109407/job/124403475433) at this head. Its log has no per-file total, so each figure is the sum of the file's per-test times.

Not covered:

- Copilot setup verification ran against a loopback stand-in for GitHub's account lookup, not a real Copilot account, and no model turn was served. The code that captures, selects and validates the runtime is the shipped code.
- musl detection was checked by running the same pattern against `/proc/self/maps` in a `node:24-alpine` container, not through the Gateway.
- Core `src/infra/npm-managed-root.ts` still builds the report, during plugin install and uninstall only.
- `extensions/llama-cpp` still builds the report during server install; it needs the glibc version, which the map does not give.
- Copilot's SDK still builds the report itself when it looks up its bundled runtime (plain Copilot runs and isolated completions, where no executable is passed). That needs a separate change. Setup verification passes the executable, so it builds none (above).
- `@openclaw/fs-safe`, an external package, builds the report when it loads its native binding, starting at Gateway startup: about 25 ms per call in the Gateway above, about 39 s in the QA driver process, the same on both sides.

prs.title: fix(clickclack): discussion rooms fail with PostgreSQL agents
prs.body:
Related: #188643, #175199

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: opening a ClickClack discussion room from Panels → Discussion fails when the Gateway's agent database family uses PostgreSQL.

## User Impact

Discussion rooms can be created and reopened with PostgreSQL-backed agents. SQLite behavior, session resets during channel creation, current-account checks, and binding commit authority are preserved. No configuration, schema, retention, or public SDK change is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The opening path still performed a synchronous session read at its effect boundaries. PostgreSQL correctly refuses that read on the Gateway thread. This uses the plugin's existing prepared-session authority helper for each effect and final binding commit, releasing each preparation in a finally block. It deliberately reacquires current session authority after HTTP instead of freezing one incarnation for the entire open. Existing FIFO, quarantine/recovery, and binding CAS owners remain unchanged.

This is separate from #188643, which fixed NUL-containing revocation keys when shared state uses PostgreSQL.

## Evidence

**Baseline:** built source `9c22cf86f68b34269e49a25a95827c1c23b52ce0`, isolated PostgreSQL 17.11, synthetic state/token, and a loopback ClickClack HTTP fixture. Actual CLI/Gateway `sessions.create` succeeded; `session.discussion.open` returned `UNAVAILABLE: PostgreSQL connections must run in a worker…` before any remote channel POST. The committed real-storage regression also fails on unchanged production source at `service-open.ts:274 → assertEngineStoreExecutionAllowed`.

Initial published head: `25e6c72731ff6134258e171a8cc59c64dc7539ce`. Its Git tree `b51a601c9703edd63bea0891dcf7c493cb8ffd11` exactly matches the reviewed, built implementation commit below; the managed publisher added its commit attribution/receipt without changing source bytes. Both commits have the exact @etzelm coauthor trailer.

**Built product at the reviewed implementation commit:** `f54f44abfa07d4a474aa27639b0109a6bcd72107`. Both official build stamps report that head and clean inputs. The executing runtime was the repository's pinned Bun fork, version 1.4.4. No Gateway handler, session reader, authority owner, or database boundary was mocked.

| Actual built Gateway case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL agents: create → discussion open → independent discussion info | Open; exactly one remote channel; persisted binding matches the PostgreSQL session row |
| PostgreSQL agents: public `sessions.reset` while the channel-create HTTP response is held | Open; lifecycle revision changes, session ID is preserved by the public reset contract, and the persisted binding remains current |
| SQLite parity through the same CLI/Gateway flow | Open; exactly one remote channel; independently read persisted binding matches the current session |

All three product cases passed and completed fixture cleanup. The three Gateway PIDs and PostgreSQL PID file were verified absent afterward. Independent SQL checks compared the binding with `session_nodes.current_session_id`; results were not inferred only from an RPC acknowledgment. The PostgreSQL product cases took 26.0s and 26.8s of test time; SQLite took 24.2s. These are behavior receipts, not performance claims.

**Focused validation:**

- New service regression uses real SQLite/PostgreSQL session and plugin-state owners; only external HTTP transport is replaced. It covers ordinary opening, a changed session ID during HTTP, and archive/removal/credential/destination changes before creation. It is red on the base and green on the repair.
- SQLite service, persistence, CAS/refusal/recovery, shutdown, and new authority tests: **69 passed in 3 files**, 75.21s wall time including preparation.
- Supported PostgreSQL conformance runner: **2 passed in 2 files**, including the new agent-storage regression and existing PostgreSQL shared-state revocation case, 36.98s wall time. The new regression itself took 1.8s. PostgreSQL catalog/trigger preflight passed.
- Conformance-planner tests: **6 passed**. Targeted production and test typechecks, scoped lint, formatting, whitespace, and the test-line budget passed. The dedicated **234-line allocation** covers the final 233-line real-storage regression and one line of phase-based reset-fixture growth; the shared ceiling is unchanged. CI seconds are not yet available.
- Fresh independent **Auto Review**, full six-file candidate against `9c22cf86…`, P0–P2: **scoped-clean**, no findings. The author simplification pass retained the existing authority owner and only the lifetime handling needed for these effects.

**CI follow-up:** the first hosted run exposed an ordinal-based reset fixture in `service.test.ts` (`session read 2`), reproduced locally as 38 passed / 1 failed. The new authority preparation intentionally adds a read and refuses a stale selected incarnation. The fixture now triggers its existing initial-read and after-create-read reset scenarios by service phase instead of read count; its binding and presentation assertions are unchanged. All **108 tests in the four affected service files** pass (63.2s command wall time), including both reset cases. Production code is unchanged from the built product proof. Follow-up targeted typecheck/lint/format, the exact 197-line test budget, author simplification, and fresh independent Auto Review of the two-file follow-up passed. No failed assertion or authority guard was relaxed. Fixture-follow-up source tree was `6aaf0b18460ad9e5d47a8eba831c3287703b6ae8` (local reviewed `cb3ccc3bcd08afeb621046ae3fa6882e1141304c`; managed published `ea0008ae395997ed69823495f54190e7d47febc0`). That prior review exposed the authority-recovery issue repaired below; latest-head CI and re-review remain separate gates.

### Authority-recovery finding repaired

ClawSweeper correctly found that an authority refusal was entering transport reconciliation. The follow-up separates preparation/adoption bookkeeping from attempted HTTP, permits ambiguous-outcome recovery only after a dispatched mutation, and re-prepares live authority before every recovery/name-conflict relist. No catch identifies errors by message, and no guard is relaxed.

The real-storage regression now counts channel GETs as well as creates. It was red on the reviewed head (4 GETs observed versus 3 expected), then green on SQLite and PostgreSQL. It proves successful ambiguous-create recovery still relists and adopts, while archive/removal/credential/destination refusal produces no follow-up GET; retirement during a failed POST produces neither relist nor binding. PostgreSQL conformance: 2/2 passed, new regression 1.945s; SQLite strengthened regression 1.759s. The exact grant is now **234 lines** (233-line real-storage regression plus one phase-fixture line), with the shared ceiling unchanged.

At clean local commit `46586bfbd0b227746dbf9545b5433f261278827c`, official built Gateway/PostgreSQL product proof was rerun: allowed open/reset-during-HTTP/info passed; public `sessions.patch {archived:true}` during the held create response refused attachment and an independent persisted-state query found no binding. Sanitized channel traces through the real HTTP client:

```text
allowed/reset: GET /api/workspaces/:workspace/channels -> POST /api/workspaces/:workspace/channels -> open/info; binding matches current PG session
archive during POST response: GET /api/workspaces/:workspace/channels -> POST /api/workspaces/:workspace/channels -> UNAVAILABLE inactive; binding absent; no follow-up channel request
```

Archive product test: 23.5s, runner exit 0; allowed reset: 26.4s, runner exit 0. An earlier archive attempt passed assertions but had a worker graceful-shutdown error; the verbose diagnostic run above completed cleanly, which does not establish a fix to that harness event. A separate attempted product credential-reload fixture was **not accepted as proof**: waiting for config.patch application while holding the plugin HTTP response caused a reload drain timeout; observing persistence alone was not equivalent to applied authority. Credential/destination retirement is therefore proven by the real-client/real-storage service boundary, not claimed as completed built-Gateway reload proof. No live account or provider was used.

Both final build stamps report local commit `46586bf…` with clean inputs. Managed published head is `a0fd38358dc454a223dc872e17177e6f26ba3719`; local source tree is `ed73f23dce42000afce2233d6accb8b203ae5959`. Production/test types, scoped lint/format, ratchet, author simplification and fresh independent Auto Review P0–P2 passed; existing CAS/refusal/recovery siblings remain green (108 tests across four files before the additional request controls). All owned Gateways and PostgreSQL were stopped.

**Known local failure, not hidden:** `test/scripts/extension-test-plan.test.ts` has three filesystem-inventory failures: owner-boundary balancing, candidate-checkout inventory, and Workboard directory/glob selection. All three reproduce after restoring both changed routing inputs to their base bytes. The ClickClack repair and test do not participate in those discovery cases. No assertions, guards, or baselines were weakened; hosted CI remains separate evidence.

**Limits:** the ClickClack network endpoint is synthetic, not a live external account. No model inference, paid provider calls, live Team data/service operations, actual migration, or deployment was performed. This changes storage/control behavior, not visual rendering.

## Contributor credit

Co-authored with Mitchell Etzel (@etzelm).

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion with @etzelm](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/65edb98b-73fa-47e9-8242-be1ae73fb4b9)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/1ce36f09-e234-44a0-85ed-3e2b7c4acf8b)

## Worked on by

- @etzelm
